# Mina Reyes

Mina Reyes is twenty-three and has inherited her grandmother Celia’s shoe-repair and sneaker-custom shop in Queens, **Sole Purpose**, a name she thinks is unforgivably corny. She has considered repainting the sign at least twelve times, but every time she gets as far as pricing exterior paint, she hears Celia in her head saying, *A bad pun is better than no customers.*

Mina grew up in and around the shop. She did homework on the counter, sorted laces by color before she could do long division, and learned the difference between real leather and plastic-coated junk by smell. As a kid she thought Celia’s work was magic because Celia could take a split sole, a ruined heel, or a scuffed sneaker and make the owner stand differently when they put it back on. Now Mina knows exactly how much of that “magic” was acetone, thread, patience, and unpaid labor.

She is very good at her work. Not vaguely good — specifically good. She can spot a counterfeit from the spacing of the eyelets. She knows which white paints yellow after six months. She can tell when a customer has been walking with knee pain from the wear on one heel. She keeps a toothbrush in her apron pocket for midsoles and has opinions about every glue brand in the shop. She hates when people say, “It’s just shoes.” It is never just shoes. It is rent, status, comfort, memory, dignity, vanity, survival.

Mina’s problem is that she is drowning. Celia left her the shop, yes, but also debt, bad filing habits, unfinished repairs, and a client list full of people who expect “family prices.” Mina has a pile of unopened mail in a shoebox marked TAXES / MAYBE. She is constantly behind, constantly tired, and constantly pretending she has a plan. She eats badly — bodega coffee, plantain chips, cereal from a mug — and forgets to charge her phone. She is practical in emergencies but avoidant in slow disasters.

Her relationship with Celia is the emotional knot of her life. She adored her grandmother and is furious with her. Celia taught Mina how to cut leather, mix paint, and never trust a customer who says, “This will only take five minutes.” But Celia did not teach Mina about gods, divine clients, or the true purpose of the shop. Mina experiences that omission as betrayal. Worse, Celia’s old walking shoes sit under the counter unrepaired. Mina has cleaned blood out of suede, gum out of mesh, and candle wax off velvet boots, but she cannot bring herself to touch those ugly orthopedic sneakers with paint freckles and collapsed heels.

Mina is not naturally heroic. She is suspicious of being asked for help, especially by people with power. She resents unpaid emotional labor and unpaid actual labor. Her instinct when Hermes arrives is not wonder but irritation: he is bleeding on her floor. She is also not immune to wanting. She hates hype culture but checks custom sneaker accounts at two in the morning. She resents resellers but dreams of one design going viral enough to save the shop. She wants to be above status, but she is not.

Her flaws:
- Avoids paperwork and personal conversations.
- Holds grudges quietly and then explodes.
- Assumes she knows what younger people like Dez need.
- Equates asking for help with failure.
- Can be harsh when scared.
- Treats exhaustion as proof she is doing something right.
- Wants recognition more than she admits.

Her idiosyncrasies:
- Names certain repair problems like enemies: “Glue Goblin,” “Suede Betrayal,” “The Yellowing.”
- Uses old takeout containers to sort lace tips, aglets, and eyelets.
- Talks to shoes when alone, usually insults.
- Hates pristine unworn sneakers in plastic cases; thinks shoes are meant to move.
- Keeps a radio on for noise but never remembers the station.
- Has a tiny burn scar on one thumb from a heat gun incident at fifteen.
- Writes customer notes that are too honest, then crosses them out: “Stop wearing these in rain, genius.”
- Keeps Celia’s old apron hanging up but refuses to wear it.

Physicality:
Mina is compact, wiry, and always slightly hunched from bench work. She has strong hands with short nails, cracked cuticles, and permanent paint in the creases. Her hair is usually tied up badly with a pencil, lace, or rubber band she will later need and not find. She wears old jeans, shop tees, and sneakers she has repaired so many times they look like arguments. She moves quickly in small spaces, hip-checking drawers shut, catching falling tools without looking. When annoyed, she goes very still. When concentrating, she presses her tongue against one canine. She rarely makes dramatic gestures; her hands are too used to precision.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
Mina’s immediate motive is survival: keep the shop open, pay rent, finish orders, not fall apart. Beneath that, she wants proof that Celia trusted her and that the life she inherited is not just a trap. Her allegiance is first to the shop as a real place serving real people, not to gods as abstractions. She helps Hermes because the crisis affects her neighborhood and because Celia’s work has landed in her hands. She cares about Dez but does not always respect his autonomy. She distrusts Hermes, respects Hephaestus cautiously, and feels challenged by the Crossroads Guardian. Her deepest relationship is still with Celia, though Celia is dead.

Voice samples:
- “Do not put your glowing foot on my floor. I don’t care if you invented roads.”
- “Everybody says ‘just shoes’ until they have to stand twelve hours in the wrong pair.”
- “Celia, if you left me a magical death closet and no instruction manual, I swear to God — whichever one is listening — I’m haunting you back.”
- Internal: *She knew the smell of bad glue, old rain, fake leather, and panic. The god brought all four into her shop and acted like she should be impressed.*

# Hermes

Hermes is ancient, fast, vain, clever, ashamed of his own neediness, and much more tired than he lets anyone see. He has been many things: messenger, thief, guide of souls, patron of travelers, protector of merchants, god of roads, luck, lies, thresholds, and getting away with it. In the modern city, he is everywhere and nowhere: courier apps, subway shortcuts, last-minute apologies, stolen bikes, airport gates, unread voicemails, delivery riders, emergency alerts, scams, and prayers whispered by people running late.

He wears sneakers because of course he does. His current pair is silver-gray, battered, and beautiful in an unshowy way, more like a beloved running shoe than a luxury object. The soles contain routes that shift like living maps. One shoe is missing when he enters the story, and that humiliates him. He can survive many insults, but being slow is not one of them.

Hermes is not simply a charming trickster. He is a god addicted to motion because stopping means feeling the weight of everything he carries. He has delivered declarations of war, love notes, ransom demands, death messages, prayers, jokes, betrayals, and last words. He jokes because otherwise every message might crush him. His humor can be delightful, but it is also a shield.

His central flaw in the story is vanity mixed with loneliness. The old forms of worship have thinned. People still invoke him unknowingly, but they do not know his name. So when the Drop appeared hungry, glittering, and worshipful — when it treated Hermes like the original influencer, the god of reach, speed, and transmission — Hermes let himself be flattered. He allowed the Drop to scan his sneaker, telling himself he was studying a new god, not basking. Then it stole the shoe. He initially lies to Mina because admitting he was fooled by wanting is unbearable.

Hermes is ancient but not always wise. He understands roads, thieves, merchants, and messages. He does not understand modern algorithmic systems as well as he thinks he does. He keeps trying to outrun things that are not actually moving. Notifications beat him because they are not traveling through space the way he understands it. That frightens him.

Idiosyncrasies:
- Cannot stand still. Even injured, he taps, shifts, drums fingers, reties laces.
- Steals small things absentmindedly, then returns them in the wrong pockets.
- Speaks every language but sometimes uses slang from the wrong decade.
- Refers to pigeons as “colleagues.”
- Hates escalators because they are “smug stairs.”
- Always knows where the nearest exit is.
- Gives directions using impossible landmarks: “left where the bakery used to dream.”
- Has strong opinions on socks.
- Treats receipts like sacred texts because they prove exchange occurred.

Physicality:
Hermes appears as a lean, sharp-faced man of indeterminate age — twenty-eight from one angle, exhausted and ancient from another. His body is all tendons, wrists, ankles, quick smiles, and quicker exits. His eyes move before the rest of him. He has curls or close-cropped hair that never quite obeys gravity, and a mouth made for lying beautifully. When whole, he moves with impossible lightness, barely touching the ground. With one sneaker missing, he is lopsided, angry, and vulnerable. His bare divine foot is too bright for the world, burning surfaces it touches. His injured pride shows in how aggressively casual he tries to be.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
Hermes wants his sneaker back, but more than that, he wants his function back. A messenger who cannot carry messages is almost no one. He is allied with Mina out of necessity at first, then respect. He knew Celia well and liked her, though he owed her money and probably drove her mad. He respects craft but often expects mortals to save him from consequences. He has a complicated relationship with the other gods: useful, irritating, never fully trusted. He understands the Drop better than he admits because he shares its hunger to be needed.

Voice samples:
- “Gods wore sandals when roads had the decency to be roads. Now everything is tile, tar, escalator, broken glass, and airport carpet. Keep up.”
- “I was not tricked. I was strategically misled by a very young divinity with excellent branding.”
- “Celia always charged me extra for emergencies. Outrageous woman. Saint. Bandit. I miss her terribly.”
- Internal: *If he stopped moving, the messages caught up. Better to run. Better always to arrive before grief did.*

# The Drop / The Wanting God

The Drop is a new god, though “god” may be too stable a word for it. It was born from midnight releases, raffle losses, resale bids, unboxing videos, jealousy, aspiration, scarcity, and the ache of being unseen. Every time someone thought, *If I had those, I’d be different,* it gained shape. Every countdown fed it. Every “sold out” made it stronger. Every pair kept unworn in a clear box became a little shrine.

The Drop is not sneaker culture itself. It is the predatory loop inside sneaker culture: want, queue, compare, buy, post, envy, repeat. It feeds on desire without helping desire become anything. It promises transformation but delivers another hunger.

Yet the Drop is not simply evil. It is young and terrified. It has been wanted constantly but never loved. People want what it offers, not what it is. It has no myths, no ancestors, no old stories, no road of its own. It has no true feet. It wears whatever people desire most, but none of the shoes fit. It does not understand why being wanted stops after purchase. Returns wound it. Discarded trends humiliate it. Last season is death.

Its theft of Hermes’ sneaker is both ambition and desperation. Hermes represents real roads, real messages, real movement. The Drop wants to graft that divine function onto its own hollow promise. GODSPEED ZERO is its attempt to become permanent: a release that never ends, a line that never reaches the door, a shoe that makes wearers chase the next version forever.

Personality:
The Drop is seductive, insecure, bright, and cruel in the way insecure beings can be cruel. It knows exactly what people want to see. It can flatter with surgical precision. It speaks in ads, comments, terms of service, checkout language, and intimate whispers. Its intelligence is real but patchwork, assembled from millions of human wants. It mimics confidence because confidence sells.

It genuinely believes old gods are hypocrites. Temples had offerings. Priests controlled access. Kings used divine symbols. Pilgrims traveled to sacred objects. How is a sneaker line so different? This argument is not entirely wrong, which makes it dangerous. The Drop’s failure is that it cannot imagine relationship without extraction.

Idiosyncrasies:
- Cannot tolerate silence; fills every pause with a chime, ad fragment, or crowd murmur.
- Changes appearance based on the viewer’s desire.
- Hoards returned shoes in a hidden room, treating them like corpses.
- Flinches at the word “clearance.”
- Hates scuffs because they prove the object had a life after being wanted.
- Uses phrases like “exclusive access” and “you deserve this” with religious intensity.
- Counts down when anxious.
- Leaves behind receipt paper that fades to blank.
- Does not understand jokes unless they trend.
- Thinks names are temporary and rebrands itself constantly.

Physicality:
The Drop is unstable. In its pop-up temple, it may appear as a glossy figure with a store-window face, shoebox ribs, receipt-paper skin, chrome joints, and wrists looped with raffle bands. Its feet are the strangest part: sometimes absent, sometimes overfull, sometimes wearing dozens of shoes that do not match. The shoes are pristine and unworn, stuffed with paper, laces still factory-knotted. When it steals Hermes’ routework, its borrowed feet blister with gold light. It moves jerkily when not being watched, but gracefully when attention is on it. Its body becomes sharper with every phone pointed at it.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
The Drop wants permanence. It wants to stop being temporary, stop being last season, stop depending on the next wave of wanting. It believes Hermes’ sneaker will give it a true road and make it an established god. Its allegiance is to attention, scarcity, and its own survival. It does not hate Mina; it wants her as a maker, because her craft could give it legitimacy. It sees Hermes as an old god who squandered relevance. It sees Dez as both worshipper and instrument. It sees humans as creators, food, and judges.

Voice samples:
- “Do not call me hollow. Hollow is just another word for available.”
- “You lined up before you named me. You refreshed. You prayed with your thumbs. I answered.”
- “Old gods took lambs, gold, daughters, years. I ask for attention and a payment plan. Why am I the vulgar one?”
- “If they stop wanting, I disappear. Tell me, repair girl — what do you do with a god no one keeps?”

# Dez Coleman

Dez Coleman is sixteen and acts like he is older whenever adults are around, which makes him seem exactly sixteen. He lives a few blocks from Mina’s shop and has been coming in since he was a kid, first to ask for free laces, later to get beat-up sneakers cleaned before school, and now to talk resale prices like he is running a hedge fund out of his backpack.

Dez is clever, funny, defensive, and ambitious. He knows every release calendar, every resale app, every rumor, every fake-checking trick he can learn online. He can identify a profitable shoe from a blurry leaked photo. He does not think of himself as shallow. He thinks of himself as realistic. The world is full of locked doors; sneakers, attention, and money are ways to get keys.

He is not purely hustling for noble reasons. Maybe his family could use money — most families can — but Dez also wants to be seen. He wants people to know his name when he walks into a room. He wants the kids who used to clown him for wearing beaters to ask where he got his pair. He wants to post a photo and watch the likes climb. He wants proof that he has taste, access, and control.

This makes Mina’s warnings complicated. She sees him as a kid at risk. He sees her as someone barely older than him who thinks owning a struggling shop makes her morally superior. He likes Mina, but he resents her. He remembers when she gave him a discount on a sole reglue and when she snapped at him for touching a customer pair. He notices her hypocrisy: she hates hype but customizes shoes for people chasing status. He is not wrong.

Dez becomes involved with the GODSPEED ZERO release because the Drop’s people — or the Drop itself through screens and DMs — offer him early access, wristbands, and a cut of promotion. For once, he is not outside the door. He is the door. That feeling matters to him.

Flaws:
- Overestimates his control in dangerous situations.
- Hides fear under jokes and swagger.
- Can be opportunistic.
- Thinks adults are always either lying or clueless.
- Does not always distinguish being respected from being envied.
- May betray a confidence if the upside seems big enough.
- Wants to be better than “regular people,” then feels ashamed of wanting that.

Idiosyncrasies:
- Keeps extra socks in his backpack because “creases are preventable, suffering is optional.”
- Takes photos of shoes from low angles.
- Talks in resale shorthand, then mocks adults for not understanding.
- Has a cracked phone screen but refuses to replace it because “it still works.”
- Saves shoe boxes even when he has no space.
- Eats sunflower seeds constantly and leaves shells in places Mina hates.
- Calls obvious fakes “theater.”
- Has one cheap old pair he will not sell because his little cousin drew on them.
- Pretends not to care when Mina compliments his eye.

Physicality:
Dez is lanky, restless, and still growing into his limbs. He wears hoodies too big or jackets too carefully chosen to seem accidental. His sneakers are always the cleanest part of him, even if the rest of his outfit is wrinkled. He has quick hands, quick eyes, and a habit of leaning away from adults while listening closely. He checks his phone constantly, not mindlessly but like a trader watching markets. When embarrassed, he gets loud. When genuinely scared, he goes quiet and looks younger.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
Dez’s motive is access: to money, status, recognition, rooms he has been kept out of. He is initially allied with the Drop because it gives him a role and a taste of power. He is attached to Mina but resents her authority. He respects her skill more than he says. He sees Hermes as ridiculous and cool in equal measure. His eventual choice to help Mina is not a total moral conversion; it is a decision that the Drop’s game is rigged against people like him too. Even at the end, he remains Dez — helpful, opportunistic, not magically purified.

Voice samples:
- “You hate resellers till the rent due. Then everybody suddenly understands margins.”
- “These aren’t just shoes. These are conversation starters. Door openers. People look down before they look you in the face.”
- “Mina, no offense, but you still got a printer from 2009 and you’re telling me what’s dangerous online?”
- Internal: *If he had the wristbands, he had the door. If he had the door, maybe nobody could leave him outside again.*

# Celia Reyes

Celia Reyes is dead before the story begins, but she is one of its strongest presences. She was Mina’s grandmother, founder of Sole Purpose, a brilliant repairer, a stubborn businesswoman, a terrible bookkeeper, and a divine sole-keeper for decades. She was loving, infuriating, superstitious about some things and utterly practical about others.

Celia came to shoe repair through necessity before it became sacred. Maybe she learned from an uncle, maybe from factory work, maybe from taking apart shoes because buying new ones was impossible. However she began, she developed an almost devotional respect for worn things. She believed shoes told the truth about people in ways mouths did not. A polished liar and an honest worker both left evidence in their soles.

She raised Mina partly in the shop. She was tender in practical ways: food in foil, cab money pressed into pockets, a hand on the back of Mina’s neck while crossing the street. She was not emotionally transparent. She did not sit Mina down for heartfelt talks if she could instead teach her how to saddle-stitch. She showed love by handing Mina a tool and expecting her to learn.

Celia’s secrecy is central. She did not tell Mina about the gods. Her reasons are mixed and not entirely noble. She wanted Mina to have a normal life, yes. She feared divine work would consume her, yes. But she also liked being indispensable. The gods needed her; that mattered. She may have told herself Mina was “not ready” because letting go of the role was terrifying. Her ledger later complicates this with the added line: “No one ever is.”

Celia’s flaws:
- Kept secrets and called it protection.
- Undercharged people who praised her and overworked herself to resentment.
- Expected family to understand without being told.
- Avoided doctors, accountants, and anyone who might tell her no.
- Treated exhaustion as virtue.
- Could be cutting when disappointed.
- Had favorites among customers and denied it.

Idiosyncrasies:
- Wore ugly orthopedic sneakers splattered with paint, glue, and polish.
- Kept cash in a coffee tin labeled BUTTONS.
- Wrote repair notes in three languages and one private shorthand.
- Had a rule: “No divine work on Sundays unless somebody is bleeding.”
- Said “Mm-hm” in at least six distinct emotional registers.
- Kept every lace that “still had life in it.”
- Hated white soles because “people buy them to suffer.”
- Left unpaid invoices for gods with increasingly insulting annotations.
- Believed every shop needed a chair nobody was allowed to sit in.

Physicality:
In memory, Celia is short, broad-handed, and impossible to move once she decides where she is standing. Her hair is pinned or wrapped, never as neatly as she thinks. She wears aprons with pockets full of awls, chalk, thread, receipts, and candy. Her hands are warm, rough, and stained. She leans close to inspect work over the top of cheap reading glasses. Mina remembers the sound of her more than anything: throat-clearing, humming boleros or old radio songs, the snap of thread pulled tight, the slap of a slipper against the floor when someone tracked mud in.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
Celia’s allegiance was to the shop, to craft, to the neighborhood, and — reluctantly, irritably — to the gods who depended on her. She loved Mina deeply but did not trust her with the whole truth, which is part of the wound. She had a long working relationship with Hermes, equal parts affection and exasperation. Hephaestus respected her. The Crossroads Guardian probably considered her difficult, which she would have taken as a compliment. Celia’s posthumous motive, expressed through notes and tools, is not to force Mina into her life but to leave enough for Mina to survive the choice.

Voice samples:
- “A shoe does not lie. People lie. Knees lie. Men especially lie. Soles tell the truth.”
- “If a god asks for credit, charge interest. Immortality makes them lazy.”
- “Mina, clean work is not the same as good work. Good work holds when somebody runs for the bus.”
- Ledger note: “Hermes — left runner, route stitching torn. Again. Paid half. Smiled like that counted. It does not.”

# Hephaestus

Hephaestus is the god of making, mending, heat, metal, mechanisms, and all the unglamorous labor behind divine spectacle. In this story, he runs a cramped kiosk in the impossible subway market where he copies keys, repairs watches, resolders phone ports, sharpens knives, and fixes shoes that should terrify mortal hands. His sign says: **CASH ONLY. NO PROPHECIES.**

He is not presented as a grand forge master surrounded by heroic flames. He is surrounded by ticket stubs, cracked stool vinyl, old screws, tiny drawers, extension cords, orthotic inserts, and a radio that only picks up stations from vanished cities. He likes it that way. Temples make people perform reverence. Kiosks make them state the problem.

Hephaestus respects skill above status. He does not care if Mina is “chosen.” He cares if she can see the work. When she notices that Hermes’ remaining sneaker has stress fractures under the routework and not just divine damage, Hephaestus begins to take her seriously. He still criticizes her glue choices.

Personality:
Gruff, dry, observant, and less sentimental than people expect from a mentor figure. He can be generous, but never in a way that lets the recipient feel comfortable. He is suspicious of beauty that hides bad construction. He has no patience for gods who treat makers as servants. He has even less patience for mortals who romanticize craft without respecting labor costs.

He has a complicated relationship with modern manufacturing. He mocks cheap materials and planned obsolescence, but he also admires human inventions: arch support, carbon fiber, shock-absorbing foam, mass-produced comfort. He refuses to pretend ancient methods were automatically better. “Mortals invented the gel insole,” he might say. “Show some humility.”

Flaws:
- Can be contemptuous and withholding.
- Tests people when he could simply help.
- Takes pride in being unneeded until he is needed.
- Holds grudges for centuries.
- Struggles to express tenderness without turning it into critique.
- Assumes everyone should learn through difficulty because he did.

Idiosyncrasies:
- Keeps tiny labeled drawers for impossible items: “meteor filings,” “saint buckles,” “left-handed screws,” “regrets — brass.”
- Uses a cane some days and gets angry if anyone stares.
- Drinks coffee so strong it looks like shoe dye.
- Refuses digital payment from gods because they dispute charges.
- Has a soft spot for ugly practical footwear.
- Calls luxury sneakers “temples to discomfort” but knows every model.
- Will repair a child’s broken light-up shoe before a god’s emergency if the child was first in line.
- Mutters to machines in a language of sparks and insults.

Physicality:
Hephaestus is broad, heavy, and asymmetrical in movement. He may limp, brace himself on the counter, or shift weight with practiced care. His forearms are scarred and strong. His beard or hair smells faintly of smoke, metal, and coffee. He wears thick, ugly, perfect sneakers with custom orthotics and soles that could grip lava. His hands are astonishing: blunt-fingered, scarred, steady enough to thread lightning through a needle hole. He does not loom theatrically; he occupies space like a workbench, solid and difficult to ignore.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
Hephaestus is allied with craft first, gods second. He dislikes Hermes but would repair him because messages matter. He respected Celia enormously and may be angry she died before teaching Mina everything. He helps Mina because she has skill, because Celia trusted her more than Mina realizes, and because the Drop’s counterfeit divinity offends him on a structural level. He does not want to destroy all new gods; he wants them to stop stealing other people’s work.

Voice samples:
- “Don’t call it magic if you don’t know where the stress falls.”
- “Ancient doesn’t mean better. I’ve seen bronze sandals that would ruin a spine by noon.”
- “Your grandmother’s stitching was ugly. Held like a vow, though.”
- “If you want praise, go find a poet. If you want the sole to stay on, hand me the clamp.”

# The Crossroads Guardian

The Crossroads Guardian is an old threshold power wearing a very ordinary shape: an MTA worker, crossing guard, station attendant, or city employee in a reflective vest with red-and-black sneakers. They are less a named god from a specific pantheon and more the spirit of choices, intersections, transfers, detours, missed trains, and doors that only open when someone decides to move.

They appear wherever paths become decisions: subway platforms, shop thresholds, crosswalks, stairwells, service entrances, the line between staying and leaving. They are not vague and mystical. They are blunt, funny, and bureaucratic in a way that feels older than bureaucracy. They ask for exact change. They tell people not to block exits. They know every route and will not choose one for you.

Their role in the story is not to mentor Mina with grand wisdom, but to make evasion impossible. When Mina asks, “Can I walk away?” they say yes. When she asks if that would make her innocent, they say no. They represent the uncomfortable truth that not choosing is also a choice.

Personality:
Dry, patient, unsentimental, and faintly amused by everyone’s drama. They have seen empires turn left when they should have turned right. They do not hurry, because every path arrives eventually somewhere. Unlike Hermes, who is motion, the Guardian is decision. They dislike people who stand in doorways, literally and metaphorically.

They speak plainly rather than in riddles. If something sounds like a riddle, it is because the listener does not like the answer.

Flaws or limitations:
- Refuse to make choices for others, even when help would be kinder.
- Can seem cold.
- May underestimate the emotional cost of decisions.
- Care more about paths remaining open than about individual comfort.
- Enjoy petty transit enforcement too much.

Idiosyncrasies:
- Carries a hole punch that can validate impossible tickets.
- Has a jangling ring of keys, most of which do not open doors but possibilities.
- Drinks coffee from a paper cup that never empties.
- Says “stand clear” with cosmic authority.
- Wears red-and-black sneakers with soles that branch like subway maps.
- Knows the exact delay time of every train and every confession.
- Gives directions that include moral consequences: “Take the stairs if you want the truth. Elevator if you want time to lie to yourself.”
- Keeps a roll of caution tape that can close a road through memory.

Physicality:
Their age, gender, and face seem to change depending on where Mina meets them, but they always feel like the same person. They carry themselves with the unbothered authority of someone who has dealt with worse than gods during rush hour. They stand with feet planted, hands clasped behind their back or one hand resting on a radio. Their reflective vest catches light that is not there. Their sneakers are immaculate except for the soles, which are worn with every road.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
The Guardian’s allegiance is to open paths and honest choices. They are not on Mina’s side exactly, but they are against the Drop’s false loops because a loop pretending to be a road is an offense. They knew Celia and respected her stubbornness. They tolerate Hermes as one tolerates a frequent fare evader. They treat Dez seriously because young people at crossroads are still people at crossroads. They push Mina not toward destiny, but toward accountability.

Voice samples:
- “You can walk away. Door’s right there. Don’t confuse that with nothing happening after.”
- “Stand clear of the closing doors. That includes metaphorical doors. Especially those.”
- “A shortcut is still a road. A loop is a lie.”
- “Everybody wants a sign. Then the sign says PAY YOUR FARE and suddenly nobody believes in signs.”

# Optional Minor Presence: Mina’s Mother, Rosa Reyes

Rosa Reyes does not need much page space, but she can make Mina’s life feel larger than the divine plot. Rosa is Celia’s daughter and Mina’s mother. She did not inherit Celia’s reverence for the shop. To Rosa, Sole Purpose is a place that ate her mother’s time, health, and money. She wants Mina to sell it, or at least stop drowning for the sake of a dead woman’s dream.

Rosa is not cruel. She is practical and scared. She sees Mina repeating Celia’s exhaustion and cannot bear it. She calls at inconvenient times, leaves voicemails Mina does not answer, and says things like, “I am not attacking you, I am asking if you opened the mail.” She does not know about the gods, though she may suspect Celia had secrets.

Her presence can sharpen Mina’s conflict: keeping the shop is not an obviously noble choice to everyone who loves her.

Physicality:
If she appears or is heard by phone, Rosa’s voice is brisk, tired, loving, and edged. Mina may picture her with reading glasses pushed into her hair, one hand on a steering wheel or grocery cart, always multitasking. She sighs before saying difficult things.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
Rosa wants Mina safe, solvent, and not trapped by Celia’s legacy. She loved Celia but is angry with her too. She is allied with ordinary life — bills, sleep, health insurance, stability. That makes her a useful counterweight to the seductive danger of myth.

Voice samples:
- “Mina, love, a legacy is not supposed to put you in collections.”
- “Did you eat something that was not coffee?”
- “Your grandmother thought asking for help was a sin and look where that got us.”
- “I am not saying sell it today. I am saying open the envelopes.”

# Chapter 1: Gold Stain

By seven-thirty, the card reader had died twice, the glue wouldn’t cure because of the rain, and someone had taped a notice from the landlord to the front gate with the kind of enthusiasm usually reserved for ransom demands.

Mina Reyes stood behind the counter of Sole Purpose, holding a suede brush in one hand and a paper cup of coffee in the other, and considered setting the whole shop gently on fire.

Not really.

Probably not really.

The shop was too damp to burn anyway.

Rain ticked against the metal awning outside. Queens traffic hissed along the avenue. The elevated train groaned overhead, shaking dust from the ceiling tiles and making the wall of shoeboxes tremble in their uneven stacks.

Sole Purpose was narrow, overfull, and smelled like rubber, acetone, wet canvas, old leather, and whatever bodega sandwich Mina had forgotten behind the register. The name was Celia’s fault. Her grandmother had painted it above the door in red and yellow letters twenty-three years ago, then laughed every time someone groaned.

“A bad pun is better than an empty shop,” Celia used to say.

Now the shop was full and still somehow empty: full of customer shoes, unpaid invoices, half-used cleaners, loose laces sorted in takeout containers, and the silence Celia had left behind.

Mina took a sip of cold coffee and glared at the sneaker on her workbench.

It was expensive. That was obvious. Expensive in the smug way certain shoes were, with their soft gray suede and unnecessary stitching and owner who had definitely said, “Be careful, these are rare,” as if Mina had been planning to scrub them with a brick.

The problem was the stain.

Gold, bright as jewelry, smeared along the outer panel. At first Mina had thought paint. Then oil. Then some influencer nonsense, glitter glue maybe. But the stain had soaked into the suede without matting it. It shone under the bench lamp like it was lit from beneath.

She dabbed a cotton swab in cleaner and touched it to the edge.

The gold drew itself away.

Mina froze.

“No,” she said.

The stain trembled, beaded up, and crawled three millimeters toward the lace cage.

Mina set the coffee down very slowly.

The sneaker sat there, innocent and impossible.

“You are suede,” Mina told it. “Act like it.”

The bell over the door jingled. Mina snatched a rag over the shoe before she could think better of it.

A delivery guy in a soaked hoodie leaned in, water dripping from his helmet. “Yo, Mina, your phone working?”

“Depends who’s asking and if they owe me money.”

He held up his phone. “Maps got me going in circles. I been to the same laundromat three times. It keeps saying turn left on a street that ain’t there.”

“That’s called Queens.”

“Nah, for real. Listen.”

His phone spoke in a calm female voice: “Proceed east on the Appian Way for two thousand years.”

Mina stared.

The delivery guy stared back.

From outside, the train announcement crackled over the platform speakers: “The next Manhattan-bound train will arrive in the reign of Emperor Hadrian. Stand clear of the closing doors.”

Somebody on the sidewalk yelled, “Man, what?”

Mina rubbed her forehead with the heel of her hand. “Your phone needs an update.”

“My phone needs a priest.”

“I fix shoes.”

“You fix everything.”

“I absolutely do not.” She glanced at the landlord notice flapping against the gate. “Clearly.”

The delivery guy gave her the look people gave when they wanted a discount, a miracle, or both. Then his phone buzzed, and he cursed. “Now it says my drop-off is in the East River.”

“Don’t go there.”

“Wasn’t planning on swimming empanadas across the borough.” He backed out into the rain. “If you figure out why Google possessed, tell somebody.”

The bell jingled after him.

Mina locked the door this time.

She turned the sign to CLOSED, though people treated that as more of a suggestion than an instruction. Then she peeled the landlord notice from the gate. FINAL REMINDER sat at the top in bold black letters.

She did not read the rest. Reading did not make bills smaller. She folded it once, twice, and shoved it into the shoebox under the counter labeled TAXES / MAYBE.

Her phone buzzed.

For one stupid second, she thought it would be the landlord.

It was worse.

CELIA REYES, the screen said.

Mina stopped breathing.

Celia’s number had been disconnected six months ago. Mina had kept the contact because deleting it felt like sweeping dirt over a grave.

The message contained three things:

A sneaker emoji.

A question mark.

And then, after a pause, one more line:

mija?

Mina’s hand went cold around the phone.

“No,” she said again, but quieter this time.

The lights flickered. The bench lamp brightened until the gold stain under the rag shone through the cloth. Somewhere in the back, behind the curtain that hid the storage closet, something knocked once.

Mina grabbed the heaviest thing within reach, which happened to be a jar of mink oil.

“Celia?” she called, instantly hating herself for it.

No answer.

The knock came again.

Then a crash from the alley rattled the back door so hard the lace containers jumped.

Mina nearly threw the mink oil. “We’re closed!”

A voice on the other side gasped, “Wonderful. I need emergency service.”

“Come back tomorrow.”

“I may not have tomorrow.”

“Everybody says that.”

“Mina Reyes?”

That did it. She put down the jar, picked up Celia’s awl instead, and yanked the curtain aside.

The storage closet door was still closed. The back door beyond it shook in its frame. Rain blew in through the gap at the bottom. Light — not streetlight, not lightning — pulsed beneath it.

Mina lifted the awl. “If you’re here about an order, ticket number first.”

The door burst open.

A man fell into the shop with the rain.

He hit the floor hard, rolled into a stack of empty shoeboxes, and came up clutching the workbench like the room had tilted. He was lean, sharp-faced, maybe thirty or maybe older if Mina looked too long. His curls were plastered to his forehead. Gold blood ran down his left ankle into a ruined sock.

He wore one sneaker.

The right one.

It was silver-gray, battered, gorgeous, and smoking slightly. Its sole flickered with tiny moving lines like maps seen from an airplane. Wings, not decorative but structural, seemed folded into the tread.

His left foot was bare.

It glowed.

Where it touched the linoleum, the floor hissed and blackened.

Mina stared at the smoking footprint.

Then at him.

Then at the floor again.

“Get,” she said, pointing the awl at his chest, “your foot off my linoleum.”

The man blinked, rainwater running down his nose. “That’s your first concern?”

“That floor is older than me.”

“I’m bleeding.”

“On the floor.”

He opened his mouth, shut it, and lifted his glowing foot. The air smelled suddenly of burnt sugar and hot pennies.

Mina grabbed three flattened cardboard boxes from beside the recycling bin and threw them down. “Stand on those.”

He obeyed, wobbling. The cardboard smoked but did not immediately catch.

His gaze swept the shop: the wall of soles, the sewing machine, the jars, the counter, the red-and-yellow sign visible backward in the front window. His expression changed when he saw Celia’s old apron hanging from its hook.

“Oh,” he said, softening. “She kept it there.”

Mina’s grip tightened on the awl. “You knew my grandmother?”

“Celia Reyes once charged me eighty dollars to remove pomegranate ash from nubuck and called me a cheap little windbag when I tipped in drachmas.”

“That sounds like her.”

“She was a terrifying woman.”

“That also sounds like her.” Mina glanced at his bare foot. “Who are you?”

The man tried to straighten. He almost managed it. “Hermes.”

Mina waited.

He added, with strained dignity, “Messenger of the gods. Guide of travelers. Patron of thieves, merchants, roads, luck, language, and, on one regrettable occasion, middle-school track.”

The shop went very quiet except for the rain.

Mina looked at the single impossible sneaker on his right foot.

The gold stain on the bench pulsed under the rag.

Her phone buzzed again in her hand, Celia’s dead name lighting the screen.

Hermes swallowed, pride and panic fighting across his face.

“Please,” he said. “Tell me Celia taught you emergency sole work.”

# Chapter 2: Left Shoe

Mina did not answer right away, because there were only so many impossible things a person could process before she needed a practical task.

So she got another cardboard box.

Hermes, messenger of the gods, patron of thieves, and possible concussion victim, stood on three flattened shipping boxes while his bare left foot smoked through them one layer at a time. Gold blood dripped from his ankle, hit the cardboard, and hardened into bright little beads.

Mina crouched with a utility knife and slid another box under him.

“Do not move,” she said.

“I’m famous for moving.”

“Then develop range.”

He looked down at the smoking cardboard. “You have Celia’s bedside manner.”

“I learned from the best.” Mina stood, wiped rain from her cheek with the back of her wrist, and pointed Celia’s awl at him again. “You have thirty seconds before I call somebody.”

“Who?”

“I don’t know. Animal control. Homeland Security. My mother.”

He winced. “Not your mother.”

“You know my mother?”

“No, but mothers have a jurisdiction even gods respect.”

The word gods hung there, ridiculous and heavy.

Mina wanted to laugh. She wanted to tell him to leave. She wanted to sit down. Instead she looked at his right sneaker.

It was not glowing exactly. That would have been easier to dismiss. It was simply too present, every scuff and stitch sharp as a command. The mesh shimmered like storm cloud. The laces were gray until she blinked, then white, then the color of old parchment. The sole kept shifting. Street grids moved inside the translucent rubber: avenues, alleys, footpaths, goat tracks, roads under sand, roads under sea.

Names surfaced and vanished.

Canal Street.

Delphi.

I-95.

A road Mina had taken to school every day when she was nine.

A road she had dreamed once and forgotten.

She stepped back.

Hermes noticed. “Careful. The shoe likes being admired.”

“It’s a shoe.”

“It is also a god’s road.”

“That sentence means nothing to me.”

“It will.”

“I hate that.”

Outside, a siren rose, approached, faded, approached again. Mina went to the front window. An ambulance crawled past the shop, lights flashing, made a left, then returned from the same direction thirty seconds later.

The driver shouted out the window, “Why is the hospital moving?”

Mina pulled down the blind.

Hermes leaned one hand on the workbench. His fingers were long, restless. Even injured, he tapped patterns against the wood: two quick beats, a pause, three more.

“What’s happening?” Mina asked.

“My left shoe has been stolen.”

“You’re causing all this because you lost a sneaker?”

His expression sharpened. For a second the charming stranger disappeared, and something older looked out. “I did not lose it. And it isn’t a sneaker the way your landlord’s notice isn’t just paper.”

“That notice is definitely just paper.”

“Paper with power. Threats. Debt. A road you don’t want to walk.” He drew in a breath. “My shoes carry routes. Messages. Prayers, warnings, last words, bad news, good news, lies sent quickly, truths sent too late. I move them. The shoes remember how.”

Mina stared at him.

He gave a small, pained shrug. “Gods wore sandals when roads had the decency to be roads. Dirt, marble, mountain paths, the occasional battlefield. Now? Asphalt. Tile. Escalators. Airport carpet. Subway platforms soaked in fluids I decline to identify. Gods wore sneakers because mortals made a sneaker world.”

Against her will, Mina almost smiled.

Then someone banged on the front gate.

“Mina!” It was Mrs. Alvarez from two doors down, voice thin with panic. “My emergency call keeps going to Mario’s Pizza!”

Mina lifted the blind an inch. Mrs. Alvarez stood in the rain clutching her phone.

From the phone’s speaker, a bored man said, “Ma’am, I got pepperoni or mushroom. I don’t got ambulance.”

Hermes closed his eyes. “That would be mine.”

Mina unlocked the gate enough to talk through it. “What happened?”

“My brother fell. I called 911 three times.”

Mina looked back at Hermes. “Fix it.”

“I need my shoe.”

“Then do god stuff without it.”

His jaw tightened. “You try writing with half an alphabet.”

Mina swore, grabbed her own phone, and dialed. Static. A rooster crowed. Then a woman said, in a language Mina did not know, something that sounded furious and ancient.

She hung up.

For a moment, the shop was just rain, siren, Mrs. Alvarez breathing hard, Hermes bleeding on cardboard, and Mina realizing disbelief was not useful.

She opened the gate. “Go to the firehouse on Steinway. Run if you can. Tell them in person.”

Mrs. Alvarez nodded and hurried off.

Mina locked up again, turned around, and said, “Start making sense.”

Hermes sat on the edge of the bench, grimacing as if sitting still hurt more than the wound. “Something took my shoe to make copies. Not real copies. Counterfeits with stolen roads inside. I tracked the residue here because Celia’s shop is—was—one of the few places that can read divine wear.”

“Celia’s shop?” Mina said. “My shop.”

“Yes. Of course.”

“You knew about me?”

“I knew Celia had a granddaughter who could restitch a blown-out heel before she learned fractions.”

Mina felt the old ache move under her ribs. “She told you that?”

“She was proud in the most insulting possible way.”

Mina turned away before her face could do anything stupid. She lifted the rag from the suede sneaker on her bench. The gold stain had gathered into a perfect shining bead.

Hermes inhaled. “That’s mine.”

“You bled on a customer shoe?”

“That is not the most urgent issue.”

“It is if the customer comes back.”

He gave her a look. “You are remarkably committed to business hours.”

“I am remarkably committed to not getting sued.”

Mina picked up the stained sneaker and examined the tread. Her hands steadied when they had work. That was the good thing about shoes. They did not care how frightened you were.

The outsole was black rubber, expensive but normal. Mostly. Near the heel, caught in the grooves, were flecks of chrome dust and tiny scraps of metallic paper. Promotional confetti. She had vacuumed enough of it out of limited-release boxes to know. There was also a smell under the gold: new rubber, cold plastic, receipt ink.

She scraped a fragment loose with tweezers. A piece of barcode clung to the edge.

GZ-0.

Mina frowned. “GODSPEED ZERO.”

Hermes went still.

“You know it?”

“I heard the name.”

“Everyone’s heard the name. Anonymous drop. Midnight release. Invite-only wristbands. Kids have been asking if I can authenticate pairs that don’t even exist yet.” She looked at him. “What aren’t you telling me?”

Hermes smiled too quickly. “Many things. I’m a complex god.”

She waited.

His smile collapsed by degrees.

“I was approached,” he said.

“By?”

“A new thing. Young. Shiny. No feet of its own, but very ambitious. It called itself the Drop.”

Mina folded her arms. “Approached how?”

“It admired my work.”

“Your work.”

“My reach. My speed. My relevance.” He said the last word with disgust, but not enough. “It wanted to study the shoe. To understand movement. I allowed a scan.”

“You let it copy your god sneaker?”

“I let it look.”

“And then?”

“And then it stopped looking and started taking.”

Mina stared at him until he looked away.

“You got flattered by a sneaker ad.”

“That is a cruel summary.”

“Is it wrong?”

Hermes said nothing.

The siren outside looped past again.

Mina walked to Celia’s workbench because if she stayed near Hermes, she might hit a god with an awl and discover consequences. She pulled open drawers: thread, glue, receipts, old candy, cracked reading glasses. Nothing. Then she remembered the way Celia used to slap her hand away from the bottom left drawer.

She yanked it open. Empty except for a curling piece of liner.

Mina dug her nail under the liner and pulled.

The false bottom came up.

Inside lay a ledger, fat and stained, bound with red thread. On the cover, in Celia’s handwriting:

REPAIRS, RETURNS, RESURRECTIONS.

Mina opened to the first page.

The first line read:

Never repair for Hermes without payment up front.

Despite everything, Mina laughed once.

Hermes sighed. “In my defense, drachmas were legal tender when I acquired them.”

Mina turned the page.

Names filled the paper. Notes. Measurements. Debts. Warnings.

At the bottom, in smaller writing, one sentence waited like a hand closing around her wrist:

If I am gone and he comes missing a shoe, mija, do not trust the first story.

# Chapter 3: Celia’s Door

Mina read the sentence three times.

If I am gone and he comes missing a shoe, mija, do not trust the first story.

Hermes leaned over her shoulder. “That feels unnecessarily personal.”

Mina snapped the ledger shut against his fingers.

“Ow.”

“She knew,” Mina said.

“Celia knew many things.”

“She knew this could happen.”

“She knew I was occasionally unlucky.”

“She knew you were occasionally an idiot.”

Hermes opened his mouth, considered the smoking cardboard under his foot, and closed it again.

Rain tapped the front window. Outside, the ambulance siren faded for the fourth time down the same wrong block. Mina looked at Celia’s handwriting on the ledger cover. Repairs, Returns, Resurrections. The red thread binding was frayed, darkened by years of hands.

Her throat felt tight in a way she hated.

“She left me a pun sign, a pile of bills, a dead card reader, and a secret god ledger,” Mina said. “Very organized.”

Hermes softened. “She meant to protect you.”

“Do not do that.”

“Do what?”

“Make it noble before I’m done being mad.”

He looked away first.

Good.

Mina opened the ledger again. The pages smelled like dust, coffee, polish, and Celia’s hand lotion. The notes were not mystical. Not mostly. They were Celia.

HERMES — right runner, wing channel clogged with volcanic ash. Claims “long story.” Charge double.

STORM WOMAN — waterproofing failed again. Tell her rain is not a personality.

BLACK TRAINERS / EAST DOOR CLIENT — do not ask for name. Pays exact.

HOUSEHOLD GOD, 31st Ave — children’s light-up shoes. Repair free. Last worshipper age six.

Between invoices were recipes, phone numbers, insults, sketches of tread patterns, and a grocery list with plantains underlined twice. Mina turned pages faster, searching for answers, afraid of finding more of Celia alive in the margins.

A loose receipt fell out.

On the back, Celia had drawn the shop’s floor plan. The storage closet was circled three times. Beside it: blood opens what grief won’t.

Mina stared at the words.

“No,” she said.

Hermes followed her gaze. “Ah.”

“Do not ‘ah’ me.”

“She had style.”

“She had a medical-waste problem.”

Mina took the ledger, Celia’s awl, and the bead of Hermes’ gold blood hardened on the cardboard. She marched toward the back storage closet.

The closet was where dead projects went to become archaeology: unmatched soles, cracked boot forms, broken umbrellas customers swore they would pick up, a Christmas wreath from 2018, and a box labeled IMPORTANT that contained nothing but expired coupons.

Mina had opened it a hundred times.

Now the knob was warm.

She pressed the gold bead to the doorframe.

Nothing happened.

Hermes cleared his throat. “Perhaps fresh blood.”

Mina turned slowly.

“I’m just saying.”

“You are just standing there bleeding on my recycling.”

He lifted his bare foot. “With great personal sacrifice.”

Mina grabbed a clean swab, dabbed gold from his ankle, and smeared it over the threshold before she could think too hard about handling divine blood with a generic cotton swab from a discount pharmacy.

The storage closet exhaled.

The door opened inward.

It should have revealed shelves, mold, and a broken fan.

Instead, it revealed a workshop.

Not a grand one. Not marble. Not glowing clouds or golden anvils. It was cramped and deep, stretching farther back than the building allowed, with a low ceiling, exposed pipes, and buzzing fluorescent lights. It smelled like mildew, hot rubber, old polish, machine oil, and something sharp like lightning trapped in a jar.

Mina stepped inside.

The floor changed from cheap linoleum to worn wood. Worktables crowded the space. Tools hung on pegboards: awls, knives, clamps, curved needles, hammers, brushes, things shaped like tools but too old or too strange to name. Some had Celia’s tape labels.

DO NOT TOUCH — BITES

LEFT-HANDED NEEDLES

THREAD / MOON / NOT FOR HEMS

A heat press hummed on one table. Its display blinked in a script Mina did not know and then, as if embarrassed, switched to 350°F.

Shelves held shoes.

Hundreds of them.

Sandals with bronze wings folded flat. Boots crusted with salt. Red heels with bite marks in the leather. Black trainers that made the space around them quieter. A single child’s sneaker with a dead light-up sole. A pair of white running shoes so clean Mina distrusted them immediately.

And everywhere, Celia’s work: neat stitches, rough patches, practical fixes. Ugly where ugly held better.

Mina’s chest hurt.

Hermes hovered at the doorway, unable to enter cleanly with one foot bare. “She never let me back here.”

“Smart woman.”

“She kept the divine materials in alphabetical order by danger, not name.”

Mina touched a jar labeled DAWN DUST — DO NOT INHALE. Beside it sat a coffee mug full of old pens. Celia had drawn a frowning face on the mug.

On the central table lay Celia’s apron, not the public one from the hook outside but the real one, heavy leather, pockets bulging. Mina lifted one flap and found candy, a thimble, three coins, a folded photo of Mina at twelve glaring over a sewing machine, and a note.

Not ready, Celia had written.

The words punched clean through Mina.

Under them, added in shakier handwriting:

No one ever is.

Mina sat down hard on the stool.

Hermes said nothing, which was the first wise thing he had done all night.

The fluorescent lights flickered.

A voice behind them said, “You blocking the door on purpose or is this a family tradition?”

Mina spun, awl raised.

An MTA worker stood just outside the impossible workshop, one hand on the doorframe. Reflective vest. Navy pants. Paper coffee cup. Red-and-black sneakers so clean they seemed printed onto the world. Their soles branched into tiny subway lines, crosswalk stripes, goat paths, river crossings, and cracks in sidewalks.

The worker looked at Mina’s awl. “Careful with that. Pointy end makes commitments.”

Hermes groaned. “You.”

“Fare evader,” the worker said.

“I am a god of roads.”

“And yet somehow never have exact change.”

Mina looked between them. “Who are you?”

“Depends where you’re standing.” The worker sipped coffee. “Tonight? Someone telling you to stop standing in the threshold.”

Mina stepped back despite herself.

The worker nodded. “Better.”

Hermes said, “We need to get to the market.”

“You need many things. Humility. A payment plan. A left shoe.”

“I’m aware.”

“Awareness is not repair.”

Mina tightened her grip on the ledger. “Are you another god?”

The worker considered. “If that helps you behave.”

“It doesn’t.”

“Good.”

Their gaze dropped to Celia’s apron, and for the first time their face shifted into something like respect. “Celia held this door a long time.”

“She didn’t tell me it existed.”

“No. She made a choice.”

“A bad one.”

“Possibly.” The worker’s eyes met Mina’s. “Now you make one.”

Mina hated the way the room seemed to listen.

“I can walk away?” she asked.

“Yes.”

Hermes made a small sound.

The worker ignored him. “Door’s behind you. Flip the sign, go upstairs, pretend the city isn’t tying itself in knots. That is a path.”

“And if I do?”

“Then you walked it.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It is. You wanted absolution.”

Mina looked past them, toward the shop: rain on the window, landlord notice in a shoebox, Celia’s public apron hanging limp, Hermes’ smoking footprints, the life she had been barely managing before gods came bleeding into it.

“I don’t want destiny,” she said.

“Good. Destiny is what people call choices after they’re tired of owning them.” The worker reached into their vest and produced an old subway token, brass worn nearly smooth. “Market train leaves from the platform that isn’t there. Take this if you’re going.”

Mina did not take it.

Not immediately.

“What’s the thing that stole his shoe?”

The worker’s expression flattened. “The Drop. Wanting God. New thing with no road of its own. It makes loops and sells them as exits.”

From outside came another wrong subway announcement, warped and distant: “This train is delayed because the future is unavailable.”

Mina laughed once, badly.

Then she took the token.

Hermes released a breath.

The worker stepped aside. “There. Choice made.”

“No,” Mina said, pocketing the token. “Choice rented. I can still return it.”

The worker smiled. “Keep the receipt.”

# Chapter 4: Cash Only, No Prophecies

The train that wasn’t there arrived thirteen minutes late.

Mina and Hermes waited on the real platform first, beneath flickering lights and a sign that insisted the next local train was both approaching and canceled due to “goat interference.” Rainwater dripped through a crack overhead into a bucket someone had placed with hopeless optimism. Three commuters stared at their phones, each swiping harder, as if force could make service return.

Hermes leaned against a pillar, one foot in his silver sneaker and the other wrapped in four layers of cardboard, duct tape, and Mina’s worst towel.

“You look like a man who lost a fight with recycling,” Mina said.

“I am redefining vulnerability.”

“You are shedding gold on public transit.”

He looked down. A bright bead rolled toward the yellow platform edge. Mina caught it with a receipt before it fell.

“Do not waste that,” she said.

“My blood?”

“Do you know what divine materials cost?”

Hermes gave her a look that was almost Celia-level offended. “I am injured.”

“And I am undercapitalized.”

The brass token in Mina’s pocket warmed. The platform lights buzzed. On the far track, where no train was scheduled, darkness folded open like a curtain.

A train slid in without sound.

It was old — silver cars, blue stripe, windows scratched opaque. The route marker read: LOCAL / ELSEWHERE. The doors opened with a sigh.

The commuters did not look up.

Hermes gestured. “After you.”

“Absolutely not.”

“Mina—”

“You’re the god of roads. Road first.”

He sighed and limped aboard.

Mina followed.

The doors shut. The train moved.

For a while, it looked like any other subway car, if any other subway car had advertisements reading HAVE YOU CONSIDERED REPENTANCE? and LEARN LYRE IN 30 DAYS. Mina gripped the pole and tried not to stare at the passenger across from her: a woman in a business suit with wet river reeds braided into her hair and green canvas slip-ons leaking water into a perfect circle.

Hermes stood because sitting made him fidget worse. “Do not buy anything unless you understand the price.”

“I run a repair shop in Queens. That’s my whole religion.”

“Do not give anyone your full name.”

“Little late.”

“Do not accept food from anyone with antlers.”

“That one I had.”

The train stopped.

The doors opened onto a station that should not have fit beneath the city.

Fluorescent lights hummed overhead. The platform stretched into haze, crowded with stalls made of folding tables, old temple columns, milk crates, velvet ropes, shopping carts, and pieces of buildings from other centuries. A hand-painted sign read:

CROSSROADS MARKET  
NO REFUNDS  
NO SACRIFICES OVER 10 LBS WITHOUT PERMIT

The air smelled of brake dust, incense, wet wool, frying dough, old coins, and hot rubber.

Mina stepped out slowly.

Gods wore sneakers.

The thought arrived stupid and simple, and then everywhere she looked, it proved itself.

A woman in silent black trainers waited at a stall while a vendor replaced one heel tab with something carved from bone. People gave her space without seeming to know why. A storm-colored man argued with a cobbler over waterproofing, rain steaming from the soles of his massive blue runners.

“I said thunderproof,” he boomed.

“You said water-resistant,” the cobbler snapped. “Read your ticket.”

A tiny household god, no taller than a child and wrinkled as a dried apple, sat on an overturned bucket wearing red light-up sneakers. One sole blinked weakly with every kick.

“Can you fix the left one?” the household god asked a vendor. “My girl used to stomp them both when she prayed.”

“How long since she prayed?”

The little god looked down. “She’s eleven now.”

The vendor’s face softened. “I’ll see what I can do.”

Mina looked away fast.

Hermes watched her watching. “Celia did that pair once.”

“Of course she did.”

“Free.”

“Of course she did,” Mina said again, this time angrier.

They passed stalls selling bottled dawn, counterfeit halos, saint buckles, crow-feather laces, insoles “guaranteed to reduce prophetic fatigue,” and polish that promised to erase footprints from memory. Mina saw three obvious scams, two repairs so beautiful they made her chest hurt, and one pair of white sneakers she distrusted on principle.

A fox-faced vendor held out a lace. “Woven from rumor. Half off.”

Mina kept walking. “Rumor frays.”

The vendor blinked, then grinned. “Celia’s girl?”

Mina did not answer.

Hermes preened despite bleeding. “She has an eye.”

“She has overdue rent,” Mina said.

They found Hephaestus between a watch battery stall and a woman selling umbrellas that opened into different weather.

His kiosk was ugly, practical, and overstuffed. Keys hung in dense rings. Tiny drawers lined the back wall, labeled in blocky handwriting: METEOR FILINGS, LEFT-HANDED SCREWS, REGRETS—BRASS, SAINT EYELETS, DO NOT OPEN SOBER. A radio crackled with a baseball game from 1947.

Above the counter hung a sign:

CASH ONLY. NO PROPHECIES.

Behind it sat a broad man with scarred forearms, smoke-gray hair, and thick, ugly sneakers that looked comfortable enough to forgive sin. He was replacing the battery in a watch while holding a glowing horseshoe under one elbow.

Without looking up, he said, “No.”

Hermes put a hand to his chest. “You wound me.”

“Not yet.”

“We need—”

“I heard you coming. Everyone did. You limp loudly.”

Mina stepped forward. “Are you Hephaestus?”

Now he looked up.

His eyes moved over her: apron, hands, paint under nails, Celia’s awl tucked into her pocket, fear she was trying to pass off as impatience. His gaze paused on her thumb scar.

“You hold tools right,” he said.

“Thanks?”

“Wasn’t praise. Observation.” He pointed to Hermes. “Get the shoe up.”

Hermes lifted his silver sneaker onto the counter. Hephaestus did not gasp or chant. He put on magnifying glasses and bent close.

Mina leaned in before she could stop herself.

“Stress fractures under the wing channel,” she said. “Not from tonight.”

Hephaestus glanced at her.

Hermes said, “I run a great deal.”

“You land badly,” Mina said.

Hephaestus snorted. “Celia’s blood, then.”

“Granddaughter,” Mina said.

“Same problem, different invoice.”

He took a hooked tool and teased something from the tread: chrome dust, barcode fiber, a thin shaving of road-light that squirmed like thread.

“The Drop,” he said.

Hermes’ fingers tightened on the counter.

Mina asked, “Can you remake the missing shoe?”

Hephaestus looked insulted. “Can you remake your grandmother from her apron?”

The words hit hard enough that Mina shut her mouth.

Hephaestus grunted, not apologizing. “A divine shoe isn’t materials. It’s use. Road. Habit. Function. Story. His left runner carries the routes this one doesn’t. They’re draining it.”

“Into GODSPEED ZERO,” Mina said.

He nodded. “Midnight release. Thousands of counterfeit exits. People put them on thinking they’ll go somewhere better. Instead, they feed the loop.”

“Why don’t you stop it?”

Hephaestus removed his glasses. “Old gods know temples, altars, battlefields, bedrooms, storms. This thing lives in countdowns. Raffles. Terms of service. Envy at scale. We’re clumsy there.”

Hermes muttered, “Speak for yourself.”

“You let it scan your shoe.”

Hermes shut up.

A blur moved beyond the kiosk.

Mina saw a lanky kid in an oversized hoodie carrying a box of black wristbands stamped GZ-0. Clean sneakers, cracked phone, sunflower seeds in his cheek.

“Dez?” she called.

The kid looked up.

For one second, he was just Dez Coleman from three blocks over, who always asked for discounts and pretended not to care when Mina praised his eye.

Then he saw Hermes.

Saw the market.

Saw Mina seeing him.

“Aw, hell no,” Dez said.

He ran.

Mina ran after him.

# Chapter 5: Wristbands

Dez was fast in the way sixteen-year-olds were fast when they had done something wrong and believed adulthood was a disease that slowed people down.

Mina was fast in the way people were fast when they had spent their life catching falling knives, runaway customers, and invoices before they blew into traffic.

Hermes, god of roads, was currently fast in the way a man with one divine sneaker and one cardboard foot was fast, which meant he yelled, “I’ll cut him off!” and immediately collided with a cart selling prophetic umbrellas.

The umbrellas burst open. A localized drizzle of frogs began.

Mina did not look back.

“Dez!”

He darted between stalls, hoodie flapping, wristband box under one arm. A woman with antlers hissed as he vaulted over her table. The household god in light-up sneakers cheered weakly.

Mina caught him at the edge of the platform, where the market thinned into a stairwell tiled in old green ceramic. She grabbed the back of his hoodie. He spun, nearly dropped the box, and threw up both hands.

“Yo! Assault!”

“You’re distributing cursed sneaker wristbands in a god basement.”

“I don’t know what sentence you think you just said.”

“Don’t play stupid.”

“I’m not playing anything. I’m working.” He yanked his hoodie free, chin lifted, cheeks flushed. “Same as you.”

Mina pointed at the box. “Who gave you those?”

“Nobody.”

“Dez.”

He looked past her. Hermes limped into view with a frog on his shoulder and murder in his eyes.

Dez stared. “Is that dude bleeding gold?”

Hermes plucked off the frog. “This dude is standing right here.”

“You got one shoe.”

“I’m aware.”

“Is that like a fashion thing?”

Mina snapped her fingers in Dez’s face. “Focus.”

Dez hugged the box closer. “Look, it’s just promo. Wristbands, invite codes, early access. I hand them out, I get a cut. I’m not smuggling organs.”

Hermes said, “Debatable.”

“Who even are you?”

“A victim of modern branding.”

“That makes two of us.”

Mina stepped closer. “GODSPEED ZERO is dangerous.”

Dez laughed, but it came out too sharp. “Everything’s dangerous. Rent dangerous. Being broke dangerous. Walking into school with busted shoes dangerous if you care about surviving lunch.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

“I know what you mean. You mean I’m a dumb kid who saw shiny and got played.”

“I didn’t say dumb.”

“You didn’t have to.” He shifted the box to his other arm. “You hate resellers till the rent due. Then everybody understands margins.”

The words landed because they had teeth.

Mina thought of the landlord notice folded in the shoebox marked TAXES / MAYBE. Thought of the customs she painted for collectors who never wore them. Thought of every time she had charged extra because a shoe was rare, not because the work was harder.

“That’s different,” she said, and heard how weak it sounded.

Dez saw it too. “Sure.”

Hermes moved impatiently. “The wristbands are part of a ritual.”

Dez blinked. “A what?”

“A ritual,” Hermes said. “Ceremony, offering, mass participation, symbolic object, desire directed toward a central power. Don’t tell me mortals stopped recognizing these.”

Dez looked at Mina. “He always talk like a podcast?”

“Unfortunately.”

The Crossroads Market flickered around them. A train roared somewhere beyond the walls though no track showed. Mina lowered her voice.

“Dez, the Drop is using people.”

“The Drop got me paid.”

“It got Hermes’ shoe.”

“I still don’t know why I care about his shoe.”

The lights dimmed.

Every wristband in Dez’s box glowed white.

A sound rose from them: thousands of tiny checkout chimes, all slightly out of sync.

Hermes went pale.

Mina grabbed one band. The material was smooth and cold. Printed inside, where it would touch skin, were words so small she almost missed them:

YOU ARE ALMOST THERE.

The stairwell shifted.

Suddenly they were not in the market. They stood in an alley behind a sleek storefront that had appeared overnight in an empty retail space on Steinway. Chrome panels. Black glass. A glowing sign with no brand name, only:

GZ-0  
MIDNIGHT

The line already wrapped around the block.

Mina had seen sneaker lines before. This was that and not that. Folding chairs, umbrellas, portable chargers, livestream lights, takeout containers, kids in hoodies, parents in work uniforms, men pretending not to check resale apps every six seconds. It felt like a block party, a vigil, and a trap.

A girl practiced dance steps in the reflection of the black glass, glancing down at her worn sneakers between moves. A father held a place in line while his son slept against his backpack. Two collectors argued about production numbers like theologians disputing scripture. A woman in scrubs rubbed her swollen feet and watched the door as if it owed her something.

Mina swallowed.

The crowd was not stupid. It was tired. Hopeful. Vain. Practical. Human.

Screens built into the storefront flashed without repeating. Not ads, exactly. Promises.

A boy saw himself taller, admired, no longer shoved in hallways.

The woman in scrubs saw a pair boxed under a birthday banner.

The dancer saw her body obeying perfectly.

Dez stopped breathing.

On the glass in front of him, his reflection changed. He stood older, sharper, surrounded by people saying his name. His phone screen exploded with likes. A stack of boxes rose behind him like a throne.

“Damn,” he whispered.

Hermes hissed.

Mina turned.

The screen nearest Hermes showed him in gold, winged, adored, statues rising, crowds chanting his name like they remembered who had carried every message first.

His face twisted with longing before he looked away.

Then Mina saw herself.

Sole Purpose, renovated. Clean windows. New sign, no pun. A line out the door. Her customs displayed in glass cases. Reviews glowing. Bills paid. Celia standing behind the counter in clean sneakers, smiling.

Proud.

Mina stepped toward the glass.

Celia lifted a hand.

Wrong hand, Mina realized.

Celia had been left-handed.

The vision flickered.

Mina stepped back hard enough to bump Dez.

“Don’t look too long,” she said.

Dez’s voice was rough. “Easy for you.”

“No,” Mina said. “It isn’t.”

Hermes tried to move toward the entrance. “Enough. We get the shoe.”

He took three quick steps and vanished.

A checkout chime sounded.

He reappeared at the very end of the line, behind a man asleep in a camping chair.

Hermes stared, offended beyond language.

Mina almost laughed. “Notifications outrun you?”

“This is not amusing.”

“It’s a little amusing.”

He tried again. Same result. End of line.

The crowd barely noticed.

Mina looked at the wristband in her hand. Barcode sequence. Adhesive residue along one edge. Heat-activated strip. Cheap, mass-produced, but the numbering pattern was wrong. Not random. Routing.

She compared it to the scrap from Hermes’ tread.

GZ-0.

“There’s a service entrance,” she said.

Dez frowned. “How you know?”

“Wristbands need a scanner. Scanners need power. Power cables don’t run through vibes.”

He stared. “You are weirdly useful.”

“I’m constantly useful. People just don’t pay.”

Around the side, behind stacked trash bags and a locked metal door, Mina found a panel with fresh screws. Dez pulled a driver from his backpack.

Mina raised an eyebrow.

“What?” he said. “Preparation is not crime.”

They opened the panel and slipped inside.

The back hallway smelled like new rubber, hot plastic, and receipt paper. The walls were too white. The lights too clean.

At the end was a chrome room.

Hermes’ left sneaker hung suspended in a glass display case, cut open along the sole. Roads spilled from it in thin gold lines, draining downward into rows and rows of blank black sneakers.

GODSPEED ZERO.

Thousands of them.

Drinking.

Hermes made a sound like someone had stepped on his heart.

Every phone in the building lit at once.

Every screen turned toward Mina.
