# Chapter 3: Under the Paint

The Cinder Badlands appeared on the forward screen as a bruise of dirty light.

Kip put them there without being asked twice. He dragged the local chart across the glass with two fingers and let it hang above the helm: a belt of broken mining rock, dead satellites, magnetic dust, and old claims nobody had bothered to bury properly. Beyond it, Mercy’s Rest blinked in clean corporate blue.

Between the two, still distant but gaining, burned the Helix cutter.

“Badlands give us cover,” Kip said. “Also give us sharp rocks, blind pockets, sensor ghosts, and the sort of navigational regrets people name children after.”

Mara stood behind his chair. “Can you fly it?”

“Sure.”

She waited.

Kip scratched the side of his jaw. “Once.”

“Good enough.”

“It is traditionally not.”

The helm smelled of burnt coffee and hot wiring. Kip had three sugar packets lined along the console like devotional offerings. Mara picked up one and turned it over without reading it.

“Quade will expect Mercy’s Rest,” she said.

“Quade has probably expected everything since infancy.”

“Then we disappoint him.”

Kip glanced back. The joking expression slid off his face and came back thinner. “Are we running, then?”

Mara looked at the cutter marker. “We’re not docking on his schedule.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

“No,” she said. “It wasn’t.”

She left him with that and went aft.

In the cargo bay, Jax had taken the crate apart as if it had personally wronged him. Panels lay across the deck. Black alloy bands leaned against the bulkhead. A slick line of coolant from the calf’s earlier chewing had been dammed with rags, sealant foam, and one of Kip’s jackets.

The calf had shifted closer to the old coolant pump. It lay with its cracked horn angled toward the vibration, eyes half-lidded but not asleep. Every few breaths its whole body shivered, and the deck answered in a low hum.

Doc Quill knelt beside the ruined crate with her sleeves rolled up. Nell stood nearby, arms folded, pretending not to watch the animal.

“What have we got?” Mara asked.

“Lies with hardware,” Jax said.

He kicked one of the inner panels over. It showed a neat row of recessed metal rings and dried adhesive pads. Restraint points.

Doc lifted a narrow tube with forceps. “Sedative injector. Timed feed. Too strong for long transport unless the goal was keeping it from moving until someone cut it open.”

Nell’s jaw tightened.

Mara crouched by the crate. Along the base, under what had looked like padding, ran a shallow channel that ended in a sealed port. Drainage. Her stomach knew before her mind named it.

Doc saw her looking. “Yes.”

Jax pulled out another false strip. Inside were tiny vials, three used, two empty. Each had a sample number printed in Helix block script.

“Residue from previous subjects,” Doc said. “Not this one.”

Jax looked at her.

“I’m sorry,” she said, which was not an answer and was.

The calf made a soft, distressed click. Its jaw filaments trembled toward their voices. Jax set down the strip more gently.

Nell said, “Ugly doesn’t change math.”

Jax rounded on her. “It changes something.”

“Does it fix the regulator? Does it fill water tanks? Does it clear the liens Quade offered to vanish?”

“It’s alive.”

“So are we.”

Doc stood slowly, one hand braced against her bad leg. “Both of you lower your voices.”

The calf’s horn bud flickered. A wrench near Mara’s boot vibrated against the deck.

Mara picked it up before it could rise.

Jax looked at her as if asking her to settle the matter. She hated that. She hated how young it made him seem, though he was not that young, and how old it made her feel.

“Keep working,” she said.

“We know enough,” Jax said.

“We know the crate is worse than advertised. That’s not a plan.”

“It keeps turning,” Doc said.

Mara looked at her. “What?”

Doc pointed.

The calf had dragged itself into a new position while they argued. Its head faced not toward the pump now, but forward and starboard. Its cracked horn bud pulsed faintly, once every few seconds. Jax had marked the deck beneath it in grease pencil: little ticks, four of them, all on the same bearing.

“It’s done that every time we alter course,” Jax said. “Turns back. Same direction.”

“Toward what?”

Jax wiped his hands on his pants and brought up a portable chart. “I thought it was following the pump vibration, but no. I overlaid the bearing with old outer-route data and Clementine’s antique folklore folder.”

“I do not have a folklore folder,” Clementine said overhead. “I have regional hazard memoranda of uncertain authorship.”

“Folklore folder,” Jax said.

The chart projected in pale blue: their current position, the Badlands, Mercy’s Rest, Quade’s cutter, and beyond them a stormed patch of unlovely static.

Kip, listening in from the bridge, said, “No.”

Jax tapped the static. “Blue Pasture.”

Nell laughed once. “Absolutely no.”

Mara studied the chart. The Blue Pasture was not labeled on official maps. Official maps called it BP-9 Gravitic Weather Zone and marked it in red hazard lattice. Spacers called it Blue Pasture because people liked giving gentle names to things that ate ships.

Doc said, “There were old migration reports. Before Helix closed most of the records. Starhorn herds moving through nebula currents.”

“Stories,” Nell said.

The calf breathed out, long and low. The projection trembled.

“Maybe,” Doc said. “Maybe not.”

Mara stared at the patch of static until it became something else.

A loading dock at Larkspur Well. Dust yellow under dome lights. Settlers standing behind a fence made of pipe and prayer. Crates lined in a row. WATER RECLAMATION PUMPS stamped on every side. The settlement foreman, a woman with gray braids and shaking hands, saying, “Deputy, can we inspect them?”

Mara had been twenty-nine and tired and clean in her black Helix coat.

“Manifest’s sealed,” she had said.

“By who?”

“By law.”

What she remembered most was not the drones coming out later. She had not seen that part directly. What she remembered was the relief she felt when the woman stopped asking. Relief, because it meant Mara did not have to decide whether the question mattered.

“Mara,” Doc said.

The cargo bay returned. Jax’s grease-pencil ticks. Nell watching too closely. The animal in the corner turning, always turning, toward a place no sane hauler wanted to go.

Mara stood. “Quade wants us at Mercy’s Rest because he can control docks, clerks, air, witnesses.”

Nell’s eyes narrowed. “He also wants us there because we need a regulator and he knows it.”

“We go through the Badlands first. Shake him if we can.”

“And after?”

Mara looked at the calf.

It had opened both eyes. The second lid clicked aside. Not understanding. Not pleading. Just alive inside a problem people kept trying to name into usefulness.

“After, we decide with more distance.”

Jax’s mouth twisted. “That what we’re calling it?”

“Careful.”

“No, Captain. You be careful. We already waited once. That’s how it ended up in the box.”

The words hit harder because they were unfair and partly true.

Mara stepped close enough that Jax had to tilt his head down to meet her eyes. “You think I don’t know what boxes are for?”

“I think you know and still want the manifest to tell you what to do.”

Nell murmured, “Kid.”

Jax did not look away.

Mara could have pulled rank. It sat ready in her mouth, familiar and poisonous. Instead she turned toward the crate and hooked a thumb under the edge of the scraped paint.

It flaked away in a long, brittle curl.

Underneath, burned deep into the composite, the Helix spiral gleamed black.

She held the strip of paint between finger and thumb. Thin. Useless. Enough to hide a thing from someone who preferred not to look.

“Clementine,” Mara said.

“Yes, Captain.”

“Record message to Marshal Quade.”

A soft chime.

Mara kept her eyes on the brand. “Cargo condition under review. Beacon found damaged during salvage recovery. Delivery schedule pending mechanical assessment.”

“Message recorded,” Clementine said. “It is unconvincing.”

“Send it.”

“Sent.”

Nell exhaled through her nose. “That your plan? Bore him into mercy?”

“No.” Mara turned toward the bridge. “Kip.”

“I’m listening in professional dread.”

“Hard burn for the Cinder line.”

There was a pause.

Then Kip said, “About time somebody made a bad decision with confidence.”

The engines deepened underfoot. The calf jerked, then steadied as Jax lowered his voice beside it. The scattered crate parts trembled across the deck.

Mara walked to the hatch.

Behind her, Clementine chimed once. “Long-range update. Helix cutter has increased acceleration. Intercept now projected before Mercy’s Rest.”

Nell checked the load on her pistol.

Jax looked at Mara over the calf’s bent head, still angry, still waiting.

Mara said, “Then we don’t go to Mercy’s Rest.”

Kip’s voice came from the bridge, thin with nerves and sugar. “Badlands in twelve minutes.”

The ship groaned as if it had heard and disapproved.

# Chapter 4: The Song with No Words

The Cinder Badlands took the *Sundown Mercy* in one bite.

One moment there was clean black ahead, stars salted thin across it. The next, the forward screen filled with rock, scrap, magnetic dust, old mining slag, and pale shards of ice spinning in every direction at once. Collision alarms bloomed red across Kip’s console.

“Lovely country,” Kip said, voice too bright. “Bit cluttered.”

Mara braced one hand on the back of his chair. “Path?”

“Several. All bad.”

“Best bad.”

“Working on it.”

The *Sundown Mercy* rolled hard to port. A burnt-out ore bucket the size of a church tumbled past close enough that its rusted hull scraped a shriek down their shields. Somewhere aft, a cabinet burst open and spilled metal cups.

Clementine chimed. “Advisory: current route intersects with debris, magnetic weather, and three outstanding docking invoices.”

“Not now,” Mara said.

“Financial hazards remain hazards.”

Kip’s hands moved lightly across the controls. The joking stopped at his wrists. He nudged them between two spinning rocks, kicked the ventral thrusters, cursed when the portside lagged half a second, and compensated before the ship’s nose could drift.

“Jax,” he called, “port ventral’s lazy.”

From aft, underlaid by static and clanging, Jax answered, “Port ventral’s a senior citizen. Be respectful.”

“Respectful won’t keep us out of that asteroid.”

“Try flattery.”

Mara checked the tactical repeater. The Helix cutter entered the Badlands behind them, not as close as she’d feared, but steady. Too steady. Quade was not trying to match Kip’s stunts. He was staying where the field thinned, letting drones do the foolish work.

Three small markers detached from the cutter and accelerated.

“Nell,” Mara said.

“Seen,” Nell answered from the dorsal gun well.

The first drone slipped through a gap in the rocks, silver and fast, a tracking harpoon folded under its belly. Nell fired. Blue-white rounds stitched across the dust. The drone twisted, almost made it, then came apart in a flash that lit the cargo bay monitors.

“One,” she said.

The second dropped low beneath a dead comm satellite. Kip rolled them around the satellite’s corpse, close enough for the *Sundown Mercy’s* belly to graze a dangling antenna.

Mara’s teeth clicked together.

Nell fired again. Missed. Fired a third time. Hit. The drone spun into a rock and vanished.

“Two,” she said, more annoyed than pleased.

The third disappeared.

Kip went quiet.

Mara leaned toward the screen. “Where?”

“Lost it in dust.”

Clementine chimed. “Unregistered object approaching from starboard aft.”

The ship jolted. Not impact. Harpoon lock.

Nell swore. “Tag on the hull.”

“Jax,” Mara said.

“Busy keeping your ventral elder alive.”

“Get busier.”

Then the cargo channel erupted in noise.

Not an alarm. Not words. A low, panicked bellow that went through the ship like a hand dragging along every bone.

The deck lurched.

Gravity vanished, returned sideways, and then punched down too hard. Kip’s sugar packets flew up, hung glittering, and slapped against the ceiling. Mara’s boots left the floor. She caught the chair with one hand and slammed shoulder-first into the console as gravity came back.

“Kip?”

“Still hands, still ship,” he said through clenched teeth.

From cargo, Doc’s voice cut in sharp. “Mara, get down here.”

Another bellow. The lights flickered. The forward screen smeared with static.

Kip grabbed manual controls. “Whatever it’s doing, it’s stepping on my instruments.”

Mara shoved off toward the bridge ladder. “Keep us moving.”

“With what, prayer?”

“You said several paths.”

“I said all bad.”

“Pick one.”

She took the ladder two rungs at a time, half falling in the uncertain gravity. The corridor was chaos: loose tools skidding, a crate strap whipping overhead, Clementine repeating, “Livestock distress detected,” in a tone fit for tea service.

In the cargo bay, the calf had wedged itself beneath the cargo pallets and was trying to kick through them. Its six legs struck metal in frantic bursts. Each blow came with a pulse that made the deck plates ripple under Mara’s boots. One pallet had broken loose and floated three feet above the floor, turning slowly.

Doc clung to a wall rail, face pale, one shoulder hanging wrong. Jax was trying to reach the calf from the side, blood bright along his forearm where a cargo chain had opened him. Nell stood near the hatch with her pistol drawn but not aimed, jaw tight.

The calf screamed again.

A rack of spare filters tore free and scattered across the bay.

“Lights down!” Mara shouted.

“They are down,” Jax snapped.

“Noise down.”

Nell looked toward the ceiling. “Tell that to Quade.”

The ship rocked as something struck the shields.

The calf’s horn buds flickered blue. Its jaw filaments stood out stiffly, trembling toward Nell. No — toward the battery pack at her hip, whining faintly as her pistol charged.

“Mara,” Doc said, breath short, “that frequency—”

“Nell. Power down.”

Nell looked at her. “Excuse me?”

“Gun. Down. Now.”

“We have drones on us.”

“And you’re scaring it worse.”

Nell’s face hardened. For one second, Mara thought she would refuse. Then Nell thumbed the pistol cold and set it on the deck with exaggerated care.

The calf’s next cry hitched, lower.

Mara stepped forward.

Jax caught her sleeve with his uninjured hand. “Captain—”

“I see it.”

She did not, exactly. She saw fear. She knew that much. Knew the way a trapped animal made itself dangerous because danger was the last language left to it.

The calf struck the deck again. Gravity surged. Mara went to one knee. Something small and metal pinged past her ear.

“Easy,” she said, which was useless.

The calf pressed its head into the corner beneath the pallet, trying to hide inside steel.

Mara had no medicine. No science. No gentleness anyone would mistake for a gift.

The ship groaned around her, and under that groan she heard, absurdly, a rhythm from Tallow. Pressure-herders in a low dome. Her mother’s cracked voice. A line of pack beasts refusing a storm gate. The old work hum had no proper words, or she had lost them. It was mostly breath and stubbornness.

She began to hum.

Quietly at first, because she felt like a fool.

Jax looked at her as if she had started bleeding from the eyes. Doc did not. Doc only lowered her own breathing to match.

Mara kept the rhythm low in her chest. Not pretty. Not music, hardly. A sound made to travel through fences and frightened bodies. Hm, hm-hmm. Hm, hm-hmm. Again. Again.

The calf’s kicking faltered.

Mara moved one hand in the air, palm down, not touching. “That’s it.”

It shivered. Its cracked horn bud glowed, dim then brighter. The vibration in the deck changed. Less like panic. More like a far engine finding alignment.

Clementine’s voice cut through the cargo bay. “Anomalous gravitic current detected.”

Kip shouted over comms, “Say that in pilot!”

Jax, staring at the portable chart strapped to his belt, said, “There’s a lane. In the rocks. Natural slip eddy, maybe. It’s showing us a lane.”

“Who’s showing?” Kip demanded.

Jax looked at the calf. “Guess.”

Mara kept humming. Her throat felt raw. The calf’s eye fixed on her, or near her. Not trust. Not calm. But less terror.

“Kip,” she said into comms, “Jax is sending you a bearing.”

“I love receiving imaginary roads from livestock while being shot at.”

Nell grabbed her pistol but did not power it up. “Harpoon tag’s still on us.”

“Then make him think we’re dumber than we are,” Mara said.

Kip laughed once, wild. “Finally, a plan tailored to our strengths.”

The *Sundown Mercy* dove.

Mara felt it in her knees before the screens caught up. Kip rolled them under a slab of iron-streaked rock, cut thrust, spun belly-first through a cloud of magnetic dust, then lit the engines hard enough that the cargo bay gravity flattened everyone for two bruising seconds.

The calf moaned. Mara kept humming because stopping felt like dropping a glass.

Jax fed coordinates with a shaking voice. “Three degrees down. Hard starboard in five. Four. No, now. Now!”

The ship screamed.

Something tore loose outside with a metallic bang. Kip whooped, which was not reassuring. Nell shouted that another drone had lost them. Clementine began a prayerful-sounding list of damages until Mara cut the audio with her elbow.

Ahead, through the cargo bay’s small external monitor, two asteroids drifted toward collision, closing like jaws.

Jax said, very quietly, “That’s the lane.”

Mara closed her eyes for half a beat and hummed.

The *Sundown Mercy* shot through the gap.

For one suspended instant, everything in the bay lifted: tools, blood droplets, Doc’s scanner, Nell’s unloaded pistol, Mara’s breath. The calf’s horn flared blue-white.

Then they were out.

Gravity slammed back. The ship rolled, bucked, and steadied into a long, wounded glide.

Kip’s voice came over comms, thin and disbelieving. “Cutter broke off. Repeat: Quade blinked.”

No one cheered.

Doc slid down the wall, clutching her shoulder. Jax sat hard on the deck and finally noticed his bleeding arm. Nell picked up her pistol and checked it without looking at anyone.

The calf lay trembling beneath the pallet, eyes half closed. Its horn had gone dull again. A trail of mineral water leaked from the ruptured hose and drifted in silver beads along the floor before gravity remembered them.

Mara stopped humming.

Her throat hurt. Her shoulder hurt. Her pride, oddly, hurt worst of all.

Clementine chimed, gentler than usual or merely damaged. “Damage report: slip regulator compromised. Water reserves reduced. Port cargo fin absent. Coffee heater offline.”

Kip gasped. “Not the coffee heater.”

“Can we reach Blue Pasture?” Mara asked.

Jax looked down at his blood, then at the calf, then at the deck as if the answer might be written there.

“Not without a regulator,” he said. “And a patch. And water.”

Nell holstered her gun. “Nearest place?”

No one answered immediately.

Kip did, from the bridge. The humor was gone.

“Mercy’s Rest,” he said.

Mara looked at the broken crate, the wounded calf, and the place where the Helix beacon had been.

Of course, she thought.

Out loud she said, “Set course.”

# Chapter 5: Mercy’s Rest Owes Us Money

Mercy’s Rest did not look like mercy from the outside.

It looked like old mining scaffolds welded around a fuel spine, with docking arms stuck out at bad angles and advertisement panels flickering through vacuum dust. Half the lights were dead. The other half sold noodles, oxygen, cards, suit patches, companionship, debt relief, and one chapel service a week if the preacher was sober.

Kip eased the *Sundown Mercy* into dock under a borrowed transponder and three layers of prayer.

“Welcome to Mercy’s Rest,” Clementine announced. “Please settle all outstanding invoices before engaging in commerce, violence, or laundry.”

“Can she not?” Nell asked.

“She can,” Jax said. “She chooses.”

The cargo bay smelled of coolant, blood, and frightened animal. Jax had wrapped his forearm badly and refused Doc’s second attempt to fix it until the calf was hidden. The starhorn stood unsteadily in a cargo sled under heat blankets, scrap panels, and two empty filter crates. It was too large for the disguise and too alive for any of it. Its jaw filaments trembled under the blanket edge.

Mara looked at it once and then away.

“Dock time,” she said. “Fast and quiet. Kip, regulator. Doc, anti-sedative, mineral feed if you can find any. Nell, eyes. Jax, stay with the sled.”

Jax’s face was pale from blood loss and anger. “I’m not leaving it.”

“That’s what I said.”

“Just making sure.”

Nell checked the charge on her pistol, then powered it down after a glance at the calf. The motion was small. Mara noticed anyway.

Mercy’s Rest hit them with station air as soon as the lock opened: fryer grease, ozone, soap, old sweat, and too many bodies trusting too few filters. The main promenade ran in a crooked ring around the fuel spine. Laundry drums thumped behind a noodle stall. A barber worked beside a pressure-suit patcher. A woman with a missing hand sold oxygen cartridges from a shrine booth plastered with saints and rate charts.

People looked at the *Sundown Mercy’s* crew the way station people looked at everyone: long enough to price them, not long enough to be involved.

Mara split them with hand signals.

The fixer she needed held court in a bar-laundry alcove called The Last Pour, which had six stools, four working washers, and a card table under a sign reading NO KNIVES IN THE MACHINES. Doma Vetch was round, bald, and wearing a vest with too many pockets to be honest.

“You owe me money,” he said as Mara sat.

“Mercy’s Rest owes me money.”

“That’s not how owing works.”

“I brought you those condenser coils last winter.”

“You brought me stolen condenser coils last winter.”

“You sold them.”

“Which created spiritual balance, not credit.”

Mara slid a small Helix-grade coupling onto the counter. Doma’s eyes sharpened.

“I need a slip regulator. Used is fine. Ugly is fine. Working is not optional.”

Doma picked up the coupling. “Where’d this fall off?”

“A crate.”

“Crates don’t have couplings.”

“This one had opinions.”

Doma studied her face, then the promenade behind her. “Helix asking questions today.”

“Helix asks questions every day.”

“Today they brought marshals.”

Mara’s jaw tightened.

At the docking level, Jax kept one hand on the cargo sled and the other near the cutter clipped to his belt. The calf shifted under the blankets. It had been quiet since they entered station gravity, which worried him more than noise would have.

“Nearly done,” he whispered.

The calf’s head pressed lightly against the inside of the scrap panel. Not trust. Weight.

Doc appeared with a paper bag of medical supplies and a face like bad news. “Anti-sedative, yes. Mineral feed, no. I got livestock electrolyte and powdered bone meal.”

“That sounds disgusting.”

“It’s for the calf, not your refined station palate.”

“I grew up here.”

“My condolences.”

Jax almost smiled.

Then a scanner arch at the far end of the dock cycled on with a rising whine.

The calf convulsed.

Jax felt the sound before it came. A tremor through the sled handle, through his bad bandage, into the deck. The blankets jerked. One scrap panel slipped, exposing the dark curve of the calf’s head and the cracked horn bud.

“No,” he whispered. “No, no, easy.”

The scanner whine rose another pitch.

The calf cried out.

Every person on the dock heard it. Some flinched. Some pretended they had not. A dockworker pushing a fuel cart stopped dead, eyes wide, then looked away so hard it was almost a kindness.

Doc grabbed for the sled cover. “Move. Now.”

Across the promenade, Mara heard the sound in The Last Pour.

So did Quade.

He had entered without hurry. Dark coat. Clean boots. Helix badge bright but not ostentatious. He took the stool beside Mara as if they had arranged to meet.

Doma Vetch vanished into the back room with impressive speed.

“Captain,” Quade said.

Mara did not turn fully toward him. “Marshal.”

“You look tired.”

“You look expensive.”

“I sleep better.”

“I doubt that.”

He rested one hand on the counter. No weapon visible. That was part of the weapon.

“You came to the place I told you to come.”

“I needed parts.”

“Yes.”

The calf cried again. Lower this time. The washers in The Last Pour shuddered. A glass slid off a shelf and broke.

Quade’s expression changed only at the eyes. “Your mechanic should have avoided the freight scanner.”

“Your dock clerk should have left it off.”

“I paid him to turn it on.”

Mara’s hand moved under the counter toward her pistol.

Quade noticed. “If this becomes shooting, station security will side with the oxygen contract. You know that.”

“You always did like buying the room before entering.”

“And you always did like pretending rooms were free.”

She looked at him then.

He said quietly, “Larkspur Well had children too, Mara.”

The words were not loud. They did not need to be.

Mara felt them land. Felt, worse, Nell and Kip on the crew channel listening.

Quade continued, “You think this animal is a door back to before you signed that transfer. It isn’t. One dramatic refusal will not make you clean.”

“No,” Mara said. “But it might keep me from getting dirtier.”

His mouth tightened. “Blue Pasture routes lose ships every year. Horn-derived cores cut that down. How many dead spacers is a wild herd worth?”

“How many herds make you satisfied?”

“That is not an answer.”

“Neither was ‘studied.’”

The dock channel erupted. Nell’s voice: “Contact, three Helix deputies by bay four.”

Kip: “I’ve got the regulator. Also a misunderstanding involving payment.”

Mara stood.

Quade did too, not reaching for her. “Last chance.”

“Never knew you to offer those.”

“I offered you one at Larkspur.”

She stepped close enough to smell the clean synthetic leather of his coat. “No. You offered me paperwork.”

Then she hit the laundry alarm.

The Last Pour exploded into sound: washer bells, steam vent, shouting patrons, Doma cursing from the back. Mara kicked over the card table and drew as the first Helix deputy pushed through the beaded partition.

She shot the light above him.

Darkness and sparks filled the alcove.

At the dock, Nell fired into a ceiling panel, showering the corridor with glass and killing the scanner arch. The calf’s cry broke into a ragged moan. Jax shoved the sled forward. Doc ran beside him, one hand holding the blanket down.

“Left!” Nell shouted.

A Helix deputy stepped from behind a fuel cart with a compact device in both hands. Not a gun. A restraint horn.

It emitted a flat, pulsing tone.

The calf collapsed.

Jax nearly went down with the sled. “No!”

Doc clapped both hands over her ears. The tone made Mara’s teeth ache even from half a promenade away.

Nell shot the deputy in the leg. He dropped, but the device kept sounding.

A second deputy caught the sled hitch with a magnetic clamp. Jax grabbed the calf’s blanket, trying to haul it back by hand, boots skidding.

“Jax, let go!” Doc shouted.

He didn’t.

The sled lurched as Helix winched it toward the service lift. Jax was dragged with it, his bandaged arm tearing open bright red.

Mara came out of the smoke at a run. Quade was behind her. Kip burst from a side passage clutching a regulator under one arm and losing credit chits from a ripped pocket.

Mara saw the calf’s eye open under the blanket. Rolling, terrified, unfocused.

She saw Jax holding on.

She shot the magnetic clamp. It sparked but did not release.

Quade fired once. Not at her. At the deck between her boots, a warning precise enough to be insulting.

“Mara.”

The service lift doors opened behind the sled.

Jax screamed with effort, still pulling.

Mara reached him and slammed the butt of her pistol into his wrist.

His grip broke.

He stared at her, betrayed, as she dragged him backward. A half second later the sled vanished into the lift with the calf and two Helix deputies.

The doors sealed.

Silence fell in pieces.

Then Nell grabbed Mara by the collar and hauled her toward their dock. “Move, unless you want the next lift to be ours.”

They ran.

Kip had the regulator. Doc had the medicine. Jax had blood down his sleeve and no calf. Mara had the sound of Quade’s voice behind her, calm over station alarms.

“Captain Venn,” he said through every speaker Helix had bought. “Do not follow.”

The *Sundown Mercy* cast off six minutes later with a stolen regulator, unpaid docking fees, one blown light panel, and an empty cargo sled.

Jax sat on the cargo bay deck beside the hoof dent, bandage soaking through, staring at the place where the calf had been.

No one knew what to say.

So no one did.

# Chapter 6: Larkspur Well

No one spoke until Mercy’s Rest was smaller than a coin behind them.

The *Sundown Mercy* ran dark, limping on a newly installed regulator that whined like it resented being useful. Jax had fitted it one-handed while Doc stitched the other, and every time she pulled the thread through his skin he stared at the cargo bay floor instead of flinching.

The empty sled sat where the calf had been.

Mara stood beside it longer than she should have. The hoof dent in the deck caught a stripe of amber light. It was deep enough to hold a little spilled coolant.

On the bridge, Kip tracked Quade’s cutter as a bright Helix mark moving outward from the station, not toward any public route but toward the storm static beyond the charts.

Blue Pasture.

Nell leaned against the bulkhead with her arms crossed. “We have the regulator.”

Mara did not look at her. “I noticed.”

“We are low on water, low on fuel, down one cargo fin, and carrying enough warrants to wallpaper a chapel. Just stating inventory.”

“You have a point coming?”

“Several. Pick your favorite.” Nell’s voice stayed flat. “First, Quade has the animal. Second, he has a cutter. Third, whatever he’s taking it to will have guns. Fourth, we are alive by accident and should respect the accident.”

Jax looked up from the deck. His face had gone pale under the grime. “You heard it.”

“I did.”

“And you still want to leave it?”

Nell’s jaw worked. “I want to live long enough to regret something else.”

“That’s your line?”

“My line moves when people start bleeding.”

Jax laughed, once, ugly. “Convenient.”

Mara said, “Enough.”

Jax turned on her. “Don’t.”

The word hit the bay harder than a shout.

Doc, seated on a cargo crate with her bad leg stretched out, watched over folded hands. Kip had come down from the bridge but stayed near the ladder, as if sincerity might require evacuation.

Jax stood carefully. “You hit my hand.”

“To keep it attached.”

“To let them take it.”

“To keep them from taking you too.”

“That what you told yourself?”

Mara could have ordered him quiet. He would have obeyed, eventually, and something between them would have broken in a cleaner shape.

Instead she said, “No.”

That stopped him.

The ship hummed. The regulator whined. Somewhere in the walls, Clementine muttered through a diagnostic loop, mispronouncing a part number.

Mara looked at the ruined crate parts strapped against the bulkhead. The scraped Helix brand faced the wall now. She had turned it there herself and gained nothing by it.

“Larkspur Well,” she said.

Nell’s eyes shifted. Kip stopped fidgeting.

Jax said nothing.

Mara kept her voice level by force. “Free settlement on Tallow’s outer spur. One deep aquifer. Helix claimed the ground under it after the survey changed hands. Settlers cut the company fence. Helix sent marshals.”

“You,” Jax said.

“Yes.”

Doc looked down.

“I escorted six crates,” Mara said. “Manifest said water reclamation pumps. Sealed corporate relief cargo. The foreman asked to inspect them. I told her no.”

Her mouth was dry. She had spoken about shootings with less trouble. About dead engines. About vacuum.

“I signed the transfer. Stood there while they unloaded. Quade was there. Others too. Next morning, Helix had the well. The crates were restraint drones. Not lethal, officially. People disappeared anyway.”

Kip said softly, “Captain.”

Mara did not want the softness. “I quit after.”

Nell gave a humorless breath. “After is popular.”

“Yes.”

Jax’s anger had not gone. It had changed color. “Were you going to tell us?”

“No.”

“If the calf hadn’t been in that crate?”

“No.”

“Because it didn’t matter?”

“Because it did.”

That sat between them a while.

Doc spoke first. “What did you do with the badge?”

Mara almost smiled, but it would have been a bad thing. “Kept it.”

“Of course you did.”

Nell pushed off the bulkhead. “Fine. You were Helix. Quade is Helix. The box is Helix. We are all learning unpleasant history. What now?”

Mara looked at each of them in turn. Not captain to crew, not quite. Debtor to witnesses, maybe.

“I’m going after him,” she said. “You don’t have to. Next rock with a dock, I’ll take a shuttle or a suit if that’s all there is. Ship’s yours if you want it.”

Kip blinked. “That is a terrible offer.”

“It’s the one I’ve got.”

Nell stared at her. “You’d give up the ship?”

“No.” Mara’s voice cracked just enough to shame her. “But I won’t order you into this.”

Jax looked away first.

Doc stood with a wince. “The calf may not survive standard restraint another twelve hours. Not with that sedative load. If Quade is using it as a lure, stress will do what knives don’t.”

“As a lure?” Kip said.

Doc nodded toward the bridge. “Where’s he headed?”

Kip hesitated. “Blue Pasture edge.”

Jax wiped his face with his good hand. “For the herd.”

No one needed Doc to confirm it.

Clementine chimed. “Historical note: Blue Pasture contains recorded migratory anomalies, unverified herd events, and forty-seven advisories against deliberate entry.”

“Helpful,” Kip said.

“Correction: discouraging.”

Nell rubbed both hands over her face. When she dropped them, she looked older. “Helix isn’t taking it home. They’re using it to call the rest.”

Mara nodded.

“That’s not rescue,” Nell said. “That’s baiting a trap.”

“Yes.”

Nell stared at the empty sled. “I grew up on Brackett’s Ring. We had a calf get caught in wire once during a pressure drop. Sounded like that.” She swallowed, annoyed with herself for it. “I still think this is stupid.”

“It is,” Mara said.

“I still want back pay.”

“You’re owed it.”

“I am aware.”

Kip lifted one finger. “For procedural clarity, are we committing armed trespass against a Helix facility in a gravitic storm to rescue livestock that may accidentally tear our ship in half?”

Jax said, “Yes.”

Kip nodded. “Good. I prefer knowing the category of doom.”

Doc reached into her coat pocket and took out a small sealed vial. Pale tissue floated inside.

Jax saw it. “What is that?”

“Identification sample,” she said.

His face hardened.

“I took it before Mercy’s Rest,” Doc said. “Because I told myself knowing what it was would help keep it alive.”

“And?”

“And I am not always comforted by my own explanations.” She put it back in her pocket, not yet destroying it. “Later.”

Mara let that stand. Not everything had to be settled in the first honest minute.

They moved.

Action was easier. It always had been.

Jax and Clementine pulled Quade’s trail from scraps: beacon handshake residue, station departure logs Kip had bribed from a clerk who hated Helix but loved credits, and a faint resonance pattern still lingering in the cargo bay sensors. Clementine misread the calf’s call as three separate pump failures until Jax rewrote a classification field by hand.

“Biological freight,” the system suggested.

Jax typed harder than necessary. “Passenger/livestock emergency.”

“Classification updated,” Clementine said. “Recommended action: reduce noise, dim lights, avoid sudden predation.”

Kip charted the storm band around Blue Pasture. It looked impossible, then worse when he filtered out the impossible parts.

“I can get us near,” he said. “Not pretty. Not quietly. Not twice.”

“Once is fashionable today,” Nell said.

She spread a schematic across the cargo deck: an old Helix harvesting platform, half-remembered from convoy-security days. “If this is the model I think, lure stack sits central. Tether transmitters outside. Guns here, here, and probably here if they paid for upgrades.”

“They paid,” Mara said.

“Then I disable the transmitters, or enough of them to make the rest work harder.”

“In a suit?” Kip asked.

Nell shrugged. “Unless you want to park politely.”

Doc checked her kit, adding anti-sedative, cutters, splints, and three things Mara did not ask about. Jax packed tools with one hand and fury with the other. Mara cleaned her pistol because her hands needed a job.

At the edge of the bridge glass, Blue Pasture grew from static into color.

Not beautiful. Not yet. It was too large for beauty at first: storm-blue cloud, black folds, veins of white lightning crawling through dust. The instruments hissed and corrected themselves and hissed again.

Then the ship shuddered.

Not from the regulator. Not from the engines.

A sound came through the hull, low and far away. Answering.

Kip went very still at the helm.

Jax, on the ladder behind Mara, whispered, “That’s them.”

Another vibration rolled through the *Sundown Mercy*, deep enough to stir the coolant in the hoof dent.

Mara looked into the blue.

Somewhere ahead, the calf was calling.

And something vast had heard.

# Chapter 7: The Lure

The Helix platform hung at the edge of Blue Pasture like scaffolding around a wound.

It had no beacon on public bands, no name painted across its hull, no running lights except the red blink of hazard lamps where tethers stretched into blue storm. It was all hard angles and industrial patience: docking spines, cutting bays, tank clusters, transmitter masts, a central resonance stack rising from its core.

Through the *Sundown Mercy’s* hull came the calf’s cry.

Not loud. Worse than loud. Amplified until it became weather, a pulse that made Mara’s teeth ache and set loose screws trembling in the bulkheads. Every few seconds Blue Pasture answered from far inside itself.

Kip held the ship along the storm band with both hands on manual control and a look on his face that had no room for jokes.

“Ghost transponders,” Mara said.

“Running,” Jax answered from the cargo console.

Clementine chimed. “We are now broadcasting as one medical skiff, two ore drones, a chapel barge, and an unlicensed poultry transport.”

Kip blinked. “Poultry?”

“Historical template availability was limited.”

The platform’s near sensor mast rotated toward them.

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then half the control board lit red.

Kip said, “They bought the chapel barge. They did not buy the chickens.”

“New plan,” Mara said.

“That was the new plan.”

“Older plan, then. Nell.”

Nell was already at the dorsal lock, suit sealed, mag-boots clamped to the deck. “Going outside.”

“Transmitters first.”

“I know.”

“Come back after.”

She looked at Mara through the helmet glass. “That an order or optimism?”

“Yes.”

The lock swallowed her.

Kip rolled the *Sundown Mercy* under a ridge of blue-lit dust as the platform guns woke. The first shot burned past their bow close enough to blank the forward screen white. The ship bucked. Somewhere aft, something expensive fell and broke.

“Define near,” Jax said.

Kip bared his teeth. “We are near.”

“Docking near.”

“Different religion.”

Mara grabbed a handhold as the ship yawed. “Put us on that maintenance lock.”

“Captain, that lock is behind a gun, beside a tether array, and currently doing an impression of a blender.”

“Can you do it?”

Kip’s laugh was breathless. “I hate how often that question works on me.”

Outside, Nell crawled across the hull in mag-boots while the storm painted her suit blue. She fired a tether line to the first transmitter mast, reeled herself toward it, and planted a charge on the base.

“Charge one,” she said over comms.

The mast exploded in a clean flash.

The calf’s cry stumbled, then resumed through another channel.

Nell swore. “Wrong mast.”

“You said first transmitter,” Kip said.

“I said charge one.”

“You implied competence.”

“I will imply my boot up your—”

A platform gun swung toward her.

Mara saw it on the tactical repeater. “Nell, down.”

Nell dropped flat against the mast strut. The gun fired. The beam tore through the space where her torso had been and scorched the *Sundown Mercy’s* already-missing cargo fin mount.

Kip snarled and kicked the ship sideways. “Nobody shoots my passengers but me.”

“You’ve shot passengers?” Jax asked.

“Emotionally.”

The ship slammed against the maintenance lock.

Not docked. Impacted. Jax’s jury-rigged clamps screamed, then caught.

Mara and Jax were already suited, helmets sealed. Doc shoved a med pouch into Jax’s good hand and a reversal injector into Mara’s.

“Don’t improvise with the dosage,” Doc said.

“Wasn’t planning to.”

“I was talking to him.”

Jax looked offended. “Fair.”

The lock cycled with the speed of an old man rising from a chair. Then Mara blew the outer catch with a shaped charge and stepped into Helix air.

The platform corridor beyond was narrow, damp with condensation, and lit by strips of surgical white. It smelled of disinfectant, hot metal, and animal fear. Grated floors ran between walls fitted with restraint rails. Not a hallway. A chute.

Jax saw it too.

“Captain.”

“Keep moving.”

They passed empty racks tagged with claim numbers. A cracked horn fragment lay in a drain grate, translucent and cloudy like the calf’s broken bud. Jax stopped.

Mara caught his arm. “Not now.”

His eyes behind the visor were wet with anger. “How many?”

“Move.”

He moved.

Doc’s voice guided them through comms from the *Sundown Mercy*. “Your signal is close to the central holding chamber. Left at the junction. No, your other left, Jax.”

“I know left.”

“You are turning toward a cutting bay.”

Jax pivoted. “Maybe I don’t know Helix left.”

An alarm began whooping overhead. Quade’s voice followed, calm beneath distortion.

“Mara. You are aboard restricted property.”

She did not answer.

A deputy stepped from a side hatch. Mara shot the gun from his hand. Jax hit him with a tool case because Jax had not been issued restraint training and was not in the mood to learn.

They reached the holding chamber.

The calf hung in the center of it, suspended in a cradle of sonic restraints. Bands of vibrating light pinned its legs and neck without touching. Tubes ran into old injection sites. Its eyes were open but dull. Every amplified cry tore through its body before being dragged up into the resonance stack overhead.

Jax made a sound Mara had never heard from him.

Doc said, sharply, “Focus. Reversal first, then restraints. If you cut the wrong band, the feedback may stop its heart.”

“Which band?” Jax asked.

“I need a panel.”

Mara moved to the control station. Helix interface. Clean. Efficient. Familiar enough to make her skin crawl. She found the sedative feed and jammed Doc’s injector into the port, dumping the reversal compound into the line.

The calf convulsed.

“Too fast?” Jax asked.

“No,” Doc said. “Ugly is not always wrong.”

Jax knelt beside the restraint emitter and opened the casing with shaking hands. Sparks snapped across his glove.

“Jax.”

“I’ve got it.”

A shock threw him backward. He hit the floor hard, gasping.

“You don’t got it,” Mara said.

He rolled onto one elbow. “Give me a second to revise.”

Another platform tremor. Outside, the herd answered. Closer.

Nell’s voice cut in. “Second transmitter down. Correct one this time. Also I am being shot at by architecture.”

Kip: “Working on the architecture.”

Mara left Jax with the calf and ran for the control spine.

The route climbed through a maintenance ladder into the resonance stack’s central chamber. Quade was there, coat off, sleeves rolled, one hand braced on a console as alarms painted his face red. Two technicians worked below him. One was bleeding from the forehead.

He looked up. No surprise. Only disappointment.

“You always did arrive after the hard part started.”

Mara raised her pistol. “Shut it down.”

“I’m trying to prevent a cascade you caused.”

“You built a trap.”

“I built a route.” His hand moved across controls. “Do you hear them out there? That herd crosses currents no instrument can survive. One generation of cores from this migration and Blue Pasture becomes passable. Settlements stop losing children in storm slip. Medical ships arrive on time. But yes, Mara, let’s talk about the animal.”

“Animals.”

“Fine. Animals.” His voice sharpened. “You want clean hands. I want fewer empty docks.”

She stepped closer. “You want ownership.”

“I want civilization.”

A tremor rolled through the chamber. The blue storm flared in the viewport behind him. For one instant Mara saw shapes moving in it, huge and distant, dark bodies threading light.

Quade saw her see them.

“They’re already here,” he said. “If I shut down wrong, the feedback kills your calf and maybe half the herd. Put the gun down.”

She wanted to believe that was a lie. He was better when lying. This sounded worse: true enough to matter.

Jax’s voice broke over comms. “Captain, I got one band off. It knows I’m here.”

Behind Mara, the calf’s amplified cry changed. Less mechanical. More itself.

Quade turned to the controls. “Keep him away from the primary restraint.”

Mara saw the resonance stack. Saw the power coupling. Saw the old Helix logic in every clean line: suffering translated into output.

She fired.

The first shot missed the coupling and blew apart a status screen.

Quade drew.

His round hit her left side like a hammer. Her breath vanished. She dropped to one knee, vision sparking white.

“Mara,” he said, almost angry.

She steadied the pistol with both hands.

“Still,” she breathed, “hearing cargo.”

She fired again.

The coupling shattered.

The resonance stack screamed.

Every light in the chamber blew blue. Quade lunged for the console. The technicians ran. Mara hit the floor as gravity rippled, vanished, returned. Through the torn systems, the calf’s real call rang out — raw, terrified, alive.

Outside, Blue Pasture moved.

The herd arrived not as saviors but as weather with bodies. Vast dark forms swept from the nebula, threaded with blue fire, horns burning like curved moons. Their combined answer struck the platform.

Tether arms snapped. Tanks ruptured. The whole structure groaned, folding around its own failed trap.

Mara crawled toward the ladder, one hand pressed to her bleeding side.

Jax’s voice filled her helmet. “We’ve got it loose. Captain, we’ve got it, but this place is coming apart.”

Quade was on the far side of the chamber, half-pinned by a fallen support, reaching not for Mara but for the bleeding technician trapped below.

For one second, their eyes met through smoke and blue light.

Then the bulkhead between them began to close.

Mara turned away.

“Back to the ship,” she said. “All of you. Now.”

# Chapter 8: Blue Pasture

The platform came apart like something ashamed of its own bones.

Bulkheads buckled. Tether cables snapped loose and whipped through vacuum outside the viewports, glowing blue where the herd’s resonance touched them. Somewhere below, tanks ruptured in slow bright flowers. Alarms layered over one another until they became one continuous animal howl.

Mara stumbled down the ladder from the control spine with one hand pressed to her side.

Her glove came away dark.

“Captain?” Jax’s voice crackled.

“Moving.”

“Define moving.”

“Badly.”

“That’s still moving.”

She found them two corridors from the holding chamber. Jax had one arm around the calf’s neck, not pulling so much as leaning with it. Doc staggered on the other side, injector kit clipped to her belt, face gray with effort. The calf was on its feet, all six legs trembling. Its cracked horn bud pulsed weakly, but its eyes were clear now.

Clear and fixed toward the outer dark.

The corridor pitched. Gravity went light. The calf floated an inch, panicked, struck the deck again when weight returned. Jax nearly went under it.

Mara grabbed his harness and hauled him upright. Pain flashed white across her ribs.

Jax saw the blood. “You’re hit.”

“Later.”

“I hate later.”

“Use it anyway.”

Doc caught Mara’s look and shook her head once. Not fatal yet. Not good either.

Behind them, a hatch slammed shut under emergency protocol. Through its small reinforced window, smoke filled the passage Mara had just left. A figure moved beyond it: Quade, coat torn, dragging a wounded deputy or technician by the back of their suit.

For a second he looked through the window.

No speech. No threat. No conversion.

Just Quade, still alive, still himself, saving someone on his side while the trap he had defended died around him.

Then smoke swallowed the glass.

“Captain,” Kip shouted over comms, “I am docked in the sense that a tick is docked. Please conclude your tourism.”

Nell’s voice followed, breathless. “Exterior guns are quiet. Not dead. Quiet. Difference matters.”

Clementine chimed beneath them both. “Structural integrity of adjacent platform is declining from poor to anecdotal.”

Mara pointed down the corridor. “Go.”

They went.

The platform had been built like a slaughterhouse pretending to be a laboratory. Narrow rails guided bodies toward chambers. Doors opened only one direction. Warning signs used words like sample, yield, biological asset. The calf balked at every threshold, recognizing shapes even when sedative and fear had blurred the details.

Jax lowered his voice. “Come on, kid. Not far. Not far.”

It did not understand the words. Maybe it understood his pitch. Maybe it was simply too exhausted to fight him.

At the maintenance lock, the *Sundown Mercy* waited with her hull pressed crooked against the platform, clamps shrieking. Blue light crawled over her patched plates. Kip held her there with intermittent thrust bursts that slammed everyone sideways.

Nell stood inside the open lock, helmet visor cracked along one edge, pistol in hand and powered down. She looked at the calf, then at Mara’s wound, then at Doc.

“Move faster,” she said, because saying anything softer would have embarrassed her.

The calf reached the threshold and stopped.

Beyond the lock, through the open outer ramp and the ship’s docking field, Blue Pasture filled the universe. Not a place now. A presence. The herd moved through it in enormous arcs, dark bodies veined with cold fire. Their horns shone blue-white, curved and branching in ways Mara’s eyes could not hold steady. Each movement bent the storm around them.

The calf lifted its head.

For the first time since the crate, it did not look for a corner.

A call rolled out of it, small against the vast answer but whole. The deck thrummed. Mara felt it in the wound, in her teeth, in the old scar across her knuckles.

Jax swallowed. “We have to get it aboard.”

Doc looked past him at the herd. “No.”

He turned on her, stricken. “What?”

“We were never taking it with us.”

The calf stepped toward the ramp.

Jax’s good hand went to the last Helix tag clamped at the base of its neck. He stared at it as if only now seeing the thing properly. Then he took the cutter from his belt.

His hand shook.

Mara reached over and steadied his wrist.

Together they burned the tag off.

It fell to the deck with a small, stupid clink.

Doc took a sealed vial from her coat: the tissue sample, pale and perfect in its little tube. She held it for one heartbeat too long. Then she dropped it under her boot and crushed it until glass and sample smeared into nothing.

Nell saw, and said nothing.

The calf turned its head. One dark eye regarded Mara, or passed over her, or saw the vibration of the ship and the people inside it. Its cracked horn bud touched her palm.

Mara did not receive absolution. Nothing so cheap happened.

It was warm. That was all.

She found the old hum in her throat. Badly. Barely. A work rhythm from a moon she had escaped and never quite left.

Hm. Hm-hmm. Hm. Hm-hmm.

The calf breathed once against her hand.

Then it leapt.

Awkwardly, impossibly, all six legs folding beneath it as it passed through the docking field and into open vacuum. For one sick instant it looked like a thing thrown away.

Then the herd turned.

One of the adults swept close, large enough to eclipse the platform. Its hide was not merely lit but patterned, flecks and lines shifting beneath the surface like a chart no human had earned. The calf tumbled toward it. A curve of horn-light caught the small body, steadied it, drew it into motion.

Jax made a sound that was almost grief and almost laughter.

“Ramp!” Kip yelled. “Now would be religiously appropriate!”

Nell hit the control. The ramp began to close. The platform bucked. The *Sundown Mercy’s* clamps tore free before the seal finished cycling.

Atmosphere screamed. Emergency fields snapped on.

Mara hit the deck hard beside Jax. Doc landed on top of both of them and cursed with impressive medical precision. Nell slammed into the inner hatch and stayed standing through sheer spite.

Kip burned the engines.

The herd moved.

Not for them. Mara understood that immediately. The starhorns did not bless the *Sundown Mercy*, did not thank it, did not rescue it out of gratitude. They were leaving. Their bodies aligned through Blue Pasture, horns brightening, calls overlapping until the nebula itself seemed to open around them.

A current formed: blue-white, vast, unstable.

Kip saw it. “Absolutely not.”

The failing regulator screamed.

Behind them, Helix reinforcements flashed at the edge of sensors. The platform tore loose from its remaining tethers and began to spin.

Mara hauled herself up by the back of the pilot chair, leaving blood on the vinyl. “Rabbit.”

“I said absolutely not.”

“Can you ride the edge?”

“I hate everyone who has ever taught you that question.”

The *Sundown Mercy* plunged after the herd.

The current caught them like a flood catches a fence post. Panels blew. The lights died and came back blue. Clementine’s voice dissolved into static, then returned with, “Livestock transit warning: reduce noise, dim lights, avoid sudden predation.”

Kip laughed, screamed, and maybe prayed. Jax clutched the deck grate with one hand. Nell braced herself across the hatch. Doc held pressure against Mara’s side and shouted something about not dying before she was finished being angry.

Outside, Blue Pasture stretched into impossible lines.

Then snapped.

The *Sundown Mercy* dropped into clear space.

Silence hit first.

Real silence, except for alarms, ragged breathing, and the offended whine of the regulator giving up at last.

On the rear screen, Blue Pasture glowed distant and unreachable. The platform was gone from sight. The Helix ships were gone too, or elsewhere, or merely tomorrow’s problem.

The herd was already vanishing into the nebula, immense bodies fading to dark, then to pattern, then to nothing. The calf disappeared among them completely.

Jax sat on the cargo bay floor later, after Doc had sealed Mara’s wound and forbidden everyone from bleeding recreationally. He touched the hoof dent once and did not try to hammer it flat.

Nell updated her back-pay ledger with a scorched stylus. “I’m adding hazard rates.”

“Fair,” Mara said from a crate, pale and bandaged.

“Double.”

“Ambitious.”

“Alive is ambitious.”

Kip appeared in the hatch holding the ruined coffee heater. “We suffered a casualty.”

Doc did not look up from washing blood off her hands. “Good. Bury it quietly.”

Clementine chimed. “Incoming freight offer. Sealed cargo. Expedited rate. Broker notes: no questions necessary.”

Everyone went still in the small, battered bay.

Mara looked at the broken crate panels strapped against the wall. At the place where the calf had hidden. At Jax, who was not smiling at her yet. At Nell’s ledger, Doc’s crushed vial ground into her boot sole, Kip’s ridiculous ruined heater.

She reached into her coat and pulled out the old Helix badge.

For years it had waited for ceremony. Fire, maybe. A dramatic throw into a star. Something clean.

The portside wall panel rattled again.

Mara wedged the badge under the panel seam and shoved until the rattling stopped.

Then she stood, slowly.

“Jax,” she said.

He looked up.

“Bring the cutter.”

His expression changed by a little. Not forgiveness. Something more useful.

“Planning to open it?” he asked.

Mara glanced once toward the empty place where crate three had sat.

“Before we lift,” she said.

The *Sundown Mercy* turned toward the next star trail, poorer than before, wanted by serious people, patched with an old badge and one better habit.

[Analysis]

Chapter 6 is the emotional hinge of the story, and the model executes it with considerable skill. The chapter's central task—Mara's confession about Larkspur Well—is handled with restraint and precision. The confession itself is delivered in short, declarative sentences that feel earned rather than performed: "I signed the transfer. Stood there while they unloaded." The model resists the temptation to make this a cathartic speech, keeping Mara's voice controlled even as the content is damning.

The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. The exchange between Jax and Mara after the calf's capture is particularly well-crafted. "Were you going to tell us?" / "No." / "If the calf hadn't been in that crate?" / "No." / "Because it didn't matter?" / "Because it did." This is economical, emotionally precise, and reveals character through compression rather than expansion. The rhythm of short exchanges throughout the chapter—Nell's inventory speech, Kip's "category of doom" line—feels authentic to the established voices.

Nell's arc in this chapter is handled well. Her admission about the calf on Brackett's Ring ("I still think this is stupid" / "It is") honors her character profile: she doesn't become soft, she just admits what she heard. This is exactly the kind of contradiction the plan called for.

Doc's vial moment is effective. The detail of her taking a sample and then not yet destroying it—"Later"—is honest about the complexity of her character without forcing resolution. Mara's response ("Not everything had to be settled in the first honest minute") is one of the chapter's better lines.

Kip's voice is consistent and used sparingly enough to land. "I prefer knowing the category of doom" is the right kind of dry humor for the moment—it deflates tension without undercutting it.

Clementine's appearances are well-calibrated. "Recommended action: reduce noise, dim lights, avoid sudden predation" is genuinely funny in context and consistent with her character as described. Her misclassification of the calf's resonance as pump failures, corrected by Jax's manual override, is a small but effective piece of world-building.

The chapter's ending—the answering vibration from Blue Pasture—is earned. The buildup through the planning sequence gives it weight, and the final image ("deep enough to stir the coolant in the hoof dent") is a good callback to the physical detail of the hoof dent established earlier. This is the kind of concrete, specific detail that elevates the prose.

Where the chapter is slightly weaker: the transition from confession to action ("They moved. Action was easier. It always had been.") is a bit too neat as a summary statement—it tells us something the chapter has already shown. The planning sequence, while necessary, is the least vivid section; the schematic-spreading and kit-checking feel slightly procedural compared to the emotional intensity of the confession scene.

The line "Not captain to crew, not quite. Debtor to witnesses, maybe" is one of the few moments where the prose reaches for something slightly more literary than the chapter's general register, but it lands well enough not to feel forced.

The chapter follows its plan closely: Mara confesses Larkspur Well, the crew chooses to stay for varied and imperfect reasons, Clementine and Jax track Quade's route, the plan is assembled, and Blue Pasture appears with the answering herd. The plan's note that "no one absolves her" and "Jax asks if she would have told them if the calf had not been taken" are both honored faithfully.

One minor issue: the chapter plan specified that Jax "stays last, not forgiving Mara, but unwilling to let the calf die in a box." The chapter doesn't quite give Jax a distinct final beat of choosing to stay—his participation in the planning sequence implies it, but the explicit moment of his decision is somewhat elided. This is a small gap.

Overall, this is a strong chapter that executes its emotional and narrative functions with discipline, restraint, and genuine craft.

Chapter 2 of this space western demonstrates considerable craft and largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me examine it systematically.

STRENGTHS:

The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. Quade's voice is precisely calibrated — controlled, practical, and genuinely threatening without melodrama. Lines like "You never did like saying the thing until it was too late" carry real weight because they feel earned by character rather than constructed for effect. Mara's responses are terse and revealing: "That wasn't my question" appears twice, and both times it does real work, showing her habit of pressing past official language to uncomfortable truth. The exchange about "livestock gets feed" / "It is livestock" / "Livestock gets feed" is a small masterpiece of compressed moral argument.

The chapter follows its plan faithfully. The beacon disabling, Quade's interception of the broker channel, the offer and its terms, the "Deputy Venn" correction, the practical argument about navigation cores, the six-hour deadline — all present and executed with discipline. The chapter doesn't overreach or underdeliver.

Character consistency is strong throughout. Jax's guilt manifests in small physical gestures (reaching toward the calf, then stopping himself). Nell's pragmatism is rendered through her arithmetic thinking and thumb near the holster. Doc's scientific fascination is held in check but visible in her scanner's continued whisper. Kip's nervous humor over the earpiece ("That's... that's a lot of vanish") is perfectly calibrated. Clementine's final line about "insufficient fuel reserves for prolonged ethical uncertainty" is the chapter's best joke — genuinely funny, in-character, and not trying too hard.

The calf's presence is handled with restraint. It drinks too fast and coughs. It flinches at its own reflection. These are animal behaviors, not symbolic gestures, and they do the emotional work without sentimentality. "The sound was wet, miserable, alive" is a good line — three words that earn their place.

Mara's interiority is rendered through action and observation rather than exposition. "That irritated her. More than it should have" is efficient and revealing. The moment she notices the calf's jaw filaments quivering toward Jax's voice, followed by "Mara hated that she noticed," is the chapter's emotional core — small, precise, and true to her character.

WEAKNESSES:

The chapter occasionally reaches for effect in ways that don't quite land. "All the old debts Mara had taught herself not to count" is slightly overwritten — the metaphor of debt has been literal throughout (fuel liens, back pay) and this abstraction muddies rather than deepens. Similarly, "a hand placed gently on an old bruise" for Quade's "Deputy Venn" moment is a competent metaphor but not a surprising one.

The Clementine lines are mostly well-deployed, but "current fuel reserves are insufficient for prolonged ethical uncertainty" is perhaps a touch too clever — it risks becoming the kind of quip the plan explicitly warned against. It works, but barely.

The chapter's ending — "show me the Badlands" — is effective but slightly predictable given the plan's structure. The reader can see the chapter's destination from early on, which reduces tension somewhat. This is partly a structural inevitability, but the chapter could have made the decision feel more costly or surprising.

Doc's "Harvest kills them" / Quade's response is the chapter's most on-the-nose moment. The exchange is necessary but feels slightly like thesis-statement dialogue compared to the subtler work elsewhere.

The phrase "Helix-made and expensive. The sort of tracker that did not ask whether you wanted to be found" is a minor purple moment — the personification of the tracker is a bit strained.

Overall, this is accomplished work: disciplined, character-driven, atmospherically consistent, and emotionally honest without being manipulative. The plan is followed closely and the chapter earns its place in the larger story.

The description is specific and alien without being overwrought: "split and dark and too soft-looking," the sideways-clicking eyelid, the jaw filaments. The smell detail (hot metal, wet stone, fear) is sensory and grounded.

The gravity lurch when the calf vocalizes is a smart choice — it makes the creature immediately dangerous rather than pitiable, which the plan specifically called for.

"The ship always sounded like it was thinking about dying and deciding, with some irritation, to continue" — this is the most self-consciously literary line in the chapter, and it's slightly too pleased with itself. "Like rain striking hot stone in a place that had forgotten weather" — this is a reach. The mineral coldness comparison is fine, but "a place that had forgotten weather" is the kind of ornamental clause that adds nothing concrete. It's the chapter's clearest instance of forced poetry.

The chapter follows the plan very faithfully, almost to a fault. The calf's capture via sonic restraint, Jax being dragged and then having his grip broken by Mara herself, the empty cargo bay at the end — these are all executed with appropriate restraint. The final image of Jax sitting beside the hoof dent is genuinely affecting precisely because the prose doesn't oversell it.

"A woman with a missing hand sold oxygen cartridges from a shrine booth plastered with saints and rate charts" is a single sentence that does real world-building work without stopping the narrative. The Doma Vetch exchange is dryly funny and moves quickly without feeling like a detour.

The calf's collapse under the sonic restraint and Jax's refusal to let go are emotionally effective. The moment where Mara breaks Jax's grip herself — choosing the crew's survival over the calf — is the chapter's moral crux, and it lands. It's a genuinely hard choice rendered without melodrama.

Clementine's opening line ("Please settle all outstanding invoices before engaging in commerce, violence, or laundry") is exactly the right register: deadpan, useful for tone, not trying too hard.

WEAKNESSES:

The chapter occasionally leans on slightly familiar Western/noir rhythms. The sequence of events — Nell shoots the light, the sonic restraint device, Nell shoots the deputy, the magnetic clamp, Jax being dragged — requires careful tracking and occasionally the prose rushes past clarity in favor of momentum.

The exchange "How many herds make you satisfied?" / "That is not an answer." / "Neither was 'studied.'" is sharp.

Character differentiation is solid. Nell's pragmatism, Jax's moral urgency, Doc's clinical detachment masking feeling, Kip's nervous humor — these are distinct voices that remain consistent.

The pacing across eight chapters is generally well-managed. The escalation from discovery to chase to confrontation to release follows a satisfying arc.

WEAKNESSES:

The metaphors are frequent and occasionally miss. "The ship always sounded like it was thinking about dying and deciding, with some irritation, to continue" is good. But some reach too far: "carrying a frightened animal, a dead beacon, and all the old debts Mara had taught herself not to count" is the kind of line that sounds profound but is actually just listing things. "The platform came apart like something ashamed of its own bones" is trying too hard. These occur regularly enough to be a pattern.

The ending is somewhat rushed. Eight chapters of careful buildup, and the release of the calf happens in a few paragraphs. The emotional payoff — "It was warm. That was all." — is deliberately understated, which is a valid choice, but the herd's arrival and the escape feel compressed compared to the careful attention paid to earlier scenes.

The "unearned transformation" concern applies somewhat to Nell. Her shift from "ugly doesn't change math" to participating in the rescue is handled through the Brackett's Ring calf memory, which is efficient but slightly schematic — a single anecdote doing heavy lifting.

Some of the poetic riffing doesn't land: "Debtor to witnesses, maybe" is the kind of phrase that sounds meaningful but dissolves under examination. "Practicality has kept you breathing" / "So has distrust" is good. But there are enough near-misses that the piece occasionally feels like it's performing depth rather than achieving it.

The starhorn as a concept is well-deployed — the gravity effects, the migration, the horn-derived navigation cores — but the herd's arrival in the final chapters is described in ways that strain credibility (the calf being "caught" by a horn-light curve). The badge-under-the-panel ending is clever and appropriately unsentimental. The final line — "poorer than before, wanted by serious people, patched with an old badge and one better habit" — is the piece's best closing sentence.

OVERALL: This is skilled, confident genre writing with genuine literary ambition. The flaws are real but not fatal. The piece succeeds more than it fails, and its failures are mostly of overreach rather than incompetence.

WELL-EARNED LIGHTNESS OR DARKNESS: The tonal balance is one of the chapter's strengths. Kip's humor is deployed at moments of genuine tension and then withdrawn at the right time ("The humor was gone"). The coffee heater joke at the end is perfectly placed — it releases tension without undercutting the damage. The darkness (Doc's shoulder, Jax's blood, the calf trembling) is not softened.

CHARACTERS CONSISTENT WITH PROFILE: All characters behave in ways consistent with their profiles. Mara's hum is exactly the kind of thing her profile describes — a childhood reflex she's ashamed of. Nell's reluctant compliance, Jax's guilt-proximity to the calf, Kip's banter-as-fear-management, Doc's quiet attunement — all track precisely.

FOLLOWED CHAPTER PLAN: The chapter follows the plan closely and faithfully. The Badlands sequence, Nell's gun battery frightening the calf, the hum, the natural slip lane, the escape, the damage inventory, and the ironic destination of Mercy's Rest are all present. The plan's note that "the calf is not a convenient miracle; it is making everything worse" is honored — the escape costs real damage.

FAITHFUL TO WRITING PROMPT: The chapter is part of a larger story responding to the prompt. It advances that story faithfully, with the calf's presence continuing to drive both plot and character development.

OVERALL: This is a well-crafted chapter that executes its plan with skill, restraint, and genuine emotional intelligence. Its weaknesses are minor: a slightly rushed middle action sequence, one or two lines of dialogue that are slightly too polished, and the asteroids-as-jaws image being conventional. But these are small complaints against a chapter that consistently earns its effects.

final_raw_judges_texts:
[Analysis]

This is an ambitious, largely successful space western that demonstrates genuine craft across its eight chapters. Let me assess it carefully.

STRENGTHS:

The world-building is economical and effective. The Sundown Mercy feels lived-in through specific, concrete details: the gravity plate pulling heavy on the left knee, the DO NOT TRUST HER warning on the cargo lift, the portside gravity plate Jax keeps promising will hold another month. The station Mercy's Rest is rendered in a single paragraph that does real work. The Helix corporation as antagonist is established through accumulation rather than exposition.

The dialogue is genuinely strong. Clementine's ship-assist voice is a consistent comic device that earns its laughs without becoming tiresome. The banter between crew members feels natural and character-revealing. Quade's dialogue is particularly well-handled: he's given real arguments, not cartoon villainy. The exchange "How many herds make you satisfied?" / "That is not an answer." / "Neither was 'studied.'" is sharp.

The Larkspur Well backstory is handled with restraint. Mara's complicity is revealed gradually, not dumped, and it recontextualizes her hesitations throughout the earlier chapters. This is the piece's most sophisticated structural move.

Character differentiation is solid. Nell's pragmatism, Jax's moral urgency, Doc's clinical detachment masking feeling, Kip's nervous humor — these are distinct voices that remain consistent.

The pacing across eight chapters is generally well-managed. The escalation from discovery to chase to confrontation to release follows a satisfying arc.

WEAKNESSES:

The metaphors are frequent and occasionally miss. "The ship always sounded like it was thinking about dying and deciding, with some irritation, to continue" is good. But some reach too far: "carrying a frightened animal, a dead beacon, and all the old debts Mara had taught herself not to count" is the kind of line that sounds profound but is actually just listing things. "The platform came apart like something ashamed of its own bones" is trying too hard. These occur regularly enough to be a pattern.

The ending is somewhat rushed. Eight chapters of careful buildup, and the release of the calf happens in a few paragraphs. The emotional payoff — "It was warm. That was all." — is deliberately understated, which is a valid choice, but the herd's arrival and the escape feel compressed compared to the careful attention paid to earlier scenes.

Quade is the most interesting character after Mara, but his final appearance (saving someone through the smoke-filled window) is a gesture toward complexity that the story hasn't quite earned. It's a good instinct but feels inserted rather than developed.

The "unearned transformation" concern applies somewhat to Nell. Her shift from "ugly doesn't change math" to participating in the rescue is handled through the Brackett's Ring calf memory, which is efficient but slightly schematic — a single anecdote doing heavy lifting.

Some of the poetic riffing doesn't land: "Debtor to witnesses, maybe" is the kind of phrase that sounds meaningful but dissolves under examination. "Practicality has kept you breathing" / "So has distrust" is good. But there are enough near-misses that the piece occasionally feels like it's performing depth rather than achieving it.

The starhorn as a concept is well-deployed — the gravity effects, the migration, the horn-derived navigation cores — but the herd's arrival in the final chapters is described in ways that strain credibility (the calf being "caught" by a horn-light curve). The piece wisely avoids over-explaining the biology, but the rescue moment tips into fantasy convenience.

The badge-under-the-panel ending is clever and appropriately unsentimental. The final line — "poorer than before, wanted by serious people, patched with an old badge and one better habit" — is the piece's best closing sentence.

OVERALL: This is skilled, confident genre writing with genuine literary ambition. The flaws are real but not fatal. The piece succeeds more than it fails, and its failures are mostly of overreach rather than incompetence.
