# Chapter 3: First Broth Needs More Salt

I boiled the knife first.

Not because I believed boiling would fix what we were about to do, but because there are rituals people accept when they have run out of certainty. Clean knife. Clean board. Clean hands. Apron tied tight enough to feel like armor.

The wrapped piece of Bloomer sat on my prep table beside the last onion.

No one looked at the onion. Everyone looked at the meat.

“Move back,” I said.

No one moved.

“Fine. Breathe on it. That’ll help.”

Nessa took Ada by the shoulders and steered her toward the dining room. Ada twisted in her grip.

“I want to see.”

“You want many things,” Nessa said. “Most of them are bad for civilization.”

“It’s not civilization if I can’t see.”

“It is exactly civilization if you can’t.”

The door swung shut on Ada’s protest. Good. I did not want her watching me be afraid.

Elsie arranged cracked spectacles on her nose and opened three old birdwatching journals across the side counter. None of them were about cooking, poison, or whatever category the Bloomer occupied, but she liked references nearby. Tuck stood at the sink washing his hands for the fourth time. Bea stayed between the table and the back door, rifle slung but ready.

Lio leaned in the threshold.

“Out,” I said.

“I’m observing.”

“No, Elsie observes. You haunt.”

“I want to know what kills us.”

“If this kills us, I’ll write you a note.”

He did not leave. Of course he didn’t.

I unwrapped the cloth.

The piece was firm, pale, almost pretty in the way raw scallop was pretty if you forgot where it came from. Blue-gray veins crossed the flesh. The fat had hardened in pearly seams. Along one edge, fire had browned the surface. That edge smelled best, which felt indecent.

Tuck swallowed. “Cut away the dark vein.”

“Which dark vein?”

“All of them?”

Elsie clicked her tongue. “Blue staining in fungi can indicate psilocybin, bruising, oxidation, or death. In this case, death is already established.”

“Thank you,” Bea said. “Helpful.”

“We discard heavily veined tissue,” Elsie said, as if she had always meant that.

I cut. The knife went through with resistance, more mushroom than meat, then caught on a band of tendonlike fiber. Not tendon. Not exactly. I refused to invent a name. Names made things stay.

The first water went into the pot with no onion, no herbs, no mercy. When it boiled, gray foam gathered at the surface.

“Skim,” Elsie said.

“I know how to boil things.”

“Boil harder.”

“I also know how to hate advice.”

We boiled it until the kitchen windows sweated and the smell changed from frighteningly good to frighteningly wrong: damp wool, cellar wall, old coins. I dumped the water into a lidded bucket for burning outside. Bea carried it away with both arms straight, as if it might whisper to her.

Second water. Salt. A twist of dried thyme that had more stem than leaf. Charcoal tied in cheesecloth. Then the onion.

I took it from the board and peeled away the soft brown outer skin. The inside was still good, sharp and white. My throat tightened. I had saved that onion through three ration meetings, two fevers, and one morning when I considered eating it raw in the pantry where no one could see.

Now I sliced it thin enough to read lies through and dropped it into monster water.

“Waste,” Lio said.

I turned with the knife still in my hand. “Say that again.”

He looked at the blade. Then at me. “I said waste.”

“It is my onion.”

“It was everyone’s onion.”

“Then everyone can enjoy being furious with me later.”

The pot simmered.

That is too gentle a word for what happened. It warmed. It deepened. The broth went from cloudy gray to amber-brown, and the fat rose in small golden coins. The smell filled the kitchen, then the hall, then the house. Doors opened. Footsteps gathered. People invented reasons to pass by.

Old Jon came in holding a mug. “If this is how we die, I’d like to say I was against it after the first bowl.”

“Out,” Bea said.

“History needs witnesses.”

“History can stand in the dining room.”

Tuck gave a sudden wet laugh, then looked ashamed.

I stirred. My stomach cramped and cramped again. Hunger, yes, but also want. Specific want. Not for food in general. For that.

That was when I became truly afraid.

Elsie held out a thimble.

“No,” Bea said.

“Yes,” I said.

“No.”

“Bea.”

Her face had gone flat, which meant terror. She came close enough that only I could hear her.

“You do not have to be first because they expect it.”

“I have to be first because it’s my pot.”

“That is stupid.”

“Yes.”

“Mara.”

“If it kills me, don’t let Jon make a speech.”

Her mouth tightened. “I hate you.”

“No, you don’t.”

“I’m considering it.”

I took the thimble.

Everyone watched my mouth. I hated them for it.

“Stop looking at my mouth.”

No one stopped.

I blew on the broth once, impatiently, and swallowed.

It burned my tongue.

“Damn it.”

Bea flinched. “What?”

“It’s hot.”

“For God’s sake, Mara.”

At first there was only pain and salt. Then the taste opened.

I have tried to write it plainly. I have failed every time.

It tasted like chicken stock after a long day. Like mushrooms fried until their edges crisped. Like the browned bottom of a roasting pan scraped up with wine we no longer had. Like venison, chestnuts, rain on warm dirt, and something darkly sweet that made my jaw ache. It was rich enough to feel kind.

It was delicious.

I wanted the whole pot.

That thought was so ugly I set the thimble down carefully, because if I threw it, everyone would know.

“Well?” Elsie asked.

I looked into the pot. Golden fat trembled on top.

“Needs more salt,” I said.

For a heartbeat nobody breathed.

Then Tuck laughed. Too loud, almost a sob. Old Jon, banished to the hall, wheezed. Someone in the dining room began crying. Bea put both hands over her face.

Lio left.

I added salt because it did need it.

Then we waited.

Elsie inspected my eyes, gums, tongue, pulse, and temper. “Tongue is gray.”

“I burned it.”

“Still gray.”

“Write down both if it makes you happy.”

“It does.”

No one else tasted until morning. That was Bea’s rule, and she held it with rifle and glare. The pot cooled on the stove under a lid weighted with a brick. I sat beside it wrapped in the curtain-quilt, sweating and chilled by turns because fear is unimaginative.

Bea sat on the floor across from me.

“You should sleep,” I said.

“You first.”

“I may die.”

“Then I’ll wake you.”

“That’s not how dying works.”

“I’m expanding my skill set.”

For a while we listened to the house. Wind in the eaves. Ada coughing below. Jon murmuring in his sleep. Somewhere outside, the burn barrel settled with a metallic ping.

Bea reached over and took my wrist. Two fingers to my pulse. Her thumb brushed the old comma-shaped burn there.

“You wanted it to be good,” she said.

I closed my eyes.

“Yes.”

Her fingers stilled.

“Before I tasted it,” I said. “When I smelled it. I wanted it. I thought about thyme.”

Bea said nothing.

“That’s the worst thing I’ve ever told you.”

“No,” she said after a moment. “But it’s on the list.”

I laughed once, badly. She did not let go.

Near dawn I dreamed of snow over roots. Not a voice. Not words. Just a dark pressure under the ground, chewing slowly.

When I woke, I was not dead.

My tongue hurt. My belly did not. My head was clear in a way it had not been for weeks. Every smell in the kitchen had edges: ash, damp wool, old grease, Bea’s coffee substitute, the broth under its brick-heavy lid.

I was ravenous.

Elsie wrote that down as if ravenous were a symptom and not the condition of the world.

We served the first round in spoonfuls.

Children first, though Nessa argued about whether poison respected age. Ada sniffed hers, suspicious.

“It smells like ham.”

“It is not ham,” I said.

“It smells like ham’s weird cousin.”

“Drink.”

She did. Her eyes widened. “Monster gravy.”

“No.”

“Monster gravy.”

“Ada.”

But the name had already jumped bowls.

Some refused. Lio stood outside in the snow rather than watch. Others took their spoonful and cried before swallowing. Tuck held his in both hands like communion and whispered, “I’m sorry,” though I did not know to whom.

By noon, no one had died.

By evening, people had half-bowls. Thin half-bowls, but warm. The dining room filled with the small, obscene sounds of appetite: spoons scraping, breath easing, someone licking a thumb and pretending not to.

No one asked for seconds aloud. They held out their bowls and looked ashamed.

I gave what I could.

That night, after the pot was washed and the brick scrubbed and Bea finally slept with one hand still on my sleeve, I opened my notebook.

My hand hovered.

Then I wrote:

First broth. Boil twice. Burn sacs. Use charcoal. More salt than you think. Do not let children name things.

Under that, smaller:

It was good.

I stared at those three words until the stove went low.

Then, because I am a coward, I crossed them out.

# Chapter 4: Yard Meat

By the third Bloomer, we had vocabulary.

That shames me more than the eating, some days. Hunger invents quickly. So does guilt. We could not stand at the table saying arm, rib, thigh, God help us, not when Ada was asking for the crispy piece and Tuck was turning gray at the sink. So we made softer words.

Cap. Shelf. Joint. Flank.

Yard meat, if we were tired.

“Corpse,” Lio said at supper, because he loved accuracy when it hurt.

Nessa pointed her spoon at him. “The children are eating.”

“The children have eyes.”

“The children also have manners, which is more than can be said for some hunters.”

Ada, mouth full, said, “Corpse tastes better than squirrel.”

“Ada,” I said.

“What? It does.”

It did.

That was the problem.

The second Bloomer came two days after the first, drawn or stumbling or unlucky into the north snare. It had too many elbows and no face worth arguing about. Bea put it down with two shots. Tuck butchered it in silence, saving only what did not twitch under salt. Elsie hovered with jars and cracked spectacles, saying “probably” until Bea told her the next probably would go in the burn barrel.

By the third, we had procedure.

Masks before yard. Gloves tied at the wrist. Sacs cut out whole and burned. Gills discarded. Blue veins trimmed unless we were too hungry, which meant trimmed less carefully than Elsie liked and more carefully than Lio trusted. First water dumped in the ash pit. Second water salted. No tasting alone.

Nessa wrote that last rule on a board and underlined it twice.

No tasting alone.

I knew whose rule it was, though she pretended it was communal.

The Lantern House changed around the food. That was the only honest way to say it. Not healed. Changed.

Smokehouse hooks that had held nothing but empty air now carried gray strips drying over applewood chair legs. The dining room candles burned with old beeswax mixed with rendered Bloomer fat and gave off a warm, garlicky smell that made Jon say grace twice by accident. Tuck labeled jars in block letters: BROTH, FAT, STEW, MAYBE, DO NOT TRUST. Elsie confiscated the MAYBE jar and then brought it back, labeled PROBABLY SAFE, which did not improve morale.

We fried caps in a skillet blackened from better years. They squeaked between the teeth. Children loved them. Adults pretended not to.

I pounded tough flank with a rolling pin until my shoulders ached, mixed it with meal dust and salt, and shaped patties no one wanted to call patties.

“Do not say burger,” I told Jon.

“I was not going to.”

“You were inhaling like a man about to say burger.”

He closed his mouth.

Ada said, “Monster burger,” and Nessa docked her half a button, which was not a recognized currency except among children and Old Jon when losing.

The food made us stronger. There was no poetry in it. People stood straighter because their bodies had fuel. Bea’s hands stopped shaking after night watch. Fenn’s wound began to close. Old Jon sang while washing bowls and only forgot half the words. Ada ran in the hall until Nessa threatened to sew her to a chair.

It also made us meaner in small ways.

The first theft was from the cooling pot. Not much. A ladle, maybe two. Enough that I noticed before breakfast and stood in the kitchen with the lid in my hand, feeling the old red anger climb my throat.

“No one leaves,” I said.

Everyone looked at everyone else. That was how communities died: not all at once, but by glances.

Nessa searched bowls. Bea searched hands. I searched faces and hated myself for recognizing hunger as motive instead of crime.

It was Fenn’s nephew, Tom, fourteen and all wrists. He had taken broth for Fenn after hearing him cry in his sleep. When he confessed, he looked ready to be beaten.

I wanted to beat him. That is the ugly truth. Not for theft. For ruining the count.

Instead I made him scrub the pot, then gave Fenn broth openly and wrote it down. Nessa objected until I asked whether she wanted fairness or numbers. She said, “Both,” because Nessa had never lacked ambition.

The second trouble was guards’ portions. Someone claimed Bea’s bowl had more meat. It did, because she had been on the wall twelve hours and because I loved her. Only one of those reasons I would admit.

“Switch with me,” Bea said immediately.

“No,” I said.

“Mara.”

“No. You need the calories.”

“So does everyone.”

“You get thicker stew when you stand between everyone and the things trying to eat us. This is not corruption. This is arithmetic.”

Lio laughed from the doorway. “Listen to the queen of arithmetic.”

“You want a throne, Marr? It’s by the sink.”

He did not eat with us then. Not openly. He stood in doorways and named the meat corpse, rot, Ren’s nightmare, anything but food. He said the smokehouse smelled like surrender. He said people smiled too much while chewing. He said we were training ourselves to love the things that killed us.

He was not wrong often enough to ignore.

One night I found him in the kitchen after midnight, crouched by the stove. The room was blue with banked coals. He had a heel of burned bread in one hand and was scraping cold broth from the bottom of the pot with two fingers.

He froze.

I froze.

The spoon rack ticked softly in the heat.

“Needs pepper,” he said.

I could have been kind. Instead I said, “Pepper died with civilization.”

He licked his fingers once, quick and furious, like he hated them. “Tell anyone and I’ll deny it.”

“Everyone already knows you’re hungry.”

“That’s not the part I’d deny.”

We stood in the dark with the pot between us.

Finally I took a chipped cup from the shelf, poured him half an inch from the reserve jar, and set it down. “Sit while you steal from me.”

“I’m not stealing if you give it.”

“Then suffer legally.”

He sat. Drank. Did not thank me. I did not want him to.

After that, he still called it corpse at meals. But once, when Ada said yard meat, he did not correct her.

The changes began so small we argued them into nothing.

Bea smelled snow before it fell.

“You always smell snow,” I said.

“Not through three walls and Jon’s socks.”

Old scars itched when spore fog rolled down from the pines. Fenn complained his wound felt full of thread. Elsie inspected it and said healing tissue often itched.

“Does healing tissue hum?” he asked.

Elsie wrote that down and told him no.

Ada claimed the woods sounded hungry.

“Everything sounds hungry to you,” Nessa said.

Ada considered this. “Maybe the woods are me.”

“No more philosophy before breakfast,” I said.

My broth tasted flat unless I cracked the kitchen window. That one I kept to myself.

The fourth Bloomer spoiled wrong.

We had caught it in a pit trap beyond the laundry line. It was fully changed, antlered with fungus, no clothing, no hands in the way hands mattered. Tuck cut clean. Elsie approved two jars with only one probably. I smoked the strips over chair legs and a broken stair rail.

By morning, the whole batch had bloomed white fuzz, thick and soft as lamb’s wool. It smelled like almonds and old socks.

“Burn it,” Bea said.

“Obviously,” I said, mourning the salt more than the meat.

Tuck carried the trays out with his face turned away. Lio watched from the fence.

“Still think it’s food?” he asked.

I was tired enough to answer honestly. “Some food kills you if you handle it wrong.”

“That comfort you?”

“No. It gives me work.”

The smoke from the ruined batch drifted into the pines. That afternoon, the Bloomers came closer.

Not many. Three, maybe four. Shapes between trunks beyond the north fence, pale caps lifting through spore mist. They did not rush. Did not shriek. Did not throw themselves against the wire.

They stood facing the smokehouse chimney.

Bea raised her rifle.

“Wait,” Elsie said.

“I hate that word,” Bea said.

The tallest Bloomer tilted its head. Or cap. Or whatever heard.

From the kitchen window, I watched steam from my cooling pots thread into the cold air and drift toward them.

“They smell it,” Tuck whispered beside me.

“Everything smells it,” I said.

Including me. Including the children. Including Lio, who stood at the fence with Ren’s scarf on his rifle and hunger in his face.

One of the Bloomers lifted a long arm.

Not waving.

Not quite.

Ada pressed her nose to the glass below me. “Maybe they want dinner.”

Nessa hauled her back so fast her boots scraped the floor.

Outside, the Bloomer lowered its arm. After a while, the shapes turned and disappeared among the pines.

No attack came that night.

That frightened me more than scratching would have.

Before bed, I opened my notebook and added a line beneath the broth recipe.

Smoke draws them.

Then, after staring at it too long, I wrote another.

Or calls them.

# Chapter 5: The Ones That Still Remember

The rule did not come before the mistake. Rules rarely do.

Before the rule, there was weather low enough to press on your teeth, four empty snares, one pot of broth stretched thin with meal, and Lio saying we had grown lazy because the monsters had started delivering themselves to our yard.

“Bloomers don’t deliver,” Bea said.

“No? Then what do you call standing under our chimney like supper guests?”

“I call it something I don’t understand.”

“That makes two of us.”

The fifth snare rang near noon.

Not the laundry line by the smokehouse. This was the birch snare beyond the north fence, outside our safest reach. Bea did not want me going. I did not want me going. But Tuck had come back from checking the line with his face the color of old paste.

“It’s caught wrong,” he said.

“What does that mean?” I asked.

He looked at his hands. “It means I need you to tell me what not to cut.”

So I went.

Bea led, rifle up. Lio moved ahead and to the left, quiet as a bad thought. Tuck carried the pole saw and an empty tarp. Elsie came because no one could stop her and because she had filled her pockets with salt, mint, and opinions. I carried my kitchen knife under my coat. It was a stupid comfort and therefore a real one.

The woods beyond the fence were beautiful in the insulting way deadly things can be. Snow lay clean over rot. Black pine trunks wore white shelves of fungus like saints’ collars. Spores drifted where sunlight struck them, golden and soft. Somewhere under the snow, water ticked or roots clicked or something chewed slowly.

“Don’t touch anything green,” Elsie said.

“Nothing’s green,” Lio said.

“Then you’re safe by accident.”

We found the snare in a hollow near the old trail marker. The wire had wrapped around one leg of the thing and pulled it half off its feet. It had not thrashed itself to pieces like the others. It sat in the snow, bent forward, breathing.

Breathing was the first wrongness.

Bloomers rasped, clicked, split. This one breathed like a person with a fever.

Fungus grew along its throat and jaw in pale plates. One arm had lengthened, fingers webbed with gray thread. Its coat hung open, stiff with frost. Beneath the growth, beneath the swelling, beneath the slick white film over the eyes, there was a face.

Not whole. Not saved.

But there.

Tuck made a sound and stepped back.

“No,” Bea said softly.

Lio’s bow was already raised.

“Wait,” I said.

He did not lower it. “For what?”

The thing’s head shifted toward my voice. Its lips moved. They were cracked, gray at the corners.

Elsie leaned in despite Bea’s hiss. “Sleeper.”

We had used the word before, but loosely. For shapes seen through fog. For bad dreams. For the infected in early days, locked in rooms while people argued mercy through doors.

Not like this. Not with one caught in our wire while our smokehouse hung full behind us.

The Sleeper wore a scarf.

Blue wool, stiff with ice, wrapped twice at the neck beneath the fungal plates. Nessa had made scarves like that from an old hotel blanket. She gave them to the south homestead last winter in trade for antibiotics.

“South Hollow,” Bea said.

No one answered.

The Sleeper breathed again, a wet pull. Its eyes rolled under the white film. It looked at Tuck, or through him, and opened its mouth.

“C—”

Wind moved through the pines.

“Cold,” Ada would have said, if she had been there. Thank God she wasn’t.

Lio drew the bowstring to his cheek. “Move.”

“Don’t,” Tuck said.

“It’s suffering.”

“Then don’t make me butcher it.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

He meant burn. Kill. End. All possible meanings hung between us.

Elsie’s face had gone hard in the way people’s faces do when they are refusing to feel curiosity. “Still aware. Some auditory response. Motor function limited.”

“Elsie,” Bea said.

“What? Naming helps.”

“No, it doesn’t,” Lio said. “It never has.”

The Sleeper’s mouth worked again. Not words this time. A hum. Thin, broken, almost nothing.

I knew it.

Not from childhood. Not from church. From our cellar stairs, where Ada hummed when she was pretending not to be afraid. Three notes up, one down. Annoying enough that Nessa had threatened to tax it.

My skin went cold under all its layers.

“Where did it learn that?” Tuck whispered.

“Maybe Ada learned it from outside,” Lio said.

I turned on him. “Don’t.”

“Why? Because then it means something?”

“Because she’s a child.”

“Ren hummed before she stopped talking.”

Bea took one step toward him. “Lio.”

He did not look at her. His eyes stayed on the Sleeper. His voice dropped. “She asked for water after her hands split. She said my name with mushrooms in her teeth. So don’t tell me where person ends like you measured it with kitchen string.”

No one moved.

The Sleeper shuddered. A small shelf of fungus cracked at its collar and released a dusting of spores. Bea pulled me back by the sleeve. Elsie covered her mouth.

Hunger spoke then. Not out loud. Worse. It spoke from inside all of us.

There was meat on the thing.

Not much, maybe. Poisoned, maybe. Wrong, certainly. But enough for broth. Enough for Ada’s bowl. Enough for Fenn’s wound. Enough for two days if watered hard and no one said the word person.

I hated that I saw it.

Tuck saw me see it. His eyes filled.

“I can’t,” he said.

“You won’t,” I said.

Lio laughed without humor. “There it is. Cook decides.”

“No,” I said. “Cook refuses.”

The Sleeper’s head lifted. The white film over its eyes had split in one place. Something dark and wet showed through.

It looked back.

That was all. Not recognition, maybe. Not pleading, maybe. But enough.

“If it remembers,” I said, and my voice sounded like someone had scraped it out of a pot, “we don’t eat it.”

Elsie closed her journal.

Bea nodded once.

Tuck sat down hard in the snow.

Lio’s bow arm trembled. “And if a child is starving?”

“They are starving.”

“If one is dying?”

I had no answer worth the air. So I said the only thing I could make true. “Not this.”

The Sleeper hummed again. Three notes up, one down.

Bea took Lio’s arrow from the string with two fingers. For a second I thought he might fight her. Then he let go.

“I’ll do it,” Bea said.

Tuck covered his face.

I turned away too late to avoid hearing.

The shot was small in the woods. The silence after was not.

We burned it there. All of it. Scarf and coat and fungal plates and the body beneath. Elsie salted the snow around the ash. Lio stood close enough that sparks landed on his boots and did not move. The smell was not savory. It was hair, wool, and bitter rot.

That difference troubled me more than if it had smelled good.

Back at the Lantern House, everyone knew before we spoke. Houses learn news from footsteps.

Nessa took one look at our faces and sent the children upstairs, which meant Ada hid on the landing.

I told them the rule in the dining room because rules need witnesses.

“No Sleepers,” I said. “Nothing with a face that knows us. Nothing that speaks. Nothing that looks back.”

Old Jon rubbed his dented mug. “What if it’s already dead?”

“No.”

“What if we’re out of food?”

“No.”

Lio sat near the hearth, Ren’s scarf still wrapped around his rifle. He had not removed his gloves. “Easy word with a full pot.”

“The pot isn’t full,” I said.

“Then it’s a stupid rule.”

“Most decent things are.”

Nessa wrote it on the board beneath NO TASTING ALONE. Her chalk squeaked.

NO SLEEPERS.

Ada appeared on the stairs. “What’s a Sleeper?”

Every adult failed her at once.

Finally Tuck said, “Someone we leave alone.”

She considered that. “Even if they’re mean?”

“Especially then,” Jon said softly.

That night supper tasted of smoke though I had washed every pot twice.

No one joked about monster gravy. Even Ada picked strings from her bowl without naming them. Lio did not eat. Or did not eat where we could see.

Near dawn, Bea woke me with a hand over my mouth.

“Quiet,” she whispered.

We went to the front gate with rifles and lantern hooded low. Snow had fallen, fresh and clean, smoothing the yard. On the packed path just outside the gate sat a dead branch as thick as my arm.

Growing from it were pale shelves of fungus, clean-edged, plump, unbruised. Arranged almost neatly.

No footprints led to it.

No drag marks.

Only thin lines beneath the snow, like roots had written their way there.

Elsie crouched, breath smoking. “Interesting.”

“If you say probably,” Bea warned.

“I wasn’t.”

Lio stared at the branch. His face had emptied. “Bait.”

“Maybe,” I said.

Ada’s voice floated from the upper window, sleepy and certain. “Maybe the woods are sorry.”

Nessa hissed her name and pulled her back inside.

I stood at the gate until my fingers hurt from cold.

The shelves smelled like broth.

I hated that too.

In the kitchen, I set the branch in a covered bowl and wrote on a scrap of tape: DO NOT TRUST.

Then I added, because apparently I had become an optimist:

YET.

# Chapter 6: The Feast They Scratched Through

The feast was not my idea.

That is what I told everyone later, when they accused me of ceremony. I did not plan a midwinter feast. I planned triage. The sixth Bloomer had fallen into the old culvert trap during a thaw and frozen again overnight, which meant half the meat had to be cooked immediately or lost. The smokehouse was too full. The salt was too low. Everyone still spoke softly because of the Sleeper.

So I made stew.

The Lantern House made it a feast because people are ridiculous if you give them enough smell.

Nessa cut paper stars from old tax forms and hung them over the dining room windows. “For morale,” she said, daring anyone to smile.

Old Jon polished the least cracked mugs and told Ada they were crystal. Ada told him crystal was transparent and he said apocalypse crystal was more flexible. Tuck brought in candles of beeswax and Bloomer fat, each one tied with string because they slumped if left unattended. Bea fixed the west shutter with one hand while eating fried cap from the other.

Lio watched all of it with the expression of a man attending a wedding between two people he disliked.

“You’re making it pretty,” he said.

“I’m making it edible,” I said.

“You put herbs in.”

“That is because I still believe in standards.”

“You put the last herbs in.”

“I said standards, not wisdom.”

He looked into the pot. “What’s that pale stuff?”

“Gate fungus.”

His head snapped up. “The bait?”

“The quarantined sample.”

“The bait.”

“Elsie tested it.”

From the corner, Elsie said, “In thimblefuls over two days, with no adverse effects except Jon claiming he heard his left knee speak French, which predates the sample.”

“My knee has always been cosmopolitan,” Jon called.

Lio stared at me.

I stirred the pot. Smoked yard meat, fried caps, barley sweepings, root scraps, onion skin saved for color, gate fungus sliced thin. A ragout, if you were generous. A thick brown argument, if you were not.

“It’s probably safe,” Elsie added.

Every head turned.

She sighed. “It is as safe as anything in this kitchen, which is to say conditionally.”

“Put that on the menu,” Bea said.

The stew simmered all afternoon. It thickened and darkened, fat shining on top in little gold windows. The smell moved through the house with hands. People followed it. Even grief followed it. Even suspicion.

By dusk, the dining room had become something almost festive and therefore almost unbearable. Paper stars trembled in drafts. Candles spat and gave off their garlicky rain smell. Bowls lined the table, numbered bottoms up. Ada’s drawing hung over the hearth: the Lantern House as a huge black soup pot, smoke curling from the chimney, little stick people safe inside. Outside the pot she had drawn Bloomers with round eyes and spoons.

“Absolutely not,” I said when I saw it.

“It’s art,” Ada said.

“It’s evidence.”

Nessa pinned it anyway.

We served children first, then sick, then wall guard, then everyone else. Nessa stood beside me with the ration ledger like a priest with a bad god. I gave Bea a thicker ladle and did not look at anyone. Tuck took only broth until I added meat to his bowl myself.

Lio came last.

For a moment I thought he would refuse. Then he held out his bowl.

No one spoke. Even Ada understood enough to shut her mouth.

I gave him stew.

He looked at it as though it had insulted Ren. Then he took a spoonful.

His face changed before he could stop it.

The ragout was better than the broth. I wish it had not been. Smoke rounded the sweetness. Gate fungus held its shape like oyster mushroom but tasted of chestnut and marrow. The little barley we had left thickened everything until the spoon stood up. It tasted like a holiday remembered by someone with blood on their hands.

Lio swallowed.

“Needs pepper,” he said.

The room exhaled.

Jon lifted his mug. “To civilization, which now has conditional stew.”

“To not calling it ham,” Bea said.

“Winter ham,” someone said down-table, maybe Fenn.

Lio pointed his spoon. “Say that again and I’ll put you outside.”

Ada whispered, “Monster holiday.”

“No,” I said.

She grinned into her bowl.

For a while, we were almost people from before. Jon sang two verses of an old road song and invented the third. Tuck told a story about a ShopMart customer who returned a turkey because it “looked judgmental.” Nessa allowed seconds by ledger and nobody argued loudly. Bea’s knee touched mine under the serving table and stayed there.

Then the scratching began.

At first I thought it was sleet against the shutters.

Scratch.

Pause.

Scratch scratch.

The room quieted one spoon at a time.

Bea rose. Lio already had his bow. Tuck stood so quickly his chair fell backward. The candles hissed.

From outside came another scrape, long and deliberate, along the north wall.

Then another at the pantry side.

Then another.

Too many branches.

Ada held her bowl with both hands. “They want seconds.”

“No,” Nessa said, though no one had asked her.

Bea moved to the hall. “Mara, cellar.”

“No.”

“Mara.”

“If everyone runs, everyone panics.”

“If everyone stays, everyone may die sitting politely.”

“Then they’ll die fed.”

She gave me a look that would have blistered paint in a better house. But she did not argue because the first shutter cracked.

Cold blew into the dining room. Candle flames flattened. Spores drifted through the gap, glittering in lamplight like gold dust.

“Wet cloths,” Bea snapped. “Masks. Now.”

Nessa moved the children with frightening efficiency. Tuck blocked the kitchen door with a cleaver in one hand and tears standing in his eyes. Elsie threw salt at the windowsill as if seasoning the apocalypse.

I kept serving.

Not because I was brave. Because my hands had learned long ago that when the room goes wrong, you keep the line moving. Bowl. Ladle. Wipe rim. Next.

“Eat,” I told Fenn, who had frozen with his spoon halfway up. “If you’re going to be dramatic, do it with calories.”

He ate.

The scratching became pounding.

Something hit the pantry wall hard enough to knock two jars from the shelf. One shattered. Broth spread across the floor, rich and steaming. The smell rose.

Outside, a wet chorus answered.

Not voices. Not howls.

Hunger recognizing itself.

My teeth hurt.

I gripped the ladle. Copper filled my mouth, sharp and sudden. The pressure moved behind my jaw toward the left, not sound, not thought, a pull.

Pantry wall.

“Bea!” I shouted. “Pantry!”

She was already heading north. “How do you—”

“Pantry!”

She believed me. That was love or tactical despair. She grabbed Lio and two guards. They reached the pantry just as the outer boards split. Something pale shoved through, all cap and fingers. Bea fired point-blank. Lio’s arrow followed. Tuck, sobbing openly now, brought the cleaver down on what remained.

The pressure in my teeth eased.

Across the room, Old Jon clutched his jaw. “Anyone else taste pennies?”

Elsie stared at him, then at me, then wrote something on her sleeve because paper was too slow.

More impacts came at the west shutter. Fenn, who had eaten two bowls, suddenly pointed before the sound arrived. “There.”

Bea reinforced there.

Nessa, mask tied crooked, held Ada against her hip with one arm and a poker in the other. Ada did not cry. That frightened me too.

The siege lasted until dawn or a year. Time broke into tasks. Salt. Boards. Bowls. Shots. Wet cloths. More stew because people shaking from fear needed warmth. The candles spat black grease onto the table. Paper stars sagged with condensation. Outside, Bloomers pressed and scratched and sang without singing.

When gray light finally seeped through the cracked shutters, the sounds thinned.

One by one, they withdrew.

No victory came. No cheering. Just people standing amid spilled broth, broken glass, and half-eaten stew, too tired to be relieved.

Bea returned from the pantry with blood on her cheek and fungal pulp on her boots. She took my face in both hands, turned it left and right.

“You knew,” she said.

“I tasted it.”

“That is not better.”

“No.”

Outside, the snow around the Lantern House was churned to dirty slush. No bodies remained where they should have fallen. Only scraps. Drag marks. And from the gate to the old compost pit behind the inn, pale shelves had risen overnight in a crooked line, plump and clean as loaves.

Lio stood beside me, looking at them.

“They came for the food,” he said.

“Maybe.”

He swallowed. “Or for the cook.”

I wanted to tell him not to be stupid.

Instead, from the dining room, Ada called, “Can we still have breakfast?”

The whole house waited for my answer.

My teeth ached. The stew pot was nearly empty. The pale shelves outside shone in the morning like something set on a table.

“Yes,” I said.

Because what else was there?

# Chapter 7: Compost

By morning, the compost pit was breathing.

Not much. Not enough for anyone sensible to call it breathing, which meant everyone sensible called it steam and avoided my eyes. But I had watched enough pots simmer to know a rhythm when I saw one.

Warm vapor rose from behind the old tool shed, where we had dumped peelings, ash, bones, first-boil water, ruined jerky, and every kitchen mistake too dangerous to save. Snow had melted in a wide, wet ring around the pit. Pale shelves grew at the edges in tidy fans. Other things grew deeper in.

Things with tooth shapes.

Things like closed eyelids.

Things that made even Elsie say nothing for almost a minute.

“Compost heats,” she said finally.

Lio snorted. “Compost doesn’t hum.”

“It can produce gases.”

“Do gases watch you?”

“Everything watches you, Marr. You make yourself interesting.”

Bea stood with her rifle across her chest, jaw set. “No one touches anything until we decide if we’re burning it.”

The word burning moved through the group like weather.

We were five: Bea, Elsie, Tuck, Lio, and me. Nessa had objected to all of us going because “if the idiots in charge get eaten, paperwork becomes impossible,” but she stayed inside with the children and the remaining guns. Old Jon was on radio watch, which mostly meant listening to static and telling it to enunciate.

I had not wanted to come. That was the truth. A cook should not have to visit the stomach she has made of the yard.

But the pale shelves from the gate led here. The Bloomers had gathered for the feast, scratched through our walls, then left us a line of food pointing to our own scraps.

That felt personal.

The pit had once been normal. Coffee grounds. Potato peels. Eggshells back when we had eggs. After the Bloom, we moved it farther from the kitchen, then farther again, until winter and exhaustion made distance negotiable. Lately we had dumped first-boil water there because carrying it to the ash trench wasted fuel and feet. Bones too dangerous for stock. Salted trimmings. The batch of spoiled strips that smelled of almonds and socks.

We had been feeding it.

I hated that I had not noticed because noticing was supposedly my job.

Tuck crouched near the edge, careful not to let his apron brush the melted snow. He looked ill.

“Smells like the meat room after a power outage,” he said. “But cleaner.”

“Helpful,” Lio said.

“I didn’t say comforting.”

Elsie used a long spoon tied to a broom handle to lift one of the clean shelves. It bruised faint gold where touched. No blue veins. No sacs. No gills. It looked like something you might buy at a farmers’ market from a woman who also sold soap.

“Edible-looking,” she said.

Bea closed her eyes. “Elsie.”

“I did not say safe.”

“Your face said safe.”

“My face is none of your business.”

Lio stepped closer with a torch. We had all seen him bring it. We had all pretended not to.

“Burn it,” he said. “Now. Pit, shed, soil, all of it.”

“And eat what?” I asked.

He turned on me. “Not this.”

“Good. What?”

His grip tightened around the torch until ash flaked from the wrapped head. “We hunted before.”

“We starved before.”

“We’re changing.”

“We were dying.”

“That was cleaner.”

“No,” Tuck said softly.

Everyone looked at him.

He did not raise his head. “Dying wasn’t cleaner. It just had less washing up.”

Lio’s mouth twisted. “You too?”

Tuck stood. His hands were damp with melted frost. “I don’t like this. I don’t like any of it. But I know waste when I see it, and I know rot, and I know when something can feed people if handled right.”

“If handled wrong?” Bea asked.

“Then it feeds on us.”

The pit answered with a soft bubble.

No one laughed.

I tasted peaches.

Not smelled. Tasted. Sour-sweet on the back of my tongue, the last jar gone lively. Then onion. Burned edge. First broth. Smoke. Bea’s coffee substitute, bitter enough to qualify as self-harm. The Sleeper’s wool scarf burning in snow.

I put a hand to my mouth.

“Mara?” Bea said.

The tastes came faster. Not memories exactly. Ingredients. Mistakes. Offerings. Everything we had thrown away because we were done with it.

The pit warmed.

Under the taste was hunger. Not a mouth hunger. Root hunger. Patient. Wide. It did not speak. It did not forgive. It did not threaten.

It wanted.

So did we.

I bent and spat into the snow until the peach taste thinned.

Elsie watched me too closely. “What did you experience?”

“Breakfast being rude.”

“Mara.”

“I don’t know.”

That was the first honest thing anyone had said all morning, and it made the air colder.

A crack sounded from the pines.

Bea raised her rifle. Lio lifted the torch and drew a knife in the same motion. Tuck stepped in front of Elsie without realizing.

A Bloomer emerged between the trees.

It was tall and deer-boned, fungus antlering from its shoulders. Its hands—no, limbs—dragged something through the snow. An infected deer carcass, half changed, ribs webbed white, eyes capped over. The Bloomer pulled it to the edge of the clearing, dropped it near the compost ring, and stepped back.

No attack.

No sound but steam and our breathing.

“Bait,” Lio whispered.

“Maybe,” I said.

“Stop saying maybe like it feeds anyone.”

“It has been feeding us.”

His face went raw. “Listen to yourself.”

“I am. I hate it.”

The Bloomer tilted its cap toward the pit. Toward us. Toward the warm kitchen window beyond the yard, open a crack because I had forgotten to shut it. Steam from our house drifted out, smelling of old stew and smoke.

Lio moved.

Not far. One step, torch up. But the Bloomer flinched, and from the trees came answering clicks. More shapes. Hidden, waiting.

Bea said, “Lio.”

His arm shook. “If we burn it, it ends.”

“No,” Elsie said. Quietly. No probably. “If we burn it, something happens. We do not know what.”

“I know what happens if we don’t.”

“So do I,” I said.

He looked at me.

“We live,” I said. “Maybe badly. Maybe not for long. Maybe less human than you’d like. But we live today. If you burn that, maybe we die cleaner. I am out of worship for clean.”

The torch shook harder.

“Ren—” he began.

“Would be hungry,” I said, and knew at once I had gone too far.

His face changed. Bea inhaled. Tuck whispered my name.

Lio stepped toward me, not with the torch now but with grief. I did not move. I deserved at least that.

Then he lowered it.

“Don’t use her mouth,” he said.

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not sorry enough.”

“No.”

That was also true.

He turned away, torch still lit but down at his side.

Bea touched my elbow once. Not forgiveness. Presence.

Tuck cleared his throat. “Butcher rules.”

We all looked at him again. He hated that.

“What?” Bea said.

“At the store, you cut away rot. You keep clean. You don’t mix. You label. You wash more than seems sane. You throw out anything that looks back.” He glanced at the pit. “Could do that.”

Elsie nodded slowly. “Controlled edge. Salt barrier. Separate deposits. Burn suspect growth. Harvest only clean shelves. Record response.”

“Or,” Lio said, “we decorate our grave.”

“Yes,” Elsie said. “That remains possible.”

We worked before courage could change its mind.

Bea and Lio held watch on the tree line. Tuck used the pole saw to cut clean shelves into a boiled sack. Elsie salted a ring around the pit, muttering measurements. I burned the tooth-things with Lio’s torch. They shriveled and popped, smelling like bitter almonds. The eyelid shapes we burned too. Anything too pink. Anything with hair. Anything that trembled toward the heat.

On one side of the pit, we laid bones and vegetable scraps. On the other, ash. No first-boil water unless sealed and marked. No Sleepers. No cloth from the dead.

At the edge of the salted ring, Lio stopped. From inside his coat he took Ren’s red scarf—not the one on his rifle, I realized, but a torn piece of it. He had carried it all this time.

He stared at it, then at the pit.

“Not there,” I said gently.

“I know.”

He buried it beyond the fence, under clean snow, away from compost and smoke.

The Bloomer watched until we finished. Then it dragged the infected deer closer to the pit and retreated into the trees.

Offering. Bait. Lesson.

Meat.

No one said any word for it.

When we turned back toward the inn, the kitchen window stood open, warm light spilling out. The whole Lantern House smelled like breakfast: broth, ash, old bread, wet wool, fear.

Ada pressed her face to the glass.

I lifted one hand to tell her to get down.

Behind me, under the salted snow, the compost pit bubbled once. Like a pot remembering the boil.

I did not wave. I did not pray. I did not make a bargain.

I went inside and washed my hands until they cracked.

# Chapter 8: Bread with Cap Meal

By the time the thaw came, we had rules enough to look civilized from a distance.

No Sleepers.

No sacs.

No first water in the kitchen drain.

No eating alone.

No dumping scraps except at the salted edge.

Burn anything with teeth, hair, eyes, fingers, or ambitions.

Taste in thimblefuls.

Label everything.

Never say winter ham where Lio can hear you.

Nessa wrote the rules on three boards and hung them in the kitchen, pantry, and back hall. Then she added SIGN FOR SECONDS beneath the kitchen list because hope had limits.

The Lantern House survived.

That sounds cleaner than it was.

We survived with gray under our tongues after broth. We survived with salt sores at the corners of our mouths and white flecks at our wrists that looked like flour until they would not wash off. We survived with Bea waking before spore winds because her jaw ached. With Fenn’s scar itching whenever something moved beyond the north fence. With Old Jon claiming the radio static had learned our supper schedule. With children who preferred fried cap to beans because beans were memory and cap was dinner.

We survived with the compost pit steaming behind the tool shed, ringed in salt, watched like a prisoner and fed like livestock.

“Not livestock,” Elsie said whenever I used that word.

“What then?”

“An unmanaged mutualistic hazard.”

“Catchy.”

“I’m still workshopping.”

Every third morning, we harvested the clean shelves that grew on the east side of the pit. Tuck cut them with a boiled blade. Elsie inspected for blue veins, sacs, hair, and anything resembling intention. Bea kept rifle watch. Lio stood farther back with a torch, as if daring the pit to become what he already believed it was.

Sometimes shapes moved in the pines. Bloomers, mostly. They came less often now and attacked less often still, provided we left bones and peelings at the salted edge before dark. Provided we burned the wrong growths. Provided we did not get proud.

Peace was the wrong word.

But then, so was war.

One morning, Ada asked if monsters liked toast.

“No,” Nessa said.

“You don’t know.”

“I know enough to discourage the question.”

Ada leaned on the prep table, chin in both hands, watching me grind dried cap into meal with the old coffee mill. “If they bring deer, maybe they want breakfast.”

“They drag deer,” Lio said from the doorway. “They do not bring them.”

“That’s what bringing is, if you’re bad at hands.”

His mouth twitched before he remembered not to let it.

“Off the table,” I said.

“I’m not on it.”

“Your elbows are trespassing.”

She removed them with theater.

We were making bread. This had become an event because flour had become a ghost. I had saved three cups, hidden in a tin labeled BUTTONS to fool children and men with no respect for inventory. The rest would be cap meal, ground fine and sifted twice. Elsie said the clean shelves were nutritionally promising. Bea said that was not a phrase she wanted near breakfast. Nessa wrote down promising and underlined it with suspicion.

The dough came together gray and stubborn.

“Looks like old socks,” Ada said.

“Then don’t eat it.”

“I didn’t say bad socks.”

Bea came in from the yard, stamping mud from her boots. The thaw made everything uglier. Snow had hidden rot with more kindness than it deserved. Now the fence posts leaned, the yard stank of wet ash, and pale threads showed in the mud where no pale threads should be.

“Storm tonight,” Bea said.

I looked at the clear slice of sky above the window. “Clouds say otherwise.”

“My teeth say otherwise.”

No one laughed. That was one of the changes. Before, we would have mocked her. Now we checked masks.

I added more salt to the dough.

Elsie, at the side counter, noticed. “You didn’t taste.”

“It needed it.”

“How do you know?”

I pressed my palm into the dough. It pushed back slightly, warm from my hands or from itself. “I know dough.”

“Mara.”

“I know dough.”

She wrote something in her ledger. She had stopped writing probably. Now her notes were worse because they were honest.

Tuck entered with three jars tucked against his chest. BROTH. FAT. DO NOT TRUST.

“Why are you bringing that last one inside?” Bea asked.

“Because it started leaking in the shed.”

“Then why are you holding it?”

He looked down, as if surprised by his own arms. “Fair.”

We all stared at the jar. Something pale pressed against the glass from inside. Not eyes. Not quite. Little closed knots, like knuckles under dough.

“Burn it,” I said.

Tuck’s shoulders loosened with relief. “Thank God.”

Lio took the jar with a cloth and carried it out. We heard the burn barrel lid clang, then the soft pop of something learning it was not invited.

The bread rose near the stove.

Slowly. Unevenly. With a faint vibration I felt through the bowl when I put my hand on it.

“If the dough hums,” Ada whispered, delighted, “do we sing back?”

“No,” I said.

Old Jon, passing with a coil of wire, said, “Depends on the tune.”

“Also no.”

He winked at Ada. “Philistines.”

I punched the dough down harder than necessary. It sighed. Everyone pretended not to hear.

For dinner we had breakfast because time had become decorative. Fried caps crisped in Bloomer fat. Broth steamed in numbered bowls. The bread came out dense, gray, and burned on the bottom where I had misjudged the coals. I scraped the black with a knife while Nessa tallied portions.

“You burned it,” Ada said.

“I improved it.”

“It smells like basement toast.”

“That’s the house specialty.”

I cut the first slice. The crumb was tight and damp, flecked with darker cap meal. Steam rose. It smelled of earth, salt, yeast, smoke, and something almost sweet. Not peaches. Nothing so kind. But close enough to make my throat hurt.

Bea took the heel because she knew I liked heels and was sacrificing badly.

I took it back and gave her the next slice, thicker.

“Corruption,” Nessa said.

“Arithmetic,” Bea and I said together.

Lio accepted his bread without comment. He spread it with rendered fat, took a bite, and chewed like a man judging an enemy’s apology.

“Well?” Ada demanded.

He swallowed. “Needs pepper.”

She cackled.

That was when someone knocked at the front gate.

Not scratched. Knocked.

Every bowl stopped halfway to every mouth.

Bea rose. Lio took up his bow. Tuck reached for the cleaver he now kept under the sideboard. Nessa began moving children with one hand while protecting her bowl with the other.

I followed Bea to the lobby, wiping my hands on my apron. The old floral wallpaper had peeled enough to show water stains shaped like maps. Through the narrow viewing slit, Bea looked out.

“One person,” she said. “Alive.”

Alive had become a category requiring confirmation.

We opened the inner door but not the gate. A woman stood outside in a torn yellow raincoat, mud to her knees, hair matted under a scarf. She was thin in the way we had been before the broth. Her eyes went from Bea’s rifle to Lio’s bow to the warm light behind us.

Then the smell reached her.

Fried caps. Broth. Bread. Fat.

Her face changed.

I knew the sequence. Revulsion first. Recognition of food second. Shame third, fast and hot.

“What are you cooking?” she asked.

No one answered.

Behind me, Ada called from the dining room, “Monster toast!”

Nessa said, “Ada Pike.”

The woman at the gate took one step back.

Lio’s mouth hardened. Bea looked at me.

My teeth ached. Not warning. Not storm. Something else. The compost pit, maybe, under thawing snow. Or hunger recognizing itself again.

I thought of the first jar of peaches hissing. The boot in the snow. The Sleeper looking back. The pit bubbling like a pot. The rules on the boards, already smudged by steam.

I thought: if she comes in, she will eat.

I thought: if she eats, she will change.

I thought: she is already starving.

“Bread,” I said finally. “Soup. Fried caps.”

The woman stared. “Caps?”

I opened the gate before anyone could turn my answer into a philosophy.

She smelled of rain, mud, and road. Human smells. Old-world smells. When she crossed the threshold, she flinched at the candles, the guns, the numbered bowls, the gray bread cooling on the table.

Then her stomach growled so loudly Ada laughed.

The woman covered her face.

“Don’t,” I said, more sharply than I meant. Softer, I added, “It does that to everyone.”

I put her at the end of the table and gave her broth first. Thimbleful. Rule was rule. Her hand shook so badly Bea steadied the cup.

She drank.

Her eyes filled. Not with horror. Not yet.

“Oh,” she said.

That was all.

After a moment, I gave her bread. Burned bottom, good middle. Ada pushed over a fried cap with great solemnity.

“For crunch,” Ada said.

Outside, something scratched once at the far fence.

Everyone heard it. No one moved.

The woman froze with the bread halfway to her mouth.

Bea touched the knife at her belt. Lio listened toward the yard. Nessa counted children under her breath. Tuck watched the back door. Elsie reached for her ledger.

I heard, beneath the thaw and the walls and the soft breathing of everyone fed for one more night, the compost pit humming.

Bea heard it too. I saw it in her jaw.

Ada opened her mouth.

I cut another slice of bread and put it in her bowl before she could ask what was singing.

This is a remarkably accomplished piece of opening chapter writing. Let me assess it across the relevant dimensions.

VOICE AND CHARACTER: Mara's voice is immediately distinctive and consistent throughout. The first-person narration achieves exactly what the plan called for: practical, sensory, dryly funny, emotionally restrained. "It smells lively" / "That means bad" is a perfect exchange that establishes her character without announcement. The voice never slips into sentimentality or self-congratulation. The detail of the last onion hidden in the flour tin, returned to twice, is excellent character work—showing her controlling streak and her private calculus of desperation without explaining it.

The Bea/Mara exchange about the gloves is intimate and loaded with history without being overwrought. Lio's entrance ("Nobody asked yet" / "You were going to") efficiently establishes his character. Jon's "texture of soap and lies" about bananas is exactly the right kind of dark humor. The dialogue rarely feels constructed for effect; it feels like people talking under pressure.

METAPHOR AND PROSE QUALITY: The opening paragraph is excellent—"Not a good hiss. Not summer trapped under glass, not syrup loosening its long gold throat." This is genuinely good prose, not purple. The metaphors are earned and specific. "Warm sadness" for mint tea is perfect. The drip hitting the bucket every thirteen seconds is a beautifully deployed detail—concrete, rhythmic, oppressive. There are occasional moments where the prose reaches slightly too hard ("a memory gone wrong" for the peach smell is a touch generic), but these are minor.

FOLLOWING THE PLAN: The chapter follows the plan closely and well. The pantry ledger falsification is revealed through dialogue rather than exposition. The numbered bowls appear. The tourist brochures as kindling are mentioned. The greenhouse failure is referenced. The scavenging party returns empty-handed. The Bloomer is caught in the laundry-line snare. The chapter ends precisely as planned—with Mara smelling mushrooms in butter from the dead Bloomer. All key characters are introduced organically. The plan's instruction to avoid over-explaining the monsters is honored; we get impressions only.

COZY-HORROR FUSION: This is where the chapter particularly excels. The horror enters the cozy spaces naturally—the bells interrupting the peach tea, the shape lurching past the kitchen window, the boot on the Bloomer's foot making everyone quieter (though this detail is saved for Chapter 2 per the plan, it's foreshadowed here). The warmth of the kitchen is real and specific: socks steaming over the stove, curtain-quilts, numbered bowls. The horror is not decorative.

ENDING: The final image—Mara's stomach cramping, her mouth watering at the smell of the dead Bloomer—is exactly right. It's the chapter's thesis delivered through sensation rather than statement. "My mouth watered anyway" is a perfect closing line: simple, devastating, and true to the prompt's central horror.

WEAKNESSES: The chapter is slightly long for what it accomplishes structurally—some of the middle section (the scavenging party's return, Fenn's injury) feels slightly rushed compared to the careful attention given to the kitchen scenes. The Sleeper's blue scarf from the south homestead, the humming of Ada's tune, the white film splitting to reveal something looking back: these details accumulate with restraint and land with real weight. The rule itself ("If it remembers, we don't eat it") arrives organically from the scene rather than being imposed on it.

The dialogue is generally excellent. Lio's speech about Ren—"She asked for water after her hands split. She said my name with mushrooms in her teeth"—is the chapter's emotional peak and earns its place. It's specific, painful, and character-revealing without being a speech. The exchange between Tuck and Lio over what "burn" means ("He meant burn. Kill. End. All possible meanings hung between us") is a fine example of compression.

Character consistency is strong throughout. Mara is practical and controlling, refusing to be made judge while accepting the role anyway. Tuck's horror at his own competence ("his hands remember where joints should be" in the plan; here "I need you to tell me what not to cut") is present. Lio's grief-sharpened suspicion is rendered with sympathy rather than caricature. Bea's quiet competence—taking the arrow from the string, doing the killing—is exactly right.

The ending with the fungal shelves outside the gate is well-executed. The tape label "DO NOT TRUST / YET" is a perfect Mara note: practical, dark, and with a dry humor that doesn't undercut the horror.

**Weaknesses:**

Some of the nature description in the woods scene tips toward the slightly overwrought: "Snow lay clean over rot. Black pine trunks wore white shelves of fungus like saints' collars. Spores drifted where sunlight struck them, golden and soft." The "saints' collars" metaphor is evocative but slightly too polished for Mara's voice, which is supposed to be institutional and practical. This is a minor issue but worth noting.

The line "Hunger spoke then. Not out loud. Worse. It spoke from inside all of us" is the chapter's weakest moment—it's the kind of portentous declaration that the writing plan explicitly warned against. It tells rather than shows, and it's slightly purple. The surrounding context already conveys this; the explicit statement is unnecessary.

"The silence after was not" (referring to the shot being small but the silence large) is a construction that works but is slightly self-conscious—it draws attention to its own cleverness.

Ada's line from the window—"Maybe the woods are sorry"—is noted in the plan as intentional, but it does risk the "mystical horror child" quality the plan explicitly wanted to avoid. It's saved somewhat by Nessa immediately pulling her back inside, but it's a close call.

The chapter follows its plan very faithfully, hitting all the major beats: the Sleeper with the recognizable scarf, the humming, Lio's speech about Ren, Mara's rule, the community's reception, the fungal offering outside the gate. The plan's instruction that the rule "should not arrive too cleanly" is honored—it arrives through fear and revulsion rather than moral clarity.

Overall this is accomplished, controlled writing that serves the story's purposes without overreaching. The flaws are real but minor relative to the chapter's considerable achievements.

This is an ambitious, sustained piece of cozy-horror post-apocalyptic fiction that largely succeeds at its difficult tonal balancing act. Let me examine it carefully across the requested dimensions.

STRENGTHS:

The voice is the piece's greatest achievement. Mara's first-person-adjacent narration (technically third-person close) is distinctive, dry, and consistent across all eight chapters. Lines like "Peach tea, I wrote on the slate board, because if you wrote hot sour water, children tended to take it personally" establish a voice that is simultaneously exhausted, wry, and deeply competent. This voice rarely falters.

The dialogue is genuinely strong. The exchanges between characters feel earned and character-specific. Lio's "Needs pepper" at the feast is a perfect moment of capitulation without surrender. Ada's "Monster gravy" and "Monster toast" function as both comic relief and thematic commentary. The Bea-Mara dynamic is conveyed almost entirely through dialogue and small physical gestures rather than exposition, which is skilled work.

The world-building is organic and well-integrated. The Lantern House feels real: the numbered bowls, the BUTTONS tin hiding flour, the burn barrel, the compost pit's evolution. The rules accumulating on the boards ("Never say winter ham where Lio can hear you") serve as both worldbuilding and character development simultaneously.

The thematic core - the ethics of survival, where personhood ends, what we owe the dead - is handled with genuine sophistication. Lio's function as moral counterweight is well-managed; he's not simply wrong, and the story doesn't pretend he is. The Sleeper chapter is the emotional peak and earns its weight.

The pacing across eight chapters is generally well-managed. Each chapter advances the situation while deepening character. The escalation from "eating the monster" to "the monster is feeding us" to "we are changing" to "someone new arrives" follows a logical and satisfying arc.

WEAKNESSES:

The piece occasionally tips into self-conscious cleverness. Some metaphors are genuinely excellent ("summer trapped under glass, not syrup loosening its long gold throat" is beautiful), but others strain: "the sort of sound a thing made when it had been waiting to disappoint you" is slightly overwrought for an opening. The frequency of aphoristic observations sometimes creates a rhythm that feels performed rather than felt - the narrator is always ready with a bon mot, which can undercut the desperation the story is trying to convey.

The "forced poetry" problem is real but not severe. Phrases like "hunger makes philosophers of people who used to complain about raisins" are genuinely good. But there are moments where the prose reaches for profundity and lands on mere cleverness: "Names made things stay" is a bit too neat. The piece has a tendency to end paragraphs and sections on aphoristic notes that occasionally feel like the author showing off rather than the character thinking.

The supernatural/horror elements are handled with admirable restraint in early chapters but become slightly muddled by the end. The "tasting through walls" ability, the compost pit humming, the Bloomers bringing offerings - these are intriguing but the story doesn't quite commit to explaining or not explaining them. The ambiguity is intentional but sometimes feels like evasion rather than mystery.

Lio's arc is the most interesting character transformation, but it's slightly rushed. His midnight kitchen scene is excellent, but his gradual acceptance of the food could use one more beat. The piece is aware of this - "Unearned Transformations" is a risk - and mostly avoids it, but Lio's final "Needs pepper" at the feast feels slightly too neat given the depth of his grief.

The new arrival in Chapter 8 is a somewhat conventional ending beat - the stranger at the gate who will now face the same choices the community faced. It's competent but the least surprising moment in the piece.

The "changes" in the survivors (gray tongues, white flecks, tasting through walls) are introduced but not fully developed. This is appropriate for a story that ends before resolution, but some readers may find it frustrating.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT:

This is genuinely accomplished work. The prompt is followed faithfully and creatively - the "cozy-horror" tonal blend is achieved and sustained, which is genuinely difficult. The characters are distinct and their actions are believable. The central ethical question (when does survival become something worse?) is explored with real intelligence. The prose is mostly excellent with occasional overreach. The piece demonstrates a writer with strong instincts and real craft.

The Bea-Mara dynamic is conveyed almost entirely through dialogue and small physical gestures rather than exposition, which is skilled work.

The world-building is organic and well-integrated. The Lantern House feels real: the numbered bowls, the BUTTONS tin hiding flour, the burn barrel, the compost pit's evolution. The rules accumulating on the boards ("Never say winter ham where Lio can hear you") serve as both worldbuilding and character development simultaneously.

The thematic core - the ethics of survival, where personhood ends, what we owe the dead - is handled with genuine sophistication. Lio's function as moral counterweight is well-managed; he's not simply wrong, and the story doesn't pretend he is. The Sleeper chapter is the emotional peak and earns its weight.

The pacing across eight chapters is generally well-managed. Each chapter advances the situation while deepening character. The escalation from "eating the monster" to "the monster is feeding us" to "we are changing" to "someone new arrives" follows a logical and satisfying arc.

WEAKNESSES:

The piece occasionally tips into self-conscious cleverness. Some metaphors are genuinely excellent ("summer trapped under glass, not syrup loosening its long gold throat" is beautiful), but others strain: "the sort of sound a thing made when it had been waiting to disappoint you" is slightly overwrought for an opening. The frequency of aphoristic observations sometimes creates a rhythm that feels performed rather than felt - the narrator is always ready with a bon mot, which can undercut the desperation the story is trying to convey.

The "forced poetry" problem is real but not severe. Phrases like "hunger makes philosophers of people who used to complain about raisins" are genuinely good. But there are moments where the prose reaches for profundity and lands on mere cleverness: "Names made things stay" is a bit too neat. The piece has a tendency to end paragraphs and sections on aphoristic notes that occasionally feel like the author showing off rather than the character thinking.

The supernatural/horror elements are handled with admirable restraint in early chapters but become slightly muddled by the end. The "tasting through walls" ability, the compost pit humming, the Bloomers bringing offerings - these are intriguing but the story doesn't quite commit to explaining or not explaining them. The ambiguity is intentional but sometimes feels like evasion rather than mystery.

Lio's arc is the most interesting character transformation, but it's slightly rushed. His midnight kitchen scene is excellent, but his gradual acceptance of the food could use one more beat. The piece is aware of this - "Unearned Transformations" is a risk - and mostly avoids it, but Lio's final "Needs pepper" at the feast feels slightly too neat given the depth of his grief.

The new arrival in Chapter 8 is a somewhat conventional ending beat - the stranger at the gate who will now face the same choices the community faced. It's competent but the least surprising moment in the piece.

The "changes" in the survivors (gray tongues, white flecks, tasting through walls) are introduced but not fully developed. This is appropriate for a story that ends before resolution, but some readers may find it frustrating.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT:

This is genuinely accomplished work. The prompt is followed faithfully and creatively - the "cozy-horror" tonal blend is achieved and sustained, which is genuinely difficult. The characters are distinct and their actions are believable. The central ethical question (when does survival become something worse?) is explored with real intelligence. The prose is mostly excellent with occasional overreach. The piece demonstrates a writer with strong instincts and real craft.
