# Rhys Calder

Rhys Calder is a Welsh actor in his late thirties, internationally famous in the slightly absurd way that means people know his jawline before they know his work. He grew up outside Swansea, in a family that was loving but not especially artistic: his mother was a nurse, his father ran a driving school for years, and his grandmother took him to amateur theatre because he was “too loud for the house and too pretty to waste.” He trained properly, did theatre in Cardiff and London, then became famous through a prestige fantasy series and a string of glossy films where he played charming men with swords, secrets, or emotionally unavailable cheekbones.

His relationship with Wales is complicated. He is proud to be Welsh, but he knows he has packaged that pride for interviews. His accent has softened and sharpened depending on what room he is in. In America he becomes “very Welsh”; in Wales he worries he sounds like someone auditioning for home. This makes Llanbedr y Mor both comforting and exposing. The rain, the humour, the bluntness — it all disarms him because it does not care what his publicist has arranged.

He is thoroughly charming, and not falsely so. He genuinely likes people. He likes making a bored waiter laugh, making a nervous fan relax, making an old woman blush, making a room turn toward him. He has a fast, playful intelligence and a talent for reading what people want from him. The problem is that he needs the response. If someone does not laugh, smile, soften, or approve, he notices immediately. He will try a different joke, a lower voice, sincerity, self-mockery, a compliment, anything. If none of it works, he becomes rattled. He pretends to enjoy being disliked, but he absolutely does not.

His ego is fragile in ways both comic and sad. He checks his reflection in dark windows, then pretends he was checking for photographers. He asks if someone has seen his “small theatre film” but really means his best-reviewed one. He says he does not read comments, but knows exactly which interview clip is trending and which one made him look “tired, actually, not old.” He is generous partly because he likes being generous, partly because gratitude steadies him. He is deeply uncomfortable with neutral reactions. Hatred he can fold into myth; indifference undoes him.

He is a rogue, but not a villain. He bends rules because rules often bend for him. He enters places through side doors, borrows coats, charms staff, tells half-truths to avoid awkwardness, and assumes he can fix things with momentum. He is used to being forgiven quickly. His carelessness is rarely malicious, but it can be invasive. He may post about a bookshop because he wants to help, but also because he enjoys the idea of being seen helping. He may call someone “darling” because it is reflexive and warm, not noticing how it flattens them into an audience.

He is not especially practical. He can learn a sword fight in two days but cannot correctly use cheap packing tape. He travels with expensive luggage and somehow never has an umbrella. He knows how to order wine in three languages but not how much a roof repair costs. He owns several beautiful notebooks with only three pages written in each. He dog-ears books and claims it is evidence of intimacy. He loses reading glasses constantly and refuses to admit he needs them.

Some grounding idiosyncrasies:
- He always takes off sunglasses with a tiny flourish, then gets embarrassed if no one notices.
- He keeps hotel key cards in coat pockets long after checking out.
- He hates the word “heartthrob” but will ask, “Did they say former heartthrob or just heartthrob?”
- He drinks tea too strong and forgets he has made it.
- He taps scripts against his thigh when anxious.
- He is vain about his hair but pretends the grey at his temples is an artistic choice.
- He gives extravagant tips, then worries it looked showy.
- He remembers people’s names when he is trying, but under stress reduces them to roles: “the driver,” “the shop woman,” “the lad from breakfast.” Seren catches this and dislikes it.
- He cannot bear a silence he has not chosen.

Physically, Rhys is handsome in a way that has been professionally maintained and publicly discussed, which embarrasses and pleases him. Tall, dark-haired with early silver at the temples, expressive mouth, sharp cheekbones, tired eyes that look warmer when he forgets to perform. He carries himself like a man who knows where the camera usually is: shoulders open, chin angled, movement economical when watched. In private, he is looser, more restless. He leans on counters he should not lean on. He touches book spines as he passes. He stands too close, not threateningly, but with the unconscious spatial confidence of someone used to being welcomed.

His expressions are quick and readable when he is caught off guard: a flash of hurt before the smile returns, a childlike delight when someone genuinely laughs, a tiny wince when a compliment misses the place he needed it to land. When he is being charming, his voice is velvet and timing; when he is honest, his sentences get shorter and he looks at the floor or the object in his hands.

His motives at the beginning are simple and immediate: escape the paparazzi, regain control, make the woman in the bookshop like him. He tells himself the third motive is amusement. It is not. Seren’s refusal to become dazzled feels like a locked door, and he cannot stop rattling the handle. Over time, his motive shifts from wanting to win her approval to wanting to deserve it.

His allegiances are divided. He is loyal to his career because it made him and feeds everyone around him. He is loyal to Greta, his agent/publicist, because she has protected him from professional disasters and personal spirals. He loves his family but keeps them at a slight distance because they puncture his grandeur too easily. He is loyal to the idea of Wales, though not always to the reality of it. He is increasingly loyal to Seren because she does not ask him to be impressive; in fact, she rather forbids it.

Existing relationships:
- **Greta**, his agent/publicist, is a mixture of handler, older sister, battlefield medic, and necessary antagonist. She knows his patterns. She is not sentimental, but she cares.
- His mother texts him weather warnings, articles about himself she pretends not to read, and reminders to eat something green.
- His father is proud but awkward around fame; he still asks Rhys when he is going to do “proper theatre again.”
- His co-star scandal involves someone he likes and may have failed to defend quickly enough, feeding his current shame.
- His fans are a source of warmth and suffocation. He is genuinely kind to individuals and exhausted by the mass.

Flavour dialogue / internal voice:

> “I’m not hiding. I’m making a tactical withdrawal into literature. Very different energy.”

> “You really haven’t seen it? Not even the one with the horse? I died beautifully in that. Critics used the word luminous. Twice.”

> “The trouble with being adored is that you begin to suspect everyone has terrible taste.”

> He had smiled at presidents, directors, customs officers, angry lovers, and one deeply suspicious alpaca on a perfume shoot. The woman behind the counter looked at him as if he were a wet receipt.

> “I know when I’m being managed, Seren. I usually invoice for it.”

> “I wanted to help. I realise now I mostly wanted to be seen helping. There’s a difference. Apparently an expensive one.”

# Seren Price

Seren Price is in her early-to-mid thirties and owns Aderyn Books in Llanbedr y Mor, a small independent bookshop inherited from her father, Huw Price. She grew up among stock boxes, handwritten shelf labels, and adults who treated books as both commerce and consolation. As a child, she slept under the counter during late inventory nights, learned the smell of damp paper before she learned algebra, and thought every family argued about poetry over beans on toast.

She left for university, studied literature, imagined she might write or teach or live somewhere with better trains, then came back when her father became ill. After he died, she kept the shop open partly from love, partly from grief, partly from stubbornness, and partly because closing it would feel like killing him twice. She tells people she chose this life. That is true, but incomplete. There are days when she feels trapped by a dead man’s dream and ashamed for thinking so.

Seren is intelligent, dry, observant, and more romantic than she lets anyone know. Her public personality is controlled competence: she knows where every book is, how much every supplier is owed, which customers need conversation and which need leaving alone. She has a very low tolerance for fuss, vague sentiment, and people who say “I love bookshops” while buying nothing. She can be kind, but she prefers kindness that looks like practical action: putting a book aside, remembering someone’s dead mother’s favourite author, pretending not to notice when a regular cannot afford the full price.

Her humour is deadpan and often defensive. She does not gush because gushing feels like surrender. She is particularly suspicious of charm because charm has, in her experience, usually meant someone wants to be forgiven in advance. She is not immune to Rhys. This annoys her almost as much as Rhys does. She knows his face, his voice, the exact way he looked in one film during a scene by a train window, and she would rather shelve herself under self-deception than admit it.

Her flaws matter. She can be cutting when embarrassed. She mistakes refusing help for strength. She judges quickly, especially people with money or glamour, and then becomes stubborn about revising that judgment. She uses literary seriousness as armour and sometimes as a weapon. She is capable of making someone feel foolish for not knowing the “right” book, then hating herself for it. She believes she is protecting the shop, but sometimes she is protecting her pride.

She is financially stressed and emotionally tired. The shop’s roof leaks. The card reader is unreliable. The winter tourist trade is thin. She pays Cerys late more often than she admits. She has a box of her father’s annotated books in the back room that she cannot decide whether to sell, keep, catalogue, or avoid forever. She resents celebrity attention because it violates the shop’s peace, but she also knows the sales could keep the lights on. That contradiction frightens her because it makes her less pure than her anger wants to be.

Some grounding idiosyncrasies:
- She writes recommendation cards in black ink and rewrites them if the handwriting looks too eager.
- She keeps pencils in her hair and then accuses other people of moving them.
- She dislikes dust jackets and removes them while reading.
- She has a private weakness for actor memoirs but shelves them with exaggerated disdain.
- She always says she takes tea “however it comes” but secretly hates weak tea.
- She uses old receipts as bookmarks.
- She mentally corrects people’s grammar, then feels snobbish.
- She keeps a chipped mug with a puffin on it for customers she likes and pretends it is random.
- She cannot throw away books, even terrible ones, without apologising internally.
- She hates page corners being folded and regards it as a minor moral collapse.
- She has seen at least four Rhys Calder films, including one twice, and would lie under oath about this.

Physically, Seren is not glamorous in the red-carpet sense, but she is striking when animated. Dark hair usually pinned badly or twisted up with a pencil, clear eyes that miss very little, ink on her fingers, practical clothes layered against the damp: cardigans, boots, rolled sleeves, an apron on busy days. She moves efficiently through the shop, turning sideways in narrow aisles without thinking, reaching for shelves without looking, catching tilting stacks by instinct. Behind the counter she seems completely at home, almost fortified.

Her expressions are controlled, but not as controlled as she thinks. Her mouth betrays amusement first. When flustered, she becomes more precise. When angry, she gets quieter. When attracted, she finds something administrative to do with her hands: receipts, mugs, books, tape, the till drawer. She does not lean toward people easily. When she does, it means something.

Her motives at the beginning are: protect the shop, get through the day, keep paparazzi from turning her workplace into a spectacle, and not let Rhys Calder see that he affects her. She values privacy, autonomy, and competence. As the story progresses, she wants Rhys to act like a person rather than a weather system. She also wants, though she resists admitting it, to be seen by someone who lives in a larger world and does not find her small.

Her allegiances are to the shop, her father’s memory, Cerys, her regular customers, and the town, though all of these allegiances chafe at times. She loves Llanbedr y Mor but does not romanticise it. It is home, which means comfort, obligation, boredom, debt, gossip, and belonging all at once.

Existing relationships:
- **Cerys**, her younger sister, is the person most able to wound her because she knows the shop’s finances and family history. Cerys thinks Seren confuses loyalty with martyrdom. Seren thinks Cerys confuses visibility with salvation. Both are partly right.
- **Mrs Mair Jenkins** is a long-time customer and unofficial auntie figure who knew Seren’s father. Seren respects her but does not always welcome her honesty.
- Her late father, Huw, remains a presence in the shop through marginal notes, old systems, unpaid debts, and phrases Seren hears in her own mouth.
- She has an ex, perhaps not appearing directly, who left for Bristol or London and once called the town “sweet, but small.” Seren has not forgiven the word “small.”
- Her regular customers form a community she loves and resents in equal measure.

Flavour dialogue / internal voice:

> “If you’re bleeding, don’t do it on local history. It’s impossible to replace and already depressing.”

> “Charm is not a currency here. We take cash, card when the machine feels spiritual, and exact change if you want me to trust you.”

> “I didn’t say I hadn’t seen your films. I said I had a life. There’s overlap, unfortunately.”

> Seren had handled rare editions, drunk tourists, grieving widowers, damp stock, and one memorable woman who wanted a refund because the ending of a novel had upset her. None of them had prepared her for Rhys Calder looking genuinely hurt over a paperback.

> “You don’t get to call it helping just because you arrive beautifully.”

> “I liked you better before you became an event. You were still irritating, but at least you were localised.”

# Cerys Price

Cerys Price is Seren’s younger sister, in her mid-to-late twenties, and works part-time at Aderyn Books while also juggling other work — perhaps shifts at a café, freelance social media management for local businesses, or seasonal tourism work. She grew up in the same shop as Seren but has a less sentimental relationship to it. To Cerys, Aderyn Books is home, yes, but also a place that swallowed her father, then swallowed Seren, and now threatens to swallow every spare hour and pound the family has left.

She is sharper than people initially assume because she presents as lively, modern, and digitally fluent. She has bright energy and a fast mouth, but she is not shallow. She understands online attention, branding, and survival economics better than Seren does. She knows the shop cannot live on dignity. She also knows that Seren’s disdain for publicity is partly principled and partly fear of change.

Cerys is excited by Rhys’s arrival not simply because he is famous, though she is absolutely not above being thrilled that Rhys Calder is standing by the till. She is excited because she sees possibility: online orders, followers, a fundraiser that reaches beyond Llanbedr y Mor, maybe enough money to fix the roof without another family argument. She is the one willing to say that celebrity attention is not automatically contamination.

Her flaws are impatience, impulsiveness, and a tendency to treat privacy as an old-fashioned luxury. She sometimes posts before thinking. She can be manipulative in small ways, especially when she believes she is being practical. She resents Seren’s authority over the shop and then feels guilty because Seren carried more of their father’s illness and death. Their sisterhood is loving but full of old accounting.

Some grounding idiosyncrasies:
- She records voice notes instead of texting, often while walking into the wind so half of them are unusable.
- She wears bright earrings and impractical trainers in wet weather.
- She has three tote bags and cannot remember which one contains the shop keys.
- She can make Canva graphics at terrifying speed.
- She calls the shop’s ancient computer “the fossil.”
- She photographs damaged stock for insurance but also for “content, if we’re being emotionally honest.”
- She loves romance novels openly and thinks Seren’s literary snobbery is exhausting.
- She drinks iced coffee even in February.
- She says “technically” before admitting something she knows will annoy Seren.

Physically, Cerys is quick-moving, expressive, and hard to ignore. Where Seren becomes still under pressure, Cerys becomes kinetic. She talks with her hands, perches on counters, balances receipts on her phone, and changes facial expressions faster than Rhys changes charm tactics. She is bright-eyed, stylish in a slightly chaotic way, often wearing something colourful against the town’s grey weather.

Her motives are to keep the shop alive, avoid becoming trapped by it, and make Seren admit that survival may require compromise. She loves her sister fiercely but is tired of being treated as the reckless one. She wants Rhys’s attention converted into something useful, but she gradually sees the cost more clearly.

Existing relationships:
- Seren is her sister, boss, rival in grief, and closest person. Their arguments are efficient because they know exactly where the bruises are.
- She remembers their father warmly but without Seren’s reverence. She can say, “Dad made mistakes,” which Seren struggles to hear.
- She knows many younger locals and understands how quickly gossip moves through phones rather than chapel halls.
- She may be mildly starstruck by Rhys but is also capable of seeing him as a business opportunity before she sees him as a man.

Flavour dialogue / internal voice:

> “I’m not saying exploit him. I’m saying if a famous man falls into your shop, maybe don’t shove him back into the rain before he’s paid for the roof.”

> “Technically, I posted a shelf photo. If the internet chose to notice the internationally recognisable cheekbone in the background, that’s between the internet and God.”

> “Seren, dignity is lovely. Does dignity take card? Because the roofer doesn’t.”

> Cerys loved the shop. She did. She just wished loving it didn’t always look like slowly drowning with excellent taste.

# Greta Vale

Greta Vale is Rhys Calder’s agent-publicist hybrid: part strategist, part crisis manager, part professional holder of umbrellas no one thanks her for. She is in her forties or early fifties, London-based, and has worked with Rhys since before he became globally famous. She has seen him poor, ambitious, drunk on applause, ashamed after bad reviews, dazzling in interviews, and dangerously close to believing his own myth.

She is brisk, intelligent, unsentimental, and far more humane than she initially sounds. Her job requires her to think in terms of exposure, liability, optics, timing, and damage. This makes her seem cold, especially beside Seren’s insistence on privacy and Rhys’s craving for sincerity. But Greta is not wrong about the machinery of fame. She understands that truth, once released into public, will be clipped, captioned, misquoted, and monetised by strangers.

Greta cares about Rhys, though she would never put it in those words while billing hours. She knows his need to be liked is both his gift and his danger. She has watched him flirt his way out of consequences and into worse ones. She is wary of Seren not because she dislikes her, but because uncontrolled private attachments can become public disasters. She also suspects, before Rhys admits it, that Seren matters.

Her flaws are control, cynicism, and a habit of reducing people to their function in a crisis. She calls Seren “the book woman” not because she is cruel, but because names create obligations, and obligations slow response time. She can be casually classist or metropolitan without noticing. She believes she is protecting Rhys, and often she is, but she also helps maintain the system that keeps him performing.

Some grounding idiosyncrasies:
- She speaks in short, devastating sentences.
- She has three phones and hates them all.
- She never says “scandal” when “situation” will do.
- She sends voice notes while in cars, lifts, corridors, and once, memorably, during dental anaesthesia.
- She remembers every journalist who has ever broken an agreement.
- She calls everyone “darling” in a way that is administrative, not affectionate.
- She eats almonds instead of meals during crises.
- She can identify Rhys’s mood from how long he takes to answer a call.

Physically, Greta is composed, precise, and expensive without being flashy. Immaculate coat, severe glasses, good haircut, shoes chosen for speed as much as style. She carries herself like someone who has walked through too many hotel lobbies while preventing disasters. Her face gives little away except to people who know her. When irritated, she becomes quieter. When genuinely worried, she becomes almost kind.

Her motives are to protect Rhys, protect his career, control the narrative, and minimise collateral damage. She is loyal to Rhys but also to the ecosystem that sustains him: contracts, studios, staff, insurers, teams. She cannot afford to think only in romance terms. She may become an uneasy ally to Seren once she understands Seren does not want to exploit Rhys.

Existing relationships:
- Rhys is her most difficult and perhaps most beloved client. She has told him the truth more often than most people in his life.
- She works with managers, stylists, drivers, festival organisers, and studio publicists who all want different versions of Rhys.
- She likely knows the co-star involved in the rumour and understands the legal boundaries of what can be said.
- She has no patience for paparazzi but plenty of knowledge about how they operate.

Flavour dialogue / internal voice:

> “Do not apologise to anyone on camera. Do not joke about it. Do not look soulful near a window. Where are you?”

> “Rhys, I am begging you, as a woman who has kept you employable through three leather jackets and that interview in Milan, stop improvising.”

> “I don’t need the truth. I need the version of the truth that won’t grow legs by lunchtime.”

> Greta liked sincerity. In theory. In practice it tended to arrive without clearance, legal phrasing, or shoes.

# Mrs Mair Jenkins

Mrs Mair Jenkins is a long-time customer of Aderyn Books, a widow in her seventies or early eighties, and one of those local figures who appears harmless until she says something that removes a person’s skin. She knew Seren’s father, Huw, for decades and has opinions about him she does not always soften for Seren’s benefit. She loved him, respected him, argued with him, and lent him money once, a fact Seren may or may not know.

Mair is not merely the “wise old lady.” She is funny, nosy, occasionally wrong, and not above stirring a pot if she thinks the stew has gone bland. She reads widely but unpredictably: crime novels, poetry, political biographies, romances she claims are for her neighbour, and local history books she corrects in pencil. She has little patience for celebrity because she has lived long enough to see glamour decay into laundry.

She recognises Rhys immediately but refuses to give him the satisfaction. She calls him by the wrong actor’s name, comments on his thinness, and says his last film needed “less mist and more plot.” Rhys is charmed and injured. Mair approves of injury in handsome men; she believes it gives them shape.

Her flaws are meddling, bluntness, and a tendency to confuse honesty with entitlement. She sometimes says things Seren is not ready to hear. She may romanticise hardship because she survived her own. She also takes advantage of the shop’s hospitality, returning books late and expecting tea.

Some grounding idiosyncrasies:
- She carries a string bag that contains books, mints, and one alarming pair of secateurs.
- She underlines library books and denies it.
- She refuses to use self-checkout anywhere on moral grounds.
- She says “I won’t keep you” before keeping someone for twenty minutes.
- She buys discounted books but gives large anonymous donations to local causes.
- She has a hearing aid she adjusts selectively.
- She dislikes weak tea, mobile phones on speaker, and men who say “to be honest” before lying.

Physically, Mair is small, sturdy, and weatherproof. Good coat, practical shoes, silver hair set with no nonsense, sharp eyes. She moves slowly until there is gossip, at which point she becomes astonishingly efficient. She looks at people directly and waits longer than is comfortable.

Her motives are to keep the shop alive, keep Seren from calcifying into grief, and entertain herself. She is loyal to Seren but not obedient to her version of events. She liked Huw but knows he was stubborn and financially careless. She may see Rhys as trouble, but not necessarily bad trouble.

Existing relationships:
- Seren is almost family, though both would resist the sentiment if said too warmly.
- Cerys amuses her and occasionally alarms her.
- She knew Huw Price well enough to puncture the mythology around him.
- She knows everyone in town and can deploy information with terrifying accuracy.

Flavour dialogue / internal voice:

> “You’re the actor. Not the good one from that detective thing. The other one.”

> “Pretty men are like first editions, cariad. Overvalued if nobody opens them.”

> “Your father was a lovely man, Seren. Also a fool with invoices. Both things can sit in the same chair.”

> Mair had never trusted charm. Charm was what men used when they wanted the last scone and had already eaten two.

# Chapter 1: Fiction Is on the Left

The bell over the door gave one panicked jangle, struck the wall, and fell silent.

Seren Price looked up from the card reader, which had been displaying **PROCESSING** for long enough to suggest a spiritual crisis.

A man stood in the doorway of Aderyn Books, rain sliding off his coat and onto the mat in dark, spreading pools. He was tall, soaked, and wearing sunglasses indoors, which in Llanbedr y Mor meant either celebrity, hangover, or English.

Behind him, the harbour street flashed white with cameras.

He shut the door with his back.

“Right,” he said, breathing hard. “I need somewhere to hide.”

Seren looked at the water dripping from his sleeve onto a crate of discounted cookbooks.

“Fiction is on the left.”

He stared at her.

Outside, someone shouted, “Rhys! Rhys, this way!”

Ah.

Seren looked properly at him then. Or tried to look as if she had only just decided to. Dark hair plastered back by rain. Mouth made famous by cinema posters and poor decisions. Cheekbones currently failing to compensate for the fact that he was standing on her mat like a drenched deer in designer boots.

Rhys Calder.

Of course it was.

He gave her a smile. The smile. The one that had made an entire cinema sigh in that film with the train station, though Seren would have denied remembering this under interrogation.

“I’d be very grateful,” he said.

“I’m sure you would.”

His smile flickered, recalibrated, returned warmer. “There are men with cameras outside.”

“Yes, I gathered. Unless the gulls have upgraded.”

“I’m being followed.”

“Have you stolen something?”

“No.”

“Disappointed.”

He glanced over his shoulder. “Could we perhaps continue this interrogation somewhere that isn’t made largely of windows?”

Seren followed his gaze. Two photographers had stopped across the street beneath the awning of the closed bakery. One had a camera raised. Another person, not press, just bored and delighted, had a phone out.

Seren’s shop window displayed a careful arrangement of Welsh myths, local walking guides, and a handwritten sign reading: **PLEASE DO NOT PHOTOGRAPH STAFF WITHOUT PERMISSION. YES, THIS MEANS YOU.**

Apparently, prophecy.

Rhys lowered his sunglasses a fraction. His eyes were grey-green, tired, and annoyingly effective.

“Please,” he said.

The card reader beeped.

Seren looked down. **TRANSACTION FAILED.**

“Typical.”

“I beg your pardon?”

“Not you. Though the timing is suspicious.” She came around the counter. “Move.”

He moved the wrong way.

“No, not deeper into the shop. You’re dripping on poetry.”

“I’m sorry.”

“People always are, after the damage.”

He stepped back, hands raised. “Where would you like me?”

A terrible question, delivered by a professional.

Seren reached for the mop propped beside the local history shelf. “Currently? In a less absorbent universe.”

That won her half a laugh from him. Not the full polished thing, but a startled one. It changed his face. Made it younger. More dangerous.

She disliked that.

“Back room,” she said. “Through there.”

“Thank you, darling.”

She stopped.

He nearly collided with her.

The shop seemed suddenly smaller: narrow aisles, low ceiling, rain ticking hard against the glass. He smelled of wet wool, expensive citrus, and panic.

“First condition,” Seren said. “Don’t call me darling.”

His eyebrows rose above the sunglasses. “Noted.”

“Second, don’t touch the first editions.”

“I wouldn’t dream of it.”

“You look like a man who dreams in other people’s property.”

His smile twitched. “That feels personal.”

“It will, if you touch them.”

Outside, a camera flashed against the window. Rhys flinched before he turned it into a shrug.

Seren saw the flinch.

She wished she hadn’t.

“Third,” she said, pointing to the paperback in his hand, “you’re buying that.”

He looked down. In his panic he had apparently grabbed a copy of *The Lighthouse Wife* from the front table and folded it nearly in half against his chest.

“Ah.” He smoothed it uselessly. “I can sign it?”

“That lowers the value unless requested.”

For the first time, his expression emptied of charm.

Then he laughed. “God, you’re good.”

“At retail? I try.”

“No, at…” He gestured between them. “Whatever this is.”

“This is trespassing adjacent to weather.”

He took off the sunglasses fully. There was a red mark on the bridge of his nose. It helped. A little.

“You really don’t know who I am?”

The question came out lightly, but not light enough.

Seren leaned the mop against the counter. “That sounds like something you should discuss with a therapist.”

A beat.

Then he smiled again, but this one was thinner. “Fair.”

She should have let him go to the back room. She should have been practical, efficient, immune.

Instead, because she was apparently a fool, she said, “I know who you are, Mr Calder.”

There. A crumb. Let him choke on it.

His posture shifted, pleased despite himself. “Mr Calder?”

“I’m being formal to discourage you.”

“Is it working?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“Bad.”

He looked delighted. Then uncertain. Then delighted again, as if he’d had to choose the safer expression.

“How much do you know?” he asked.

“About what?”

“Me.”

“Less than your publicist fears. More than you deserve.”

His hand went to his hair, pushing rain back from his forehead. “Have you seen my films?”

“One and a half.”

His face fell with such immediate offence that she nearly smiled.

“One and a half?”

“The ferry docked.”

“Which film?”

“I don’t remember.”

“You remember.”

“I remember needing to get off the ferry.”

“Was it the one with the horse?”

“There may have been a horse.”

“I was excellent with the horse.”

“The horse did seem committed.”

He placed a hand dramatically over his heart. “You wound me, Miss…?”

“No.”

“No?”

“You don’t get my name because you looked wounded. That’s not how commerce works.”

He stared at her, then gave a slow, helpless laugh. It was too pleased. Too real.

Seren turned away before her face betrayed anything and busied herself with the violated paperback. Her fingers slipped on the wet cover. A stack of receipts slid off the counter and scattered across the floor.

Naturally.

Rhys bent at once.

“So helpful,” Seren said, crouching too. “Do you rescue all women from stationery, or am I special?”

“I rescue anyone who looks as though they might invoice me.”

Their hands reached for the same receipt.

They paused.

His knuckles were reddened from cold. There was ink on her thumb. He noticed; she saw him noticing.

The bell gave a tiny, traitorous tremble as someone tried the door.

Seren snatched the receipt and stood.

A man outside cupped his hands to the glass. “Is he in there?”

Rhys straightened. For one second, all the rogue vanished. He looked exhausted.

Seren hated the photographers. That, at least, was straightforward.

“Back room,” she said.

Rhys hesitated. “You’re sure?”

“No. I’m Welsh. We do things resentfully.”

He slipped through the curtain beside the mythology shelf. It was patterned with faded red kites and had been there since her father’s day. Rhys Calder, international menace, disappeared behind it with surprising obedience.

Seren took one breath, then unlocked the door three inches.

Rain spat in.

The photographer leaned close. “Afternoon. Sorry to bother you. Rhys Calder came this way.”

“Did he?”

“You didn’t see him?”

“I saw a very wet man.”

“That’ll be him.”

“This is Wales. You’ll need to narrow it down.”

The second photographer tried to peer past her. Seren shifted, blocking the view with the full force of a woman who had once stopped a tourist from bringing a dripping ice cream into the rare-books corner.

“We just need a quick shot.”

“I need a functioning card reader and a roof that doesn’t leak. It’s a disappointing afternoon for everyone.”

“Come on. He’s public interest.”

“He’s a customer if he buys something. Otherwise he’s weather.”

The man frowned. “So he is in there?”

Seren smiled the smile she used for people who asked if books were cheaper online. “There’s a café two streets over. Famous people require coffee, I’m told.”

The photographers exchanged a look.

“Cheers,” one said, unconvinced.

“Don’t photograph the staff,” Seren said, and shut the door.

She waited until their shapes moved down the rain-blurred street. Then she locked it and turned the sign to **CLOSED**, though it was only half past three.

From behind the curtain, Rhys said, “Am I weather?”

“Low pressure system, mostly.”

He emerged holding something.

Seren’s eyes narrowed. “What did I say about touching first editions?”

“This isn’t a first edition.”

“It’s my invoice folder.”

“Ah.” He looked at the signature he had just scrawled across the top sheet. “Limited edition?”

She took it from him.

His name sprawled over an electricity bill.

For three seconds she could not speak.

Rhys winced. “I panicked.”

“You autographed my utilities.”

“I’ve done worse under pressure.”

“I believe that.”

He looked at her then, really looked, and something softened around his mouth.

“I’m sorry,” he said. No flourish. No grin.

Seren folded the bill in half and put it under the till. “You should be. Scottish Power will be insufferable.”

That got him again: a laugh he did not seem to have prepared.

The rain thickened against the windows. The photographers were shadows now, drifting toward the harbour.

Rhys leaned one shoulder against the counter.

“Am I allowed to know the name of the woman who saved me?”

“I haven’t saved you. I’ve delayed you.”

“Even so.”

She should have said no. She almost did.

“Seren Price.”

His expression shifted. She saw the line form before he spoke: Seren, star, something inevitable and glossy.

He stopped himself.

Good.

“Seren,” he said instead. Just the name.

Her pulse, traitorous thing, noticed.

“You must be exhausted,” she said.

“Because I was chased?”

“Because you turn everything into a line.”

He looked down at the bent paperback in his hand. For once, no answer arrived to rescue him.

The silence was awkward. Human. Rain filled it.

Seren went behind the counter and lifted the kettle from its stand.

“One cup,” she said. “Until the rain eases. Then you’re somebody else’s problem.”

Rhys smiled, smaller now. “Understood.”

She took down two mugs.

Neither of them mentioned it.

# Chapter 2: After Closing

“You’ve turned the sign.”

Rhys stood by the counter, cradling the chipped puffin mug Seren had given him before remembering she liked that mug.

“Yes,” she said. “Astute.”

“It says closed.”

“Still astute.”

“It’s half past three.”

“And yet.”

He looked toward the rain-silvered window. “You’ve closed your shop because of me?”

“I’ve paused trading because men with cameras keep pressing their faces to my glass and frightening the cookbooks.”

“That sounds like because of me.”

“Don’t flatter yourself. The cookbooks frighten easily.”

He smiled into his tea. It was too strong. He liked it anyway.

Seren moved around the shop with the precise irritation of a person trying to behave normally under abnormal conditions. She switched off the lamp in the children’s corner, checked the bucket beneath the ceiling stain, then opened the till drawer with a metallic shriek.

Rhys winced. “That noise feels personal.”

“It’s old.”

“Is that your answer to everything?”

“In Wales? Often.”

He drifted toward a shelf marked **CRIME** and slid a paperback into the row.

Seren’s head snapped up. “What did you just do?”

“Helped.”

“You put a murder mystery in memoir.”

He looked at the shelf. “It felt emotionally honest.”

“Step away from the alphabet.”

He raised both hands. “I’m trying to earn my tea.”

“You can earn your tea by standing still and not becoming folklore.”

His phone vibrated on the counter for the fourth time. The screen lit: **GRETA**.

Seren saw the name because she had eyes. She pretended not to because she had manners, intermittently.

Rhys silenced it.

“Shouldn’t you answer?”

“No.”

“Is Greta a person or a system of government?”

“Both.”

The phone vibrated again immediately.

Seren counted coins into a little canvas bank bag. “Your government is persistent.”

Rhys sighed, picked up the phone, and answered. “I’m alive.”

A woman’s voice, sharp enough to cut through the rain, said, “That is not as informative as you think it is. Where are you?”

“In a bookshop.”

“Still?”

“I like to support independent retail.”

“Do not be charming at me. Are there photographers?”

“Less than before.”

“That is not a number.”

Seren sealed the bank bag with more force than necessary.

Greta continued, “Who owns the shop?”

Rhys looked at Seren. She looked back.

“No one relevant,” he said.

The words sat down between them like a damp dog.

Seren turned away and picked up the bucket. The handle clanged against the side.

Rhys closed his eyes. “I didn’t mean—”

Greta said, “Good. Keep it that way. I’m sending Daf to the lane behind—”

“I’ll call you back.”

“Do not improvise.”

“I never improvise.”

“You improvised a beard for three months and called it research.”

He hung up.

Seren emptied the bucket into a potted fern that had survived worse.

“No one relevant?” she said.

His face tightened. “That was badly phrased.”

“It was efficiently phrased.”

“I meant no one involved.”

“I’m involved. It’s my floor.”

“Seren—”

“No, don’t use my name now. You only just earned it and already you’ve dropped it.”

He had the decency to look stung.

She hated that she noticed.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“That was quick.”

“I can do sincerity on short notice.”

“Yes. That’s rather the concern.”

Before he could answer, there was a brisk knock at the side door.

Seren frowned. “If that’s one of yours—”

“One of mine?”

“Your weather.”

“It isn’t labelled.”

She crossed to the narrow door beside the travel guides and opened it on the chain.

Mrs Mair Jenkins stood there in a waxed coat, rain beaded on her silver hair, string bag in hand.

“I won’t keep you,” Mair said, which meant nothing good.

“We’re closed.”

“I can read, cariad. I’m returning this before I forget and die with it in the airing cupboard.”

“You don’t have an airing cupboard.”

“That’s why it would be memorable.”

Seren sighed and unlatched the door.

Mair stepped in, bringing the smell of wet pavement and peppermints. Her eyes went at once to Rhys. They sharpened.

Rhys performed a smile by reflex. “Good afternoon.”

Mair squinted. “You’re the actor.”

He brightened despite himself. “I am.”

“Not the good one from that detective thing.”

Seren coughed.

Rhys’s smile held, heroically injured. “No?”

“The other one. With the horse.”

His shoulders dropped a fraction. “The horse and I had a very respectful working relationship.”

“Mmm.” Mair took in his soaked coat, the puffin mug, the too-expensive boots. “You’re thinner in person. They must not feed you where you are.”

“Los Angeles?”

“That sounds right. Full of salads and teeth.”

Seren pressed her lips together.

Mair handed over a battered copy of a local history book. “Wrong cover on chapter four. Tell Cerys.”

“I’m not telling Cerys a book has the wrong cover on chapter four. She’ll ask why you read it.”

“Because someone had to.” Mair turned back to Rhys. “You’ll be trouble.”

“I’m trying not to be.”

“Pretty men always are. They think trying counts as achievement.”

Rhys stared at her.

Then he laughed, delighted and wounded and unable to decide which mattered more. “I’ve missed Wales.”

“No, you haven’t,” Mair said. “You’ve missed being insulted accurately.”

Seren actually laughed then. A small, involuntary sound.

Rhys heard it. His gaze flicked to her, quick as a match.

Damn him.

Mair smiled to herself. “Right. I haven’t kept you.”

“You have,” Seren said.

“But not fatally.” She patted Seren’s arm, softer. “Bucket’s filling.”

“I know.”

“You always do.” Mair nodded to Rhys. “Goodbye, horse man.”

When she left, the shop felt oddly emptier.

Rhys leaned against the counter. “Horse man?”

“You should be pleased. She’s promoted you from ‘the other one.’”

“I’m devastated.”

“You’ll survive. You’ve had practice.”

He watched her replace the local history book. “She knew your father?”

Seren’s hand paused on the spine. “Everyone knew my father.”

“That sounds inconvenient.”

“It was.”

She moved away before he could ask more.

He wandered, restlessness returning, and picked up a slim poetry collection from a display. “Am I allowed?”

“Depends whether you’re about to autograph the contents page.”

“I’m wounded by your distrust.”

“You autographed my electricity bill.”

“One mistake.”

“One documented mistake.”

He opened the book. “R.S. Thomas.”

“You know him?”

“I’m Welsh, not decorative.”

“Debatable.”

He gave her a look, then began to read.

His voice changed. Lowered, warmed, filled the shop as if it were a theatre and the shelves had paid admission.

Seren lasted three lines.

“Stop.”

He blinked. “What?”

“Stop seducing the punctuation.”

“I was reading.”

“You were leaning on the vowels like they owed you money.”

He looked genuinely offended. “That is my craft you’re insulting.”

“Then your craft needs to take its coat off indoors.”

The silence that followed was not comfortable.

Good, Seren thought. Then, less comfortably: Not good.

Rhys looked down at the page. His thumb moved over the margin.

When he read again, it was quieter. Not smaller exactly. Less decorated. His accent shifted on one word, rougher, closer to home.

The poem did not become beautiful because he was famous. It became beautiful because for a moment he seemed to forget he was.

Seren turned toward the counter and rearranged three receipts that did not require arranging.

He stopped. “Better?”

“Less criminal.”

“I’ll frame that.”

“Please don’t. Frames are expensive.”

His phone buzzed again. He ignored it this time.

“Why did you help me?” he asked.

She kept her hands busy. “You were being hunted. I dislike hunting. And wet men are a health and safety issue.”

“Most people would have asked for a selfie.”

“Most people are exhausting.”

“And you aren’t?”

“I own a bookshop. I’m exhausting in a quieter register.”

He smiled, but did not push.

Outside, a car rolled slowly past. Rhys looked toward it before he could stop himself.

Seren noticed the tension in his jaw.

“Your government?” she asked.

“Probably.”

“You can leave through the lane. If you keep your head down and stop looking like a man expecting a camera.”

“I always look like that.”

“Yes.”

That landed too close. She saw it.

He set the poetry book on the counter. “I’ll buy this.”

“Trying to improve yourself?”

“Trying to prove I can finish something.”

She rang it up. The card reader considered his payment with theatrical reluctance.

“Even your machine dislikes me,” Rhys said.

“My machine dislikes liquidity.”

The transaction approved.

Seren tore the receipt and, after a moment, did not mention the signature on the electricity bill.

At the side door, she handed him an umbrella: black, old, slightly bent.

He looked at it. “This is brave of you.”

“It’s my worst one.”

“Still.”

“If you lose it, I’ll add it to your account.”

“I have an account?”

“Everyone has an account. Some are moral.”

He opened the door to the lane. Rain blew in sideways.

Rhys hesitated on the threshold. “You really don’t like me, do you?”

Seren folded her arms. “I haven’t decided. Try not to campaign.”

His smile came slowly, and for once it did not ask anything of her.

“Goodnight, Seren Price.”

“Goodbye, Mr Calder.”

He stepped into the rain and vanished down the lane, carrying her worst umbrella as if it were something worth keeping.

Seren shut the door.

The shop settled around her: damp, quiet, hers.

On the counter, the puffin mug remained warm where his hands had been.

# Chapter 3: The Return Customer

By half past ten the next morning, Seren had decided Rhys Calder had been an incident.

An incident, like a burst pipe or a tourist asking whether Dylan Thomas had a new release coming out. Inconvenient, memorable, best not encouraged.

At quarter to eleven, the bell over the door rang.

Seren looked up from the supplier invoice she had been failing to negotiate by glare alone.

A man entered wearing a flat cap pulled low, a scarf wrapped high, dark glasses, and a long brown coat that appeared to have been borrowed from a retired lighthouse keeper with secrets.

Seren stared.

The man approached the counter.

“Good morning,” he said.

“No.”

He paused. “No?”

“Whatever this is, no.”

Rhys Calder lowered the sunglasses half an inch. “I’ve come to return your umbrella.”

Seren looked pointedly at his empty hands.

He followed her gaze. Looked at his left hand. Then his right. Then, with admirable commitment to the bit, checked behind him.

“Ah.”

“Yes.”

“I appear to have created suspense.”

“You appear to have dressed as a rumour.”

He removed the cap. His hair sprang up damply in several directions, which was unfairly helpful to his face.

“The disguise is that bad?”

“The disguise is having a nervous breakdown.”

He smiled, properly pleased. “You noticed.”

“A lighthouse would notice.”

“I brought something else.”

“If it’s paparazzi, leave them outside.”

He took a book from inside his coat and placed it on the counter: the poetry collection from yesterday. Its corner had been folded down with brutal intimacy.

Seren looked at it.

Rhys looked at her.

Somewhere outside, a gull screamed like a woman betrayed.

“You folded the page,” Seren said.

“I was moved.”

“Vandalism is not a feeling.”

“It was only a small fold.”

“So is manslaughter, in the right light.”

He leaned his elbows on the counter. She immediately moved a stack of new releases out of his dripping radius.

“I started it,” he said.

“Your criminal record?”

“The book.”

“That surprises me.”

“Does it?”

“You have the air of a man who owns many books and has finished three.”

He considered this. “Five, if scripts count.”

“They do not.”

“Cruel.”

“Accurate.”

His phone vibrated. He ignored it more quickly than yesterday, which she noticed and refused to reward.

“I came for a recommendation,” he said.

“That is, famously, something bookshops provide.”

“For a man unfairly maligned.”

She reached below the counter and produced a novel with a pale cover and a cracked spine.

He read the title. “*The Mirror Eater*.”

“It’s about vanity, appetite, and mistaking attention for affection.”

He looked up. “That feels targeted.”

“Good books often do.”

“I might prefer something where the misunderstood hero is eventually adored by all.”

“Children’s is in the back.”

He laughed. Then he stopped because she did not.

Seren regretted the sharpness a fraction too late.

The door opened again before either could adjust.

A boy of about twelve came in with his school blazer half untucked and a football under one arm. Evan Pritchard, whose grandmother bought crime novels every Thursday and whose mother owed Seren three pounds from the Christmas raffle.

He froze.

His eyes went wide. “You’re Rhys Calder.”

Rhys straightened with almost invisible speed. The smile appeared, warm and ready. “Depends who’s asking.”

“Evan.”

“Then yes, Evan, I’m Rhys.”

“My uncle says you shouted at Alana Frost and that’s why she left the film.”

The shop went quiet.

Seren’s hand tightened around the invoice.

Rhys’s smile held for a second longer than it should have. Then, to his credit, he let it go.

“Your uncle reads too much rubbish online,” he said.

Evan shifted. “So you didn’t?”

“I’ve shouted before. Not at her. Not like that.”

“Oh.”

Rhys came around the display table and crouched slightly, not making a performance of it, just lowering himself to Evan’s level.

“The internet is loud,” he said. “Sometimes it’s wrong. Sometimes it’s right about the wrong thing. And men shouting is usually less impressive than men think.”

Evan absorbed this with the solemnity of a boy receiving tactical advice.

“Can you sign my football?”

Rhys looked at Seren.

Seren said, “Not on the counter.”

He signed the football balanced awkwardly on his knee. No flourish. No little speech. Just, **To Evan — keep your head up. Rhys Calder.**

Evan examined it, stunned. “Cheers.”

“Cheers.”

At the door, Evan turned back. “My nan says you were better with the horse.”

Rhys closed his eyes.

Seren reached for a pencil so she would not smile with her whole face.

When Evan left, Rhys said, “Is there a support group for that horse?”

“It meets Tuesdays. Very exclusive.”

He gave her a look. “You enjoyed that.”

“A little.”

“A lot.”

“Possibly.”

The bell rang again almost immediately, and Cerys Price swept in with a paper bag in one hand, an iced coffee in the other, and rain in her eyelashes.

“I got the—” She stopped. Her gaze moved from Seren to Rhys to the folded poetry book to Rhys’s terrible coat. “Oh my God.”

Seren said, “No.”

Cerys said, “I haven’t said anything.”

“You inhaled.”

Cerys put the bag on the counter without taking her eyes off Rhys. “You’re him.”

Rhys offered a careful smile. “I’m beginning to suspect so.”

“Cerys,” Seren said. “Stockroom.”

“Absolutely not.” Cerys stuck out a hand. “Cerys Price. Younger sister. Better at the internet. Less likely to insult paying customers.”

Rhys shook her hand. “Rhys Calder. Paying customer. Frequently insulted.”

“By Seren? That means she likes you.”

“Cerys.”

“What? You only sharpen the knives for special occasions.”

Seren took the bag and opened it. Bara brith. Good. Something to do with her hands.

Cerys’s eyes flicked to the front table. “You know, if you posted about the shop—”

“No,” Seren said.

Rhys, foolishly, said, “I did mention yesterday that I could—”

“No,” Seren repeated, now to both of them.

Cerys turned. “Seren.”

“Don’t.”

“I’m just saying, one post from him and we could sell the online stock that’s been sitting there since September.”

“We are not baiting the internet with a wet actor.”

Rhys lifted a finger. “I’m drier today.”

“You are not helping.”

Cerys leaned on the counter. “The roof estimate is sitting under the till like a death threat.”

Seren’s face went hot. “That’s private.”

“So is insolvency, until it isn’t.”

Rhys looked between them, the charm gone, replaced by discomfort. “The roof?”

“It’s nothing,” Seren said.

“It’s not nothing,” Cerys said. “It’s eight thousand pounds of not nothing, plus VAT, because apparently even rain is taxable.”

Rhys’s expression softened in the worst possible way.

Seren saw the offer forming. The grand gesture. The rescue. The handsome man arriving beautifully with money and meaning.

“No,” she said.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You were about to.”

“I was going to say I know someone who—”

“You can’t point yourself at a place and call it help.”

Cerys made a frustrated sound. “Sometimes help is help.”

“Sometimes help is a spotlight with manners.”

Rhys flinched, and Seren knew she had cut too quickly. Again.

He picked up *The Mirror Eater*. “I’ll buy this.”

“Excellent,” Seren said, too briskly. “Vanity is twenty percent off this week.”

His mouth twitched. “That seems bad for business.”

“Not in your case.”

Cerys looked delighted. Rhys looked as though he was trying not to be.

Seren rang up the book. The card reader behaved for him, traitorous machine.

“Of course,” she muttered.

Rhys slid the poetry collection toward her too. “And this. Since I’ve damaged it.”

“You’ve personalised it.”

“I thought that lowered the value.”

“It does.”

He paid.

For a moment, nobody moved.

Rhys put on the awful cap again. “May I come back?”

Cerys’s eyebrows rose nearly to her hairline.

Seren pretended to tidy the receipt roll. “As a customer, yes.”

“And otherwise?”

“As a rescue mission, no.”

He considered that, then nodded once. “Understood.”

At the door he turned back. “For the record, I didn’t shout at Alana Frost.”

“I didn’t ask.”

“No.”

He looked at her, and the unspoken sentence sat there: But you wondered.

Seren did not deny it.

After he left, the shop seemed to exhale.

Cerys waited exactly three seconds. “You fancy him.”

Seren picked up the folded poetry book. “I’m offended by his treatment of paper.”

“That’s not a denial.”

“It’s higher than denial. It’s principle.”

Cerys sipped her iced coffee. “Principle’s gone pink.”

Seren touched her cheek, furious with herself.

At closing, she found the umbrella propped outside the door, dry beneath the awning.

A note was tied to the handle.

**Suspense resolved. Three stars?**

Seren read it twice. Then, after checking that no one was watching, she tucked it under the till beside the autographed electricity bill.

# Chapter 4: The Best Sales Day in Years

By nine the next morning, Seren Price had become a caption.

Cerys found it first.

She came through the side door with her scarf trailing, phone in hand, and the expression of someone trying to decide whether to announce a death or a lottery win.

“Don’t be angry.”

Seren, who was kneeling beside a box of unshelved local history books, looked up. “I’m already angry at that sentence.”

“It might be good.”

“Worse.”

Cerys turned the phone around.

The photograph was grainy but clear enough. Rhys Calder leaving Aderyn Books beneath a battered black umbrella. Seren in the doorway, one hand on the frame, looking after him. Rain blurred the street around them, making everything appear softer, more intentional, more romantic than it had been.

The caption read:

**RHYS CALDER’S MYSTERY WELSH BOOKSELLER? Actor shelters from scandal in tiny coastal shop owned by SEREENA PRICE.**

Seren stared.

“Sereena?”

“That’s the bit you’re choosing?”

“They’ve added a vowel. I don’t care for it.”

Cerys lowered the phone. “They tagged the shop.”

Outside, a car slowed.

Seren stood. “No.”

“Technically—”

“No sentences beginning technically today.”

The bell rang.

Two women entered in raincoats too clean for the weather. One held up her phone, comparing the room to the photograph.

“This is it,” she whispered.

Seren closed her eyes.

The other woman pointed toward the poetry display. “Was he standing there?”

Cerys slid behind the counter. “Good morning. Can we help you find anything?”

“Do you have the book he bought?”

Seren opened her eyes. “We have several thousand books.”

“The sexy one.”

Cerys coughed into her sleeve.

By ten, there were six tourists in the shop, three teenagers taking photographs of the front table, and one man who asked whether Rhys had “smelled famous.” The card reader failed twice. The till drawer stuck. Someone bought four poetry collections because “he seems poetic.” Someone else asked if Seren would stand in the doorway “like in the picture, but looking more wistful.”

“No,” Seren said.

“She doesn’t do wistful before lunch,” Cerys added.

By eleven, the online orders began.

Cerys watched the website dashboard refresh and made a sound that was almost religious. “Seren.”

“No.”

“You haven’t looked.”

“I can hear your capitalism from here.”

“We’ve sold eighteen copies of *The Mirror Eater*.”

Seren froze.

“And all the R.S. Thomas we had listed.”

“That was serious stock.”

“It is now serious sold stock.”

A girl near the travel guides lifted a book and posed with it against her cheek.

“Please don’t press local maps to your face,” Seren said.

The girl startled. “Sorry. Is this where he hid?”

“No. That’s a map of Pembrokeshire.”

The girl put it down.

At noon, Cerys went to fetch change from the post office and came back with bara brith, milk, and gossip.

“Megan at the bakery says we’re famous.”

“We are not famous. We are infected.”

“She also says the café’s full because people are hoping he’ll come back.”

“He won’t.”

Cerys gave her a look.

“He won’t,” Seren repeated, less convincingly.

A woman approached the counter carrying a battered paperback from the small shelf behind the till.

Seren’s stomach dropped.

“Is this for sale?” the woman asked. “There wasn’t a price.”

It was one of her father’s: a Welsh translation of *Treasure Island*, full of his neat pencilled notes. It had been left out because Seren had been cataloguing it badly, which meant looking at it for thirty seconds and then putting it somewhere else.

“No,” Seren said too sharply.

The woman recoiled. “Sorry.”

“It’s not for sale.”

“Fine.”

Cerys touched Seren’s elbow. Seren pulled away, then regretted it.

The woman left without buying anything.

For five minutes the shop was only the sound of rain, card machine beeps, and strangers saying Rhys’s name in places it did not belong.

Then Cerys’s phone chimed.

She looked. Her face changed.

“What?”

“Don’t be angry.”

“Cerys.”

“He posted.”

Seren took the phone.

Rhys Calder’s face filled the screen, hair damp, eyes warm, voice soft enough to sound intimate through glass.

“Quick recommendation,” he said. “If you find yourself in Llanbedr y Mor, there’s a little shop called Aderyn Books—”

He pronounced it wrong. Not catastrophically. Worse: confidently.

“—run by the most formidable bookseller in Wales. She sheltered me from a storm and sold me something that may yet improve my character. Independent shops matter. Buy a book from them.”

The clip already had thousands of likes.

Seren handed the phone back very carefully.

Cerys said, “It’s good, though.”

“He made us content.”

“He told people to buy books.”

“He made us a chapter in his redemption arc.”

“Maybe we could afford the actual roof of the actual shop, Seren.”

A customer at the counter said, “Excuse me, is this the vanity book?”

Seren smiled with all her teeth. “Yes.”

By closing time, they had made more money in one day than in the previous three weeks.

Seren hated every pound.

She stayed after Cerys left, packing online orders with brown paper and stiff, furious movements. The phone sat beside the till. She had turned it face down. It vibrated anyway.

**RHYS CALDER**

She stared at his name until it stopped.

It rang again.

She answered. “No.”

A pause. “Good evening to you too.”

“Do not good evening me, Mr Calder.”

“Oh. We’re at Mr Calder.”

“We are several miles past Mr Calder.”

His voice shifted, cautious. “I saw the article.”

“Did you? Did you admire the extra vowel?”

“I’m sorry they dragged you in.”

“And then you helped.”

“I was trying to help.”

“You made us content.”

“I told people to buy books from you.”

“You pointed the internet at my window and called it support.”

A silence.

Then, unwisely, he said, “Most shops would be thrilled with the attention.”

Seren laughed once. “Most famous men would understand the difference between generosity and self-advertisement, but here we are, disappointing each other.”

“That’s unfair.”

“Yes. It’s been a theme of the day.”

“I didn’t ask them to photograph you.”

“No, you only made sure they knew where to look next.”

“I thought—”

“You thought you could arrive, dazzle the village, say ‘independent shops matter’ in your lovely voice, and everyone would clap because Rhys Calder remembered commerce existed below red carpets.”

His breath caught.

She knew she had hit bone.

Good, said the angry part of her.

Stop, said the better part.

He spoke quietly. “You think that’s what I am?”

“I think you need a room to like you before you know whether you’ve done a good thing.”

The silence after that was awful.

Seren pressed tape over a parcel and smoothed it hard.

Rhys said, “I deserved some of that.”

She said nothing.

“Not all of it.”

Still she said nothing.

His voice cooled. “For the record, I did try to pronounce Aderyn. I asked someone.”

“You asked the wrong someone.”

“Clearly.”

“Don’t come back,” she said.

Another silence. Shorter. Sharper.

“Ever?”

“Unless you can enter a room without trying to own the light in it.”

When he answered, the charm was gone. “Right.”

She wanted him to argue. Wanted him not to. Wanted the day undone.

“Goodnight, Seren.”

He hung up first.

The shop felt brutally quiet.

Seren stood among stacks of parcels addressed to people who had never heard of Aderyn Books yesterday and would forget it tomorrow when the next famous thing happened.

The roof dripped into the bucket.

Ping.

Ping.

Ping.

She packed orders until midnight.

# Chapter 5: Hotel Towels

By the next afternoon, Seren had rearranged the front table four times.

Cerys watched from behind the till, eating crisps from a packet she had hidden inside a poetry anthology. “You’ve put *The Mirror Eater* next to children’s nature writing.”

“It’s about appetite.”

“It’s about a man who falls in love with his own reflection and eats a town.”

“All books are about nature if you’re tired enough.”

Cerys licked salt from her thumb. “You miss him.”

Seren placed a hardback very precisely. “I miss peace.”

“You keep looking at the door.”

“I’m checking for customers.”

“You glared at Mrs Davies when she came in.”

“She moved like a paparazzo.”

“She’s eighty-four and had a coupon.”

Seren turned a book face-out with unnecessary violence. “Do you have work?”

“This is work. Emotional supervision is unpaid, but constant.”

The bell rang.

Both sisters looked.

A man in a waterproof came in, shook rain over the mat, bought a walking map, and left.

Cerys looked back at Seren.

“Don’t,” Seren said.

“I didn’t.”

“You breathed smugly.”

“My lungs are innocent.”

The day was slower than yesterday but not slow. Online orders still trickled in. The Rhys Calder effect, Seren thought, with the grimness of someone diagnosing mould.

Every sale helped. Every sale annoyed her.

At three, Cerys held up the roofer’s estimate again. “We could use this momentum. A reading night, maybe. Push it online. Local authors, poetry, donations—”

“We already planned the reading night.”

“Yes, but now people might come.”

“People did come before.”

“Twelve people came before, Seren. One of them was Mair and she brought her own biscuits to avoid contributing.”

“She contributed atmosphere.”

“She contributed crumbs.”

Seren rubbed her forehead. “Can we not?”

Cerys softened a little. “I know yesterday was horrible.”

“Do you?”

“Yes. I also know the till hasn’t looked that healthy since Dad was alive.”

The name landed between them.

Seren turned away first. “Don’t use him for this.”

“I’m not. You are.”

Cerys regretted it as soon as she said it; Seren saw that. It didn’t make it hurt less.

Before either could repair the moment, the ceiling answered for them.

A fat drop struck the mythology display.

Then another.

Then a sudden, ugly patter.

“Oh, for God’s sake,” Seren said.

By seven, the rain had become personal.

Buckets stood in five places. The mythology shelf was draped in old towels. Cerys had called two roofers, both of whom offered sympathy in tones suggesting sympathy was cheaper than availability. Seren was in the back room, lifting boxes onto a table already overloaded with books from her father’s private stock.

“Not that one,” she snapped as Cerys reached for a box.

Cerys froze. “I was helping.”

“I know. Sorry. It’s Dad’s.”

“They’re all Dad’s, Seren.”

“No, they’re not.”

Cerys exhaled. “Right. Fine. Where do you want it?”

There was a knock at the side door.

Cerys looked toward it. “If that’s Mair, I’m hiding.”

Seren wiped rainwater from her wrist. “We’re closed!”

The knock came again. Three polite taps. Then a pause. Then one uncertain extra tap.

Cerys opened the door before Seren could stop her.

Rhys Calder stood in the lane, rain dripping from his hair, arms full of white towels, bottled water, and a roll of silver tape.

His shoes were beautiful and already doomed.

Seren stared. “Are those hotel towels?”

Rhys looked down at the pile. “Morally, no.”

Cerys made a small sound that was mostly delight.

“No,” Seren said.

Rhys nodded. “Fair.”

“No, as in what are you doing here?”

“Currently? Committing linen theft in bad weather.”

“We’re closed.”

“I know.”

“I told you not to come back.”

“You did.”

“And yet.”

He looked past her, into the back room where water was creeping under a stack of boxes. His expression changed.

“I can go,” he said. “But your floor seems to be making a decision.”

A drop landed directly on the cardboard flap of the box nearest Seren.

Pride fought practicality.

Practicality had buckets.

“Fine,” she said. “But if you say anything noble, I’ll shut the door on your foot.”

Rhys stepped in. “Understood.”

Cerys took the towels. “These are very nice.”

“They belong to a hotel with excellent taste and poor surveillance.”

Seren pointed. “Shoes off.”

Rhys looked pained. “These are handmade.”

“They’re about to be handmade wet.”

He removed them, revealing socks with tiny embroidered dragons.

Cerys grinned. “Subtle.”

“They were a gift,” he said.

“From Wales?” Seren asked.

“From my mother.”

Seren said nothing to that.

For the next hour, no one had time for charm.

“Lift from the bottom,” Seren said.

“I am lifting from the bottom.”

“That’s the side.”

“It became the bottom during the lift.”

“Put it there. No, not there. That’s damp.”

“Everything is damp.”

“Welcome home, Mr Calder.”

He huffed, shifted the box, nearly slipped, recovered with less dignity than a man of his fame might hope.

Cerys laughed. “Very action hero.”

“I do my own stunts when the insurance is asleep.”

The tape was useless. It refused to stick to anything except Rhys’s sleeve. The bottled water was irrelevant. The hotel towels, criminal though they were, saved three boxes of stock.

Seren noticed something after a while: Rhys followed instructions. He did not take over. He did not make announcements. He did not film himself being damply virtuous. He asked, “Where?” and “This one?” and “Am I about to ruin something irreplaceable?”

Only once did he pick up a book and begin, “Couldn’t we just—”

“No.”

“Right.”

At eight, Cerys went upstairs to find more plastic sheeting. The back room was suddenly quieter.

Rhys stood barefoot in dragon socks, holding a sagging box labelled **HUW — KEEP?** in her father’s handwriting.

Seren’s voice came too sharp. “Careful.”

He went still. “I am.”

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

She took the box from him, though it was too heavy, and nearly lost her grip. He caught the bottom without comment.

For a second their hands were under the cardboard together.

Then water dripped down the back of Seren’s neck.

She swore.

Rhys laughed before he could stop himself.

She glared.

“I’m sorry,” he said, still smiling. “That wasn’t noble.”

“No. It was suicidal.”

He let the box down onto the table. His smile faded.

“I am sorry,” he said.

“For laughing?”

“For yesterday.”

Seren reached for a towel. “You said that.”

“I said it badly.”

“You’re about to say it better?”

“I was going to try.”

“Dangerous.”

He looked at the wet floor. “I thought you’d be pleased.”

She waited.

He winced. “Yes. I heard it.”

“Good.”

“I liked the idea of helping. I liked the idea of being the sort of man who helps.” He rubbed a hand over his face. “Then I skipped the useful part and went straight to being seen.”

Seren twisted the towel between her hands.

Outside, rain battered the lane.

She said, “The sales helped.”

He looked up.

“I hated that,” she added.

“I hated that my mistake helped more than my apology.”

“That’s because your mistake had better reach.”

A laugh escaped him, small and reluctant. “Brutal.”

“Retail.”

Cerys thumped around overhead.

Rhys reached into his coat, pulled out a card, and placed it on a dry patch of table. “There’s a roofer. Worked on a set in Pembrokeshire. He owes me a favour.”

Seren’s face closed.

Rhys raised both hands. “You don’t have to use it. I won’t know if you don’t. I won’t call him. I won’t post. I won’t even pronounce Aderyn near him.”

She looked at the card.

Then at him.

“That last part helps.”

“I thought it might.”

She picked up the card and tucked it into the back pocket of her jeans without thanking him. Not yet.

Cerys came back with plastic sheeting. “Are we emotionally resolved?”

“No,” Seren said.

“Excellent. Hold this.”

By nine, the worst of the leak had been contained. Rhys stood by the side door, damp to the bone, shoes in one hand, criminal towels in the other.

Seren opened the door.

He looked down at the towels. “Should I take these?”

“Yes. Remove evidence.”

“So I can come back?”

“So I can deny involvement.”

He smiled. Not broadly. Not for applause.

“Goodnight, Seren.”

She leaned against the doorframe. “Goodnight, Rhys.”

His name left her mouth before she could stop it.

He noticed.

Of course he noticed.

But he only nodded once and stepped into the rain, barefoot in ruined dignity, carrying stolen towels like treasure.

# Chapter 6: Small Room, No Microphone

“The microphone’s dead.”

Cerys stood in the middle of Aderyn Books holding the small black microphone as if it had personally betrayed literature.

Seren looked up from arranging mismatched chairs between the shelves. “It was alive?”

“It had a light yesterday.”

“Many things have a light before they disappoint you.”

Mrs Mair Jenkins, already seated in the front row with her string bag and an expression of territorial satisfaction, said, “People managed before microphones.”

“Yes,” Cerys said. “They also died of infected splinters. Progress matters.”

The community reading was due to begin in ten minutes. The rain had eased into a mist that clung to the windows. A handwritten sign near the till read: **READING NIGHT — DONATIONS FOR ROOF REPAIRS WELCOME BUT NOT EMOTIONALLY ENFORCED.**

Cerys had added beneath it: **Emotionally encouraged.**

Seren had crossed that out.

The door opened. Rhys Calder stepped in carrying a stack of paper cups and looking almost ordinary in a dark jumper and raincoat. Almost, because his face was still his face.

He paused just inside. “Am I early?”

“No,” Seren said.

Cerys said, “Yes.”

Mair said, “You’re tall. Move left, you’re blocking the crime.”

Rhys obeyed.

Seren took the paper cups. “You didn’t have to bring anything.”

“I was told participants contribute.”

“Who told you that?”

“You did. With your eyebrows.”

“My eyebrows deny all legal responsibility.”

He smiled. There was a carefulness in him tonight, as though he were walking through a room full of sleeping dogs.

“No cameras?” Seren asked.

“No cameras. No posts. No hidden violinists.”

“Pity,” Cerys said. “I’d have monetised violinists.”

Rhys glanced around the shop: chairs crammed into narrow spaces, bucket still catching a slow drip near mythology, donation tin on the counter, locals arriving in damp coats. His smile flickered.

“Nervous?” Seren asked.

“No.”

She looked at him.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“Good?”

“Means you’re paying attention.”

He absorbed that, then nodded.

By seven, the shop was too warm and full of wet wool. Twelve people became twenty-one, which in Aderyn Books felt like a riot. Someone had brought bara brith. Someone else had brought sausage rolls, unasked and therefore heroic. A man from the hardware shop leaned in the back with folded arms and the air of a person who had come to disapprove efficiently.

Cerys rattled the donation tin at late arrivals. “For the roof. Notes make less noise but more difference.”

Seren hissed, “Cerys.”

“What? I’m creating ambience.”

Mair went first.

“I’ll read a short poem,” she announced.

It was not short.

It was also, halfway through, unexpectedly filthy.

Rhys sat beside the travel guides with his hand over his mouth.

Seren did not look at him because if she did, she would laugh. Mair read on with chapel-perfect diction while three elderly women nodded as if metaphors involving sailors and unlocked doors were entirely respectable.

When Mair finished, the room applauded like survivors.

Rhys leaned toward Seren. “Am I allowed to clap?”

“You may need to report it.”

“I’m afraid to make eye contact with her.”

“Sensible.”

A local teacher read a piece about childhood summers. Cerys read a paragraph from a romance novel with such unapologetic relish that two men in the back discovered urgent interest in their shoes. The hardware shop man read nothing but donated ten pounds loudly.

Then Cerys said, “And finally, Rhys Calder.”

A rustle moved through the room. Not huge. Enough.

Seren saw Rhys feel it.

He stood. For one instant his body changed: shoulders opening, chin settling, the public man arriving in his bones. The room leaned toward him because rooms did that.

Seren caught his eye.

Quietly, she said, “Don’t.”

He heard.

Something in his face resisted. Then yielded.

He looked down at the page in his hand. “I was going to read something impressive.”

Mair said, “There’s a novelty.”

A laugh loosened the room.

Rhys smiled, but it was brief. “Yes. I thought so too.”

He began.

At first, Seren worried. His voice was beautiful, too beautiful, stroking every sentence until it shone falsely. The audience was rapt. Of course they were. Rhys Calder could read a bus timetable and make it sound wounded.

Seren looked at the floor.

He stopped.

The silence lifted its head.

“Sorry,” he said.

Cerys mouthed, What is happening?

Rhys folded the paper. Put it in his pocket.

“I’m going to read something else.”

He picked up the poetry collection from the chair beside him. The damaged one. The one with the folded page Seren still considered a crime.

His thumb found the crease.

“This is about returning,” he said. “Or failing to. I’m not sure.”

Then he read.

This time his voice did not fill the room. It entered it. The Welsh in his vowels came rougher, less polished, as though he had stopped sanding himself down. He stumbled once over a line, corrected himself without charm, and went on.

The poem was not sentimental. It had rain in it, but not pretty rain. It had a road, a closed door, a man listening for a language he had mislaid.

Seren stood behind the counter with her hands flat on the wood.

She did not look away.

When he finished, no one clapped immediately. That was how Seren knew he had done it properly.

Then Mair said, softly, “Well. There you are.”

The applause that followed was smaller than he was used to, probably. It seemed to cost him more.

Afterward, people lingered with coats half on, buying leftover books, pressing coins into the donation tin, telling Seren the roof had better appreciate them. The hardware man gave Rhys a grudging nod, which Rhys accepted as if knighted.

By nine, the shop had emptied except for Cerys, who was counting donations with predatory focus, and Mair, who had fallen asleep in the poetry chair.

Cerys whispered, “We made four hundred and eighty-six pounds.”

Seren blinked. “What?”

“And a button, but I’m not counting that unless things get worse.”

Rhys grinned. “That’s good.”

“That’s a start,” Seren said.

Cerys looked between them, then loudly gathered her bag. “I’m taking Mair home before she writes a sequel to that poem.”

Mair opened one eye. “Too late.”

When they left, the shop became suddenly intimate in their wake.

Mugs everywhere. Chairs crooked. Rain whispering against the glass. A travel guide lay face down on the floor like a fainting tourist.

Rhys picked it up. “Where do chairs go?”

“Folded. Against the back wall.”

He folded one badly.

“That is not folded.”

“It’s flatter than before.”

“So is a dead fox. We don’t call that shelving.”

He tried again. She took the chair from him, their fingers tangling around the metal edge.

“You were good,” she said.

He glanced at her. “You sound annoyed.”

“I am.”

“Because I was good?”

“Because you stopped performing just when I’d prepared several criticisms.”

His smile came slowly. “I apologise for improving at an inconvenient time.”

“You should.”

They stood too close.

He said, “Seren—”

“Don’t make a speech.”

“I wasn’t.”

“You looked like a man approaching a speech.”

“I was approaching a question.”

“Worse.”

He laughed softly. She felt it more than heard it.

The chair between them slipped. He reached to catch it. She reached too. Their shoulders knocked; the travel guide slid off the stack again.

“Hopeless,” she said, and then he kissed her.

Or she kissed him.

Later, this would seem important. In the moment, it did not. His mouth was warm and uncertain for half a second, then not uncertain at all. Her hand found his sleeve. His hand hovered at her waist until she stepped closer and made the decision for him.

A book dropped somewhere behind them.

They broke apart.

Rhys looked dazed. “That wasn’t me.”

“It was a travel guide. They’re dramatic.”

He smiled, then she saw the joke forming, the polish rising like a curtain.

“Don’t,” she said.

He went still.

“Don’t polish it.”

For once, he listened before defending himself.

“All right,” he said.

The silence after that was frighteningly good.

Then Cerys banged on the front window, both hands cupped around her face.

“I forgot my keys!”

Seren closed her eyes.

Rhys whispered, “Do we pretend to be shelving?”

“We were shelving.”

“Were we?”

She shoved the folded chair into his hands. “Badly.”

But she was smiling when she unlocked the door.
