# Intention

The piece will be an 8-chapter short story of approximately 8,000 words total: compact, dialogue-forward, politically tense, and grounded in human detail. It will serve the original prompt directly: colonial Mars is being mined by corporations using leased indentured labour; Azra, an exotic decay-accelerating metal, has triggered a gold rush and arms race; Arthur Neegan, a first-generation Martian settler and mining engineer, discovers his small claim sits atop an immense Azra vein; an armed but polite Antarean retinue removes him from his home and draws him into off-world intrigue.

The story will open with Arthur already aboard the transfer vessel, as requested, wondering what he has become involved in. The armed descent on his home will be presented immediately through recent memory, not as a distant flashback. This will reconcile the prompt’s two opening instructions while keeping the first chapter active and disorienting.

The governing mode will be classic science fiction: rational pressure, institutional menace, technology with political consequences, and a climax built on thought rather than battle. The prose should have a retrofuturistic texture—orbital transfer craft, analog gauges, punch-card archives, sealed Martian cottages, atomic calculators, oxygen ledgers, printed contracts, polished diplomatic habitats—but it should avoid becoming decorative pastiche. The atmosphere will be restrained, lucid, and slightly formal, with dry humor and civilized threat. The story should feel like people under pressure speaking carefully because every word may become evidence.

The main voice will stay close to Arthur’s perception. Arthur is not a chosen hero or natural revolutionary. He is a tired, proud, technically competent Martian engineer who owns very little except his claim, his tools, and his stubbornness. His flaw is that he has mistaken independence for innocence. He dislikes the corporations and avoids leased labour, but he has still benefited from the colonial machinery around him. He begins by thinking in terms of property and survival. He ends by thinking in terms of custody, risk, and obligation.

Arthur’s emotional stakes will be concrete. His home, Neegan Spur, is not simply “land”; it is a patched pressure cottage made from old cargo cylinders, an aging pump he can diagnose by sound, a legal patent his parents fought to keep, and the one place on Mars where he does not owe anyone permission to breathe. Voss’s offer must genuinely tempt him: money, protection, repairs, recognition, revenge against Heliox, and the release of named workers. His final refusal to sell exclusive control will therefore cost him something real.

The principal Antarean figure will be Minister Cyrene Voss of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. She will be elegant, dangerous, and sincere in selected ways. Antares is not evil for evil’s sake. It fears Earth’s energy and weapons monopoly and remembers previous embargoes that killed outer-colony civilians. Voss wants Arthur’s claim because exclusive Azra access would free Antares strategically—and allow it to build the drives and weapons needed to survive a coming confrontation. Her initial move is the first “Azra gambit”: obtain legality before rivals can move by force. She is coercive, but not stupid; courteous, but not kind.

The corporate antagonist will be Heliox-Levant Resource & Atmosphere, usually called Heliox. Its representative, Director Sef Trane, will not speak like a villain. He will speak like a manager of indispensable systems: oxygen contracts, hospitals, transport liens, lease labour, risk allocation. His moral horror lies in the blandness with which he makes exploitation sound like infrastructure. Heliox must be frightening because it is embedded in Martian survival, not because it twirls a mustache.

Mira Saye will be an indentured survey technician whose knowledge and testimony are essential. She will not exist only to awaken Arthur’s conscience. She has her own agenda: to expose falsified Azra survey data, find out what happened to two “reassigned” surveyors, and prevent another mineral rush from consuming workers under the name of opportunity. She distrusts Arthur’s property rights even while needing them. She will force the anti-indenture provision into Arthur’s final plan, so the labour victory is not Arthur benevolently saving workers, but the result of pressure from someone whose life has been shaped by the system.

The Martian Provisional Council, represented by Commissioner Ada Lorne, will be weak but not foolish. Lorne knows the old Founding Compact and knows Mars has legal powers it cannot usually afford to enforce. She cannot move first without risking blockade, debt collapse, or oxygen retaliation. Arthur’s valid private patent creates a rare procedural opening. Her later ratification of his gambit should feel like a dangerous political act, not paperwork.

The Earth faction will be represented by an envoy from the Bureau of Radiological Equilibrium, informally “the Equilibrium Office.” Earth’s argument will not be absurd: Azra is a dual-use material capable of destabilizing the weapons balance. Earth wants containment. Its hypocrisy is that containment conveniently means Earth control.

Azra’s science will be clear but not overexplained. It is an exotic metallic lattice that catalyzes radioactive decay, releasing in hours or days what certain isotopes would normally release across years or centuries. This makes it valuable for interstellar drives, nuclear waste processing, isotope batteries, and weapons. Arthur’s technical insight will be that the vein beneath Neegan Spur is not merely a pile of ore. Its natural matrix moderates its catalytic effect. If fractured and extracted according to ordinary corporate models, it could create lethal decay cascades in old settlement waste stores and isotope infrastructure. The science should be discovered through practical engineering signs: bad counters, spoiled calibration sources, aged components, suspiciously smoothed survey data, and Arthur’s knowledge of how equipment fails.

The sabotage chapter will provide danger but not become an action spectacle. A false maintenance drone or illicit drilling charge will breach a shaft and threaten a localized Azra-isotope event. Arthur and Mira will survive through engineering, improvisation, and mutual dependence. The saboteur’s identity will remain unresolved. The point is not mystery-solving; the point is that once Azra becomes strategically valuable, every faction has both motive and deniability.

The climax will be Arthur’s counter-gambit. He will use the claims of all factions against them, but the legal solution must not feel magical. It will be seeded through the Neegan family’s old patent, Lorne’s guarded hints, and the Founding Compact. Arthur’s move works because it gives every major power a second-best outcome preferable to another faction’s monopoly. He dedicates Neegan Spur’s Azra formation to a Martian Hazard Trust: no exclusive corporate, Earth, or Antarean ownership; transparent isotope accounting; international inspection; Martian technical stewardship; and, at Mira’s insistence, no indentured labour in Azra extraction or processing because coerced consent cannot authorize extreme hazard work.

The ending will be cautiously unresolved. Arthur will not “fix Mars.” The trust will be provisional, contested, and surrounded by loophole-seeking powers. Heliox will angle for service contracts. Earth will demand inspectors. Antares may have anticipated the trust as an acceptable fallback. The Azra labour leases will be suspended, not all indenture abolished. Mira’s freedom will be real but incomplete. Arthur will return to a home that is no longer private, watched by towers, drones, and committees. The final note will be hope as pressure management, not triumph: Mars has gained a foothold, not victory.

The story will avoid common artificial neatness. Characters will not all speak in the same voice. Themes will be dramatized through contracts, airlocks, debts, injuries, and choices rather than stated repeatedly. The prose will favor concrete images over grand declarations: red dust in a cuff, an old pump clicking, a printed contract clause, a worker’s lease mark, a pressure gauge trembling. The big picture will always be anchored in something small enough to touch.

# Chapter Planning

## Chapter 1 — The Invitation

Arthur Neegan is aboard an Antarean transfer vessel, watching Mars shrink through a thick glass port. The cabin is too clean, all polished alloy, brass-rimmed pressure dials, and a soft atomic hum behind the wall. Red dust from his work cuff floats loose in the air, an absurd little piece of home following him into orbit.

He is not locked in, exactly. The door opens. The corridor beyond contains polite armed men.

Arthur thinks back to an hour earlier, when three sleek skimmers settled outside his pressure cottage at Neegan Spur. The cottage is described in quick, personal detail: cargo-cylinder walls, an old pump left half-disassembled, his mother’s framed patent copy, dust needling at the outer seal. The Antarean insignia—a star within a laurel—marked the skimmers. The “diplomatic” retinue carried sidearms and pressure rifles but spoke with immaculate courtesy. Their officer never said Arthur was under arrest. He said Arthur’s presence was urgently requested in an off-world consultation.

Arthur asked whether he could refuse. The officer replied that refusal would introduce “avoidable complications.”

On the transfer vessel, Arthur needles his escort with practical questions. Is his home sealed? Who shut down the pump? Is this about Heliox? Is it about the assay from his lower bore? The escort avoids the word Azra until Arthur says it first. The silence tells him more than an answer.

Through Arthur’s thoughts, we learn the essentials without an exposition dump: he is a first-generation Martian, a mining engineer, owner of a poor independent claim called Neegan Spur. The claim was thought nearly worthless until a deep survey returned impossible Azra readings. Arthur had barely had time to distrust the numbers before Antares arrived.

The chapter ends as the vessel docks with a rotating diplomatic habitat in high orbit. Arthur glimpses Antarean cutters berthed behind ceremonial screens. Their gun ports are covered but not hidden. A steward informs him that Minister Voss is ready.

## Chapter 2 — The Offer

Arthur is brought into the Antarean legation: a curved chamber with star maps, filtered light, old-fashioned paper documents, and a viewport showing Mars like a rust-red coin below. Minister Cyrene Voss greets him as though he is an honored guest rather than a man escorted by armed guards.

This is the early dialogue-heavy scene. Voss explains, through careful conversation rather than lecture, that Arthur’s claim sits atop the richest Azra formation yet found. Arthur remains skeptical, dry, and literal. He says he owns forty-seven square kilometers of basalt, debt, and failing seals. Voss says that was true last week.

Voss describes Azra’s significance in terms Arthur understands. It accelerates radioactive decay. In a drive, it can release decades of isotope energy in weeks. In waste processing, it can burn poisons down toward stability. In weapons, it can ruin every comfortable calculation of deterrence. Earth wants containment. Heliox wants extraction. Antares wants legal custody before either can impose a monopoly.

She makes her offer. Antares will buy out Arthur’s debts, rebuild Neegan Spur, guarantee him protection, pay him a fortune, and purchase the release of specified indentured survey crews, including several whose names Arthur recognizes from Mars work ledgers. In return, he must sign a custodial mineral lease granting Antares extraction jurisdiction beneath his claim. The document is printed on actual paper, heavy and formal.

Arthur asks why she does not simply take the mine. Voss answers that force without title is war, and war is expensive. Legitimacy is cheaper, rarer, and currently belongs to him.

The conversation hints at larger intrigue: Earth observers are en route; Heliox has filed a fraud challenge to Arthur’s patent; two surveyors vanished after questioning anomalous readings; Antares believes the strategic balance may collapse within eighteen months. Voss admits Antares wants to prevent war if possible and win it if not.

Arthur does not sign. He asks for the complete survey record and time on his own ground. Voss allows twelve hours and warns him that politeness has a half-life.

Alone afterward, Arthur reads the contract. He is less alarmed by the money than by one repeated word: jurisdiction. Antares is not merely buying ore. It is asking him to make part of Mars legally foreign.

## Chapter 3 — Claims and Counterclaims

Arthur returns to Mars under Antarean escort but not Antarean control. The moment he lands, he discovers that every institution has moved while he was in orbit.

His bank access is frozen pending strategic mineral review. Heliox-Levant Resource & Atmosphere has filed a challenge claiming the original Neegan patent was improperly surveyed. The Equilibrium Office from Earth has issued a radiological containment advisory. The Martian Provisional Council has summoned him to Dome Lowell. Corporate drones hover near his cottage, and Council constables apologize while refusing to leave.

At Dome Lowell, Arthur meets Commissioner Ada Lorne, who is tired, procedural, and sharper than she first appears. She tells him the Council has authority over Mars “in the same way a man in a leaking suit has authority over his breathing.” She cannot protect him openly unless there is a public legal record.

Arthur is then approached by Director Sef Trane of Heliox. Trane is blandly reasonable. He reminds Arthur that Heliox built half the oxygen infrastructure, owns the nearest refining plant, operates the emergency hospitals, and manages most labour transport liens. He offers a partnership: Arthur keeps a title, Heliox takes operations. If Arthur refuses, Heliox will pursue the patent challenge and argue incompetence.

Arthur also meets Mira Saye, an indentured survey technician. She helped process the deep scan of Neegan Spur. She tells Arthur Heliox smoothed away anomalous readings before submitting public data. She knows of two surveyors listed as “contractually reassigned” after objecting. One was her friend. She does not trust Arthur, but his patent may be the only legal wedge available.

Mira shows Arthur a lease ledger. Workers are charged for air, tools, suit wear, medical treatment, and transport delays. Debt does not decay. Arthur is uncomfortable; he has avoided using leased labour, but he recognizes how much of Mars runs on it.

The chapter ends when Arthur learns that his lower bore has been sealed by injunction “for safety.” He decides that any place everyone wants him not to inspect deserves inspection immediately.

## Chapter 4 — The Vein Beneath

Arthur and Mira enter Neegan Spur through an old maintenance adit omitted from modern Heliox maps. The chapter shifts from offices and contracts into physical Mars: pressure doors, frost at seams, dust in suit joints, the silence beyond the tunnel skin, and the familiar bad temper of old machinery.

Arthur’s competence is shown through action. He knows which gauge reads low in cold weather, which support rib was patched after a quake, which emergency line still carries power if kicked twice. Mira proves equally competent with survey equipment and data handling. Their alliance is practical before it is trusting.

In the lower bore, Azra appears as dark metallic threadwork in the rock, violet where the lamps strike it. The instruments misbehave. A calibration source loses activity too quickly. An old isotope tag becomes useless. A counter casing warms, then dies. Arthur realizes these are not random failures.

Mira produces partial raw data she copied before Heliox locked her out. The corporate models treat the Azra as extractable ore. But the untouched vein appears moderated by its natural matrix—basalt, ice salts, and secondary metals in a configuration that damps the catalytic effect. Fracture and refine it too quickly, and the decay acceleration may spike. Worse, early settlement waste stores and isotope batteries lie scattered beneath this district in poorly mapped caches from the first desperate decades of Mars construction.

The danger is not “the mine will explode” in a simple way. It is worse: nobody knows how far a mismanaged decay cascade might propagate through old radiological infrastructure.

Arthur records physical evidence on an old spool, because networked data can be altered. Mira notices fresh vibration through the rock: unauthorized drilling or tunneling nearby. Someone else is already trying to reach the vein.

The chapter ends not with a speech, but with Arthur and Mira standing in the dark, listening to a machine that should not be there.

## Chapter 5 — The Balance of Decay

Arthur brings his evidence into the open, but every faction turns it into ammunition.

At a sequence of tense meetings in Dome Lowell, the Equilibrium Office argues that Arthur’s findings prove Azra must be placed under Earth-supervised radiological containment. Trane argues they prove only Heliox has the infrastructure and trained labour force to mine safely. Voss argues that Antares has superior containment technology and that delay merely gives Earth time to convert “safety” into monopoly. Commissioner Lorne hears them all and says as little as possible.

The chapter should feel claustrophobic despite its political scale: stale committee air, bad coffee, sealant stains behind official banners, guards outside every door. Arthur grows increasingly irritated by people who discuss his home as a theater of strategic necessity.

Mira confronts him after one meeting. Arthur’s emerging plan focuses on title, hazard, and extraction control. Mira points out what he has omitted: the people who will be sent down with drills. If the new arrangement permits indentured labour, it is only Heliox with cleaner stationery. Arthur says adding labour terms may break the legal mechanism. Mira asks what the mechanism is for, if not to decide who gets buried.

Lorne quietly gives Arthur access to a punch-card archive containing the Martian Founding Compact. Arthur already knows parts of it from his parents’ old water-rights battle, but now he sees a clause concerning privately patented land containing a planetary hazard resource. If valid title and public danger are established, the owner may dedicate the resource to a local hazard trust under Martian charter authority.

The clause is old, originally meant for unstable reactor salts and sealed bio-labs. Applying it to Azra is risky. But every faction has already made part of the argument Arthur needs: valid title, strategic danger, need for oversight, Martian charter jurisdiction.

Arthur realizes the shape of his counter-gambit. It is not clean. It may fail. It will certainly make him enemies. He adds Mira’s labour condition to his notes anyway.

## Chapter 6 — The Broken Seal

Before Arthur can force a tribunal, Neegan Spur is attacked.

A maintenance drone with forged Heliox credentials enters an auxiliary shaft near the lower bore. It carries an isotope charge designed not simply to explode, but to interact with exposed Azra and create a radiological emergency. The purpose is ambiguous: kill Arthur, discredit his competence, force Earth containment, justify Antarean intervention, or render the claim unusable. Several factions could benefit.

Arthur and Mira are underground when the breach occurs. The chapter becomes tense and practical rather than cinematic. Pressure drops in one passage. A seal alarm fails because its isotopic trigger has aged out. Dust and frost move the wrong way. Arthur curses not like a hero, but like a man who knows exactly what repair was overdue.

Mira is essential. She identifies the drone’s power signature from survey equipment. Arthur calculates that if they can place a small moderated Azra-bearing sample near the drone’s isotope battery without exposing the main vein, they may drain the battery fast enough to prevent the charge from reaching threshold. It is dangerous and partly improvised.

The plan works, but not cleanly. Mira is injured sealing a manual pressure door. An old maintenance worker or constable near the surface dies in the confusion, giving the event weight. Arthur gets Mira out through the old adit as Heliox security, Council constables, Earth observers, and Antarean guards converge, each demanding custody of the site and evidence.

The aftermath is uglier than the crisis. Trane calls it proof that independent management is unsafe. Earth calls it a containment incident. Voss calls it attempted strategic sabotage. Lorne, seeing that the narrative will be stolen unless fixed publicly, grants Arthur’s demand for an emergency tribunal under the Founding Compact.

The chapter ends with Arthur, exhausted and shaking, refusing medical evacuation until the evidence spool is logged in the Council record.

## Chapter 7 — The Azra Gambit

The tribunal convenes in Dome Lowell’s old assembly rotunda, built from surplus pressure shells and dressed up with flags. It is public by compact law, transmitted on delay across Mars and to orbital platforms. This is the intellectual and political climax.

Each faction presents its case.

Trane, smooth and grave, argues that the sabotage proves Arthur lacks operational capacity and that Heliox must assume control for public safety. The Earth envoy argues that Azra is a strategic radiological material requiring containment under the Bureau of Radiological Equilibrium. Voss argues that Arthur’s private title is valid and that he may legally grant custodial jurisdiction to Antares. Lorne listens under visible pressure from all sides.

Arthur is not a polished speaker. He is tired, bruised, and angry enough to be plain. He accepts selected claims from each party:

- Antares is correct that the Neegan patent is valid.
- Earth is correct that Azra is a planetary-scale strategic hazard.
- Heliox is correct that extraction cannot be left to an isolated private operator.
- The Council’s own compact is correct that Mars retains charter authority over planetary hazards.

Because all parties have entered claims under these premises, Arthur invokes the old hazard-resource clause. He dedicates the Azra formation beneath Neegan Spur to a Martian Hazard Trust. The trust forbids exclusive ownership or jurisdiction by any corporation, foreign power, or diplomatic corps. It permits licensed access under transparent isotope accounting, multinational inspection, and Martian technical stewardship.

Trane attacks the clause as obsolete. The Earth envoy threatens nonrecognition. Voss sees the trap first and asks several surgical questions, testing whether Arthur has left Antares any access. He has. Not exclusive access, but enough. She does not endorse him, but she stops short of destroying the argument.

Then Mira, injured but present, gives brief testimony about falsified data and leased survey crews ordered into hazard zones. Arthur introduces the added provision: no indentured labour may be used in Azra extraction, transport, or processing. Hazard consent under debt lien is not consent. Existing Azra leases are suspended pending review.

This nearly breaks the room. Trane is furious beneath his calm. Lorne must choose. She ratifies the trust provisionally under emergency charter authority, not because it solves everything, but because it is the only available mechanism that prevents immediate seizure.

The chapter ends with Voss quietly telling Arthur that he has made himself a player in a game that kills players. Arthur replies that mines kill men who pretend pressure is not there.

## Chapter 8 — Red Dawn, White Fire

The final chapter shows aftermath rather than victory.

The Martian Hazard Trust survives its first week because every faction prefers it to a rival’s monopoly. Antares files for licensed access. Earth files for permanent inspection rights. Heliox files three appeals and, almost immediately, offers “non-exclusive technical services.” The Council announces the trust in careful language that sounds braver than its members feel.

The anti-indenture provision has real but limited effect. Azra-field labour leases are suspended. Some workers walk free for the first time in years; others discover freedom does not automatically provide housing, transport, or medical credit. Mira’s own lien is suspended, then challenged, then provisionally voided because her testimony becomes protected under the trust charter. She accepts a paid technical post with the trust, not as Arthur’s grateful follower, but as someone determined to keep the new system from becoming the old one with cleaner seals.

Arthur returns to Neegan Spur. His cottage still stands, but it is no longer wholly his. Survey towers ring the ridge. Council monitors occupy a temporary dome. Antarean and Earth observers pretend not to watch each other. The old pump he left half-disassembled has been repaired badly by someone who did not know its moods.

Voss sends, or delivers in person, a final message. She admits nothing improper. She notes that Antares can work with the trust, for now. Arthur realizes she may have accepted this outcome as her second-best result from the beginning: no Earth monopoly, no Heliox monopoly, legal access preserved. His victory is real, but not absolute.

Mira and Arthur share a brief, unsentimental exchange. She does not thank him extravagantly. She says the trust is a start, and starts are dangerous because people mistake them for endings. Arthur accepts this.

The final image returns to small maintenance against vast consequence. At dawn, red light spreads over the Martian plain while white work lamps burn over the sealed lower bore. Beneath the basalt, Azra waits—fuel, weapon, cure, poison, depending on who touches it and why. Arthur kneels at his airlock and cleans dust from the seal. Mars has not been saved. But for the first time, it possesses something Earth, Antares, and the corporations need and cannot simply take.

The story closes on that uneasy balance: not triumph, but pressure held—for now.

# Arthur Neegan

Arthur Neegan is a first-generation Martian settler, though “settler” has always sounded too grand to him. His parents arrived under transport liens during the hard years after the first domes went permanent. His mother, Rilla Neegan, worked fourteen years in atmospheric maintenance before she owned her own breath. His father, Callum, was a bore engineer who believed land patents mattered because they were one of the few promises Earth had made to Martians in writing. Arthur inherited that belief, though he would never call it sentimental.

He grew up at Neegan Spur, a marginal independent claim outside Dome Lowell, in a pressure cottage assembled from two retired cargo cylinders and a connecting sleeve his father welded badly but proudly. Arthur knows every sound in the place: the west seal’s dry click in cold weather, the pump’s double-stutter before a filter jam, the way dust ticks against the viewport before a pressure front.

He is a mining engineer by training and temperament. He trusts instruments, but only after he has learned how each instrument lies. He is not a visionary. He thinks in gradients, tolerances, fractures, loads, seals, debts, and maintenance schedules. His idea of luxury is a full spare-parts drawer and coffee that has not been recycled through six municipal contracts.

Arthur is proud, but his pride is quiet and stubborn rather than flamboyant. He has spent years being treated as quaint by corporations and inconvenient by administrators. Independent patent holders like him are relics: too small to matter, too legally entrenched to easily absorb. He knows this and resents it. He also secretly cherishes being overlooked. Being ignored has let him remain free.

His flaw is that he has mistaken independence for moral innocence. He avoids using leased labour and dislikes Heliox’s indenture system, but he has still bought cheap parts manufactured by leased workers, used corporate roads maintained by debt crews, and paid oxygen rates subsidized by labour he does not want to think about. He tells himself he is not responsible for the whole world. The story forces him to confront the convenience of that excuse.

He is tempted by Voss’s offer more than he admits. He imagines replacing the cottage seals, paying off inherited claims fees, buying out the neighbouring abandoned lot so no corporation can build a relay tower over his horizon, maybe even seeing one of Earth’s oceans before his bones become too Martian for the trip. The temptation embarrasses him, so he disguises it as suspicion.

Arthur has a dry, economical wit, mostly defensive. He dislikes speeches, especially his own. When angry, he becomes quieter and more precise. His questions tend to be practical in a way that makes abstract people uncomfortable: who sealed the pump, who signed the maintenance order, who pays for air if the mine is locked down, who is liable if a worker dies?

He keeps his mother’s paid-off transport lien in a metal box with his land patent. He claims this is because “documents matter on Mars,” but he has polished the box more often than necessary. He hates imported fruit because diplomats serve it as if it proves civilization. He has an old habit, learned from his father, of touching the inner doorframe before cycling an airlock.

Physically, Arthur is lean and tough in the Martian way: long-limbed, slightly narrow through the chest, with the economical movements of someone raised in lower gravity and confined spaces. He is in his late thirties or early forties, though Martian dryness has put fine lines around his eyes. His hair is dark with iron-gray already at the temples, usually cut badly by his own hand. His hands are scarred, nails kept short, fingertips rough from gloves and tools. He carries himself without swagger, but he has the stillness of a man who knows panic wastes oxygen.

He interacts with the world through touch and sound. He taps gauges, listens to pumps, tests seals with two fingers, turns unfamiliar objects over before trusting them. In diplomatic rooms, he looks slightly misplaced but not intimidated; he treats polished furniture like machinery whose purpose he has not yet identified.

Motively, Arthur begins by wanting his claim back, his home intact, and everyone with uniforms off his land. His allegiance is first to Neegan Spur, then to Mars as he understands it: not flags, but pressure skins, working pumps, paid debts, and promises kept because the alternative is vacuum. He mistrusts Heliox from old disputes, mistrusts Earth because Earth writes laws from a safe gravity well, and mistrusts Antares because Voss is too honest about wanting him.

His relationship with Mira begins as wary necessity. She has data he needs; he has title she can use. He initially dislikes how she judges him, because her judgment is partly accurate. Over time, he comes to respect her competence before he fully understands her anger.

His relationship with Voss is adversarial but intellectually charged. She treats him as significant before anyone else does, and he knows that this too is a tactic. He dislikes being manipulated but cannot dismiss her arguments.

Flavor dialogue / internal monologue:

> “I don’t mind a man pointing a gun at me if he’s honest enough to call it a gun. It’s when he calls it procedure that I start counting exits.”

> “The pump was still open on the kitchen floor. That bothered him more than the rifles. Rifles were someone else’s stupidity. An open pump was his.”

> “You keep saying jurisdiction, Minister. Ore I understand. Money I understand. Jurisdiction is what a man asks for when he means to move the walls.”

> “Mars doesn’t forgive bad arithmetic. You can call it policy if you like, but if the seal fails, policy freezes with the rest of you.”

# Cyrene Voss

Cyrene Voss is Minister Plenipotentiary of the Antares Diplomatic Corps, a title that sounds ceremonial until one notices that Antarean diplomats travel with armed cutters, encrypted legal teams, and authority to negotiate mineral concessions under naval protection. She was born on Eos Cincture, one of the Antarean belt habitats, to a family that still remembers the fuel embargo of 2179 as a massacre conducted with invoices. Her younger brother died during that crisis, not from violence but from a “logistical delay” in isotope shipments that shut down hospital reserve power for nine hours. Voss does not mention this unless it serves a purpose, but it shaped her.

She believes dependence is a form of occupation. To her, Earth’s control of energy and strategic materials is not stability; it is a leash. Antares must have Azra because without it, the outer colonies remain politically adolescent, forever requesting permission from older powers. She is entirely capable of coercion in the service of this belief. She does not think of herself as cruel. She thinks cruelty is what happens when sentimental people refuse to count consequences.

Voss is disciplined, observant, and almost impossibly polite. Her courtesy is not warmth; it is control. She speaks in complete sentences, rarely raises her voice, and leaves silences where other people rush to fill them. She likes definitions. She believes power resides in the right word placed in the right document at the right time.

Her flaw is that she reduces human beings to strategic variables while sincerely intending to save them from larger horrors. She can describe the freeing of indentured workers as both a moral good and a useful inducement without seeing, or perhaps without allowing herself to see, the violence in that duality. She admires Arthur because he is not easily categorized, but she also tries to categorize him repeatedly: owner, legitimacy source, colonial independent, bargaining instrument, possible ally.

She has small rituals. Before negotiations, she removes one glove and places it beside the document she wants signed. Nobody knows if this is superstition, habit, or theater. She drinks mineral water warmed slightly above room temperature because cold liquids were rationed in her childhood habitat. She dislikes open flame, even simulated flame. She corrects imprecise treaty citations with the same calm she uses when ordering guards into position.

Voss’s physicality is controlled and elegant. She is in her forties or early fifties, tall by inner-system standards but slender in the long-boned Antarean way. Her hair is silver-black, worn close to the head or pinned in a severe coil. Her face is fine-featured, composed, and more expressive around the eyes than the mouth. She often appears motionless, but her stillness is active, like a pressure door holding against vacuum. She does not fidget. She turns her head before she turns her body. When she smiles, it is usually to acknowledge a point scored rather than to comfort.

She dresses in diplomatic black and deep blue, with the Antares laurel-star at the throat or cuff. Her clothing is austere but expensive, designed to function in variable gravity. She interacts with rooms as if she has already memorized them: entrances, vantage points, who stands where, who can overhear.

Her allegiance is to Antares, but not blindly to every Antarean superior. She serves the strategic survival of her polity as she understands it. If her government gives reckless orders, she may satisfy them by indirection. She wants Arthur’s signature because it would give Antares a lawful foothold. If she cannot have exclusive jurisdiction, she may accept a trust that denies Earth and Heliox exclusivity, because second-best outcomes are still outcomes.

Her relationship with Arthur is one of mutual testing. She respects his practical intelligence but underestimates his capacity for political imagination. She finds his suspicion refreshing because it is concrete rather than ideological. He irritates her because he asks who will fix the pump when she is discussing fleet deterrence.

She views Mira as dangerous in a different way: not powerful legally, but morally clarifying. Voss is careful around people who can collapse euphemism into accusation.

Flavor dialogue / internal monologue:

> “There are three currencies in crises, Mr. Neegan: force, time, and legitimacy. You possess the third. I possess enough of the first to value it properly.”

> “Do not mistake candor for kindness. I am honest with you because dishonesty would waste hours we may not have.”

> “Earth calls it equilibrium when every scale is kept in its own hand.”

> “She had learned early that people forgave threats more readily than ambiguity. A rifle could be negotiated with. A delay in oxygen shipment was merely administration.”

# Mira Saye

Mira Saye is an indentured survey technician under a Heliox-Levant transport lien. She was born in Dome Lowell’s labour quarter, which means she has technically never been transported anywhere, but inherited debt is flexible when written by people who own airlocks. Her mother signed a medical lien after a decompression injury; the debt rolled, accrued, and was converted into family obligation under a clause called “continuity of care.” Mira can recite the clause from memory with the flat bitterness of someone who has had it quoted at her since childhood.

She is very good at her work. Survey technicians live between data and danger: checking bore readings, calibrating instruments, smoothing signal noise, tagging hazard anomalies, and knowing when a number means bad equipment versus bad rock. Mira has a fierce technical intelligence, but unlike Arthur, she has never been allowed to convert competence into autonomy. Her skill has mostly made her more valuable to the people who own her contract.

Her immediate agenda is specific. Two surveyors, Tavin Ro and Els Cador, objected to Heliox’s handling of anomalous Azra readings beneath Neegan Spur. Soon after, they were listed as reassigned to an outer shaft, then dead in a pressure accident with sealed records. Mira believes they were silenced or sent knowingly into danger. She copied fragments of raw survey data before her access was cut. She needs Arthur’s patent because his legal standing can force the data into public record.

Mira is not automatically noble. She is angry, guarded, and capable of using people. At first, she sees Arthur as a patent with legs. She does not care about his sentimental attachment to Neegan Spur, at least not initially. To her, property is the language by which people like Arthur are heard and people like her are priced. She resents needing him.

Her flaw is that she can mistake distrust for clarity. She has survived by assuming every promise is a trap, and she is often right, but not always. She sometimes refuses help because accepting it feels like another form of debt. She has a habit of reducing free people to hypocrites before they have finished speaking. Arthur infuriates her because he is not as guilty as she wants him to be, and not as innocent as he thinks.

She has small grounding traits. She hoards pencil stubs because network slates can be remotely wiped. She writes figures on her inner sleeve in tiny shorthand. She never stands directly under overhead piping if she can avoid it. She dislikes being offered coffee by officials; coffee is what supervisors give workers before asking for “voluntary” overtime. She can sleep sitting up in a corridor, but only facing the door.

Physically, Mira is in her late twenties or early thirties, compact and wiry, with a face made sharper by fatigue rather than age. Her hair is usually cropped close or tied back under a work cap. She has a small scar along her jaw from a cracked helmet ring and a pale mark on the inside of her wrist where lease scanners often read her contract tag. Her movements are quick, economical, and slightly defensive. She occupies little space until she chooses not to.

She does not have Arthur’s stillness or Voss’s composure. Her expressions are fast: a flash of contempt, amusement, calculation, then blankness when she remembers who may be watching. When handling equipment, she becomes calmer. Instruments do not become kind, but at least they fail according to laws.

Her allegiance is first to herself and the people trapped under the same system. She is not initially a Martian nationalist; Mars is where she has been bound. Over the story, she may begin to see a difference between Mars as corporate prison and Mars as a possible political community, but she remains skeptical. Her relationship with Arthur grows from mutual utility to grudging respect. He listens to equipment; eventually, he learns to listen to her. Her relationship with Lorne is wary because Council officials have often apologized while signing nothing useful. She despises Trane because he represents the system’s smiling face. She is cautious around Voss, who may offer more than Heliox ever did but still sees people as pieces.

Flavor dialogue / internal monologue:

> “Free men always say they don’t use leased labour. Then they step over the floor we welded and breathe the air we scrubbed.”

> “I don’t need you to be decent, Neegan. I need you to be documented.”

> “Debt doesn’t decay. That’s why they like it better than uranium.”

> “She trusted numbers more than promises, but even numbers could be beaten into shape by the person who owned the table.”

# Director Sef Trane

Sef Trane is regional extraction director for Heliox-Levant Resource & Atmosphere, the corporation that owns or services much of Mars’s mining, oxygen distribution, medical evacuation, and labour leasing infrastructure. He came up through logistics, not geology, which he considers an advantage. Geologists fall in love with rock. Trane cares about throughput, liability, and continuity.

He was not born rich. That matters to him. His grandparents were contract technicians, and he uses this fact when useful to imply he understands labour. What he does not say is that his family bought out its liens by becoming enforcers of the same system. Trane believes Mars was built by disciplined obligation. He regards anti-indenture sentiment as emotionally satisfying but historically illiterate. In his mind, everyone on Mars owes someone: oxygen, debt, maintenance, law, sacrifice. Heliox merely keeps the accounts legible.

He is dangerous because he is genuinely competent. Heliox does own the heavy equipment, emergency shelters, transport routes, hospitals, and refining networks that small claimants rely on. When he says Arthur cannot safely mine Azra alone, he is correct. His bad faith lies in converting that truth into a claim of ownership.

Trane’s personality is smooth, patient, managerial. He almost never threatens directly. He offers risk analyses, partnership frameworks, transitional arrangements, and liability shields. He speaks of human beings as “personnel assets,” “contracted capacity,” or “continuity labour.” He does not think this language is evasive; he thinks it is civilized.

His flaw is moral abstraction hardened into policy. He has spent so long viewing survival as a system problem that individual suffering appears to him as unfortunate noise. If pressed, he can become coldly contemptuous. He dislikes Arthur because independent patent holders are inefficient and because Arthur’s stubbornness exposes the coercion beneath Heliox’s polish. He dislikes Mira more because she knows the paperwork from the inside and refuses to be grateful for “care.”

Trane’s idiosyncrasies are subtle. He adjusts cuffs when negotiations turn unpleasant. He has an excellent memory for dates of contract revisions but forgets workers’ names unless they are legally relevant. He dislikes dust and uses a small static brush on his sleeves after visiting outer settlements. He always reads the liability appendix first. He uses the phrase “with respect” when he means “you are being irrational.”

Physically, Trane is in his fifties, compact, well-fed by Martian standards, with smooth skin that suggests access to good medical care and humidity. He keeps his hair clipped and his beard, if any, precisely trimmed. His suits are practical corporate gray with subtle reinforcement for pressure transitions. He smiles often and warmly, but the warmth does not reach his assessing eyes. He stands too close to people of lower status and gives important people generous space.

He carries himself like someone accustomed to secure rooms and functioning climate control. Unlike Arthur and Mira, he does not instinctively check seals. He assumes systems work because people like him authorize them to work.

His allegiance is to Heliox, but more deeply to the worldview that Heliox embodies: survival through hierarchy, debt, and managed scarcity. He wants Neegan Spur because Azra will make whichever institution controls extraction indispensable. He is willing to falsify, bury, delay, or reclassify data, but he prefers not to spill blood in visible ways. Visible blood creates hearings.

His relationship with Arthur is superficially cordial. He offers Arthur dignity as long as Arthur accepts subordination. His relationship with Mira is one of ownership denied; he will speak to her as a misled employee rather than an adversary because recognizing her as an adversary grants her status.

Flavor dialogue / internal monologue:

> “No one breathes independently on Mars, Mr. Neegan. Some of us are merely honest enough to invoice it.”

> “Heliox is not asking for your home. We are offering to relieve you of a risk no private citizen can responsibly carry.”

> “Indenture is an ugly word for deferred transport cost. Mars was not built by poetry.”

> “With respect, Commissioner, moral indignation has never moved a ton of ore or patched a hospital dome.”

# Commissioner Ada Lorne

Ada Lorne is a senior member of the Martian Provisional Council, an institution that has remained “provisional” for so long that the word is now a joke, an insult, and a legal trap. She was born in Dome Lowell to schoolteacher parents who believed Mars would become self-governing within their lifetime. She no longer believes in timelines, but she has not stopped believing in documents.

Lorne is a lawyer by training and a survivalist by experience. Her career has been spent negotiating between corporate necessities, Earth mandates, local anger, and the brutal physics of Martian dependency. She knows which clauses are dead, which are sleeping, and which might wake if someone creates the right public record. She is often mistaken for timid because she speaks cautiously. In reality, she has learned that one reckless sentence can cost a dome its credit rating or delay an oxygen shipment.

She is tired, but not defeated. Her office is in a converted pressure shell behind the assembly rotunda. The carpet does not reach the corners. Her desk has three obsolete terminals because each accesses a different pre-standardization legal archive. She keeps tea in a thermos because the Council machine dispenses something that tastes like boiled insulation. She has a private list of “laws we might yet use,” and the hazard-resource clause is on it.

Her flaw is procedural caution bordering on paralysis. She has watched too many brave gestures become dead workers and unpaid invoices. She sometimes waits so long for a viable opening that people suffer in the meantime. Mira sees this clearly and does not forgive it. Lorne does not forgive herself either, but self-reproach is not policy.

She has idiosyncrasies that reveal her mind. She annotates printed statutes in three colors: blue for active law, red for dangerous ambiguity, green for political leverage. She remembers children’s names from dome school visits but forgets meal times. She taps her thumb against her forefinger when someone lies with technical accuracy. She hates the Council’s ceremonial banners because they hide sealant stains badly.

Physically, Lorne is in her sixties, short, spare, and slightly stooped from a lifetime of low-gravity posture and desk fatigue. Her hair is white, worn cropped close. Her face is lined, with deep brackets around the mouth from holding back both laughter and fury. She has a soft voice that forces people to quiet down if they want to hear her. She moves slowly, not because she is weak, but because haste has become, to her, a luxury of the unaccountable.

She dresses plainly: dark tunics, old Council insignia, pressure boots polished but worn. She interacts with the world through papers, archives, and small acts of maintenance. She will straighten a crooked seal notice while discussing interplanetary sanctions.

Her allegiance is to Mars as a political entity that barely exists yet. Not Mars as romance, not Mars as corporate asset, not Mars as Earth’s frontier, but Mars as a place whose inhabitants must someday possess enforceable rights. She cannot say this too loudly. She needs Arthur because his private patent gives her a lever the Council does not otherwise have. She needs Mira because testimony from labour can turn hazard law into more than property defense. She distrusts Voss but recognizes Antares as a counterweight. She despises Heliox dependency while relying on Heliox oxygen.

Flavor dialogue / internal monologue:

> “The Council has authority over all Mars. Unfortunately, authority and oxygen arrive in different containers.”

> “A dead law is often only a law no one has been desperate enough to use correctly.”

> “Do not ask me for courage, Mr. Neegan. Ask me for procedure. Courage without procedure is how Mars gets memorial plaques.”

> “She had learned to fear men who said history demanded haste. History did not have to check pressure seals afterward.”

# Envoy Tomas Rusk

Tomas Rusk is the Earth representative from the Bureau of Radiological Equilibrium, the agency responsible for strategic isotope control, nuclear waste treaties, decay-catalyst licensing, and quiet interventions under the pleasant name of stability. He is not military, though he works closely with military offices. He thinks in containment zones, escalation ladders, audit trails, and unacceptable variance.

Rusk was born on Earth, in the Andean Administrative Corridor, under open sky. He has never fully adjusted to habitats. On Mars he is careful, slightly stiff, and privately unsettled by the idea that a wall thickness can be the difference between meeting and obituary. He tries not to show this because Martians despise Earthborn claustrophobia. He does not dislike Mars, but he does not understand loving it.

His motives are not merely imperial. He has seen classified projections of Azra-enabled weapons: compact decay charges, sabotaged isotope grids, accelerated waste blooms, drive cores converted into bombs. He genuinely believes uncontrolled Azra access could trigger a civilization-scale disaster. His problem is that “controlled” always seems to mean controlled by Earth, because Earth still imagines itself the adult in the room.

Rusk’s personality is precise, dry, and bureaucratically severe. He is less smooth than Trane and less elegant than Voss. He does not seduce; he classifies. He becomes impatient with colonial grievances when strategic risk is being discussed, which makes him sound arrogant even when he is frightened. He believes procedure prevents apocalypse, and unlike Lorne, his procedures come backed by fleets and sanctions.

His flaw is paternalism. He can recognize danger but not the danger of his own authority. He sees Arthur’s property rights as parochial, Mira’s labour concerns as important but secondary, and Martian autonomy as desirable only after the crisis is contained. Every crisis, however, extends the period before autonomy.

He has small habits. He carries a sealed packet of Earth tea and dislikes the mineral taste of Martian water. He sanitizes his hands after touching public railings, then feels foolish and does it anyway. He records verbal summaries after every meeting, speaking in numbered points. He has an old burn scar on one hand from a training accident involving a mishandled isotope capsule, which partly explains his caution.

Physically, Rusk is in his forties, broad-shouldered and compact, with Earth-normal musculature that looks heavy on Mars. He moves a fraction too forcefully in low gravity and occasionally catches himself against furniture. His hair is close-cropped, his face clean-shaven, his expression habitually narrowed as if reading fine print. His clothes are official but not luxurious: dark pressure-adapted suit, Equilibrium Office badge, radiation dosimeter always visible.

He interacts with the world through measurement. He checks exposure readouts compulsively. He asks for definitions. He wants maps, perimeters, inventories, and chain-of-custody records. He is disturbed by Martian improvisation, especially when it works.

His allegiance is to Earth and to the doctrine of radiological stability. He is suspicious of Antares, dismissive of Heliox’s profit motives, and frustrated by the Martian Council’s weakness. He regards Arthur as an accidental hazard custodian and Mira as a witness whose testimony matters only after material containment. Over the story, he may come to grudgingly respect Arthur’s technical evidence, though not his politics.

Flavor dialogue / internal monologue:

> “A material that changes half-life changes strategy. A material that changes strategy changes the probability of war. You may call that politics. My office calls it arithmetic.”

> “Local title is not a containment protocol.”

> “I am not here to steal your mine, Mr. Neegan. I am here to prevent it from becoming a weapon before anyone admits it already has.”

> “Mars made him feel surrounded by engineering that had been allowed to develop opinions.”

# Optional Supporting Figure: Lieutenant Maro Hest

Lieutenant Maro Hest is the Antarean security officer who leads the retinue to Arthur’s home and later shadows him aboard the transfer vessel. He is not a major political actor, but he can humanize Antares by showing the machinery beneath Voss’s diplomacy.

Hest was raised in a rotating habitat where discipline was not ideology but survival practice. He is young enough to still believe in the elegance of Antarean service, old enough to have done things under diplomatic cover that trouble his sleep. He is scrupulously polite because Antarean field doctrine teaches that unnecessary insult creates unnecessary variables.

He is not cruel. This does not make him safe. He will hold a rifle on Arthur’s doorway while apologizing for the inconvenience. He will ensure Arthur’s home pump is sealed correctly before departure because leaving it open would be wasteful and dishonorable. Arthur notices this and dislikes him less than he wants to.

Physically, Hest is young, narrow-faced, and precise in movement. His armor is polished but used. He keeps his helmet under one arm when protocol allows, making eye contact instead of hiding behind the visor. He has a small habit of checking seal indicators twice, perhaps from a past failure.

His allegiance is to Voss and Antares. He does not know the whole game and does not ask to. His presence in chapter one and possibly later scenes can reinforce the “diplomatic in name only” quality of Antares without turning every Antarean into a faceless guard.

Flavor dialogue:

> “You are not under arrest, Mr. Neegan.”
>
> “Then I’ll stay.”
>
> “That is among the complications I was instructed to avoid.”

> “I sealed your pump before we left. Badly, perhaps. I am not a miner.”

# Chapter 1 — The Invitation

Mars was shrinking behind glass, and Arthur Neegan could not decide which offended him more: that he had been taken from it, or that from this height it looked so small.

Not small, exactly. No world was small when one lived under its weather and paid for its air. But through the transfer vessel’s observation port Mars had become a rust-red coin set beneath a pane of black crystal, its scratches and basins flattened into geography fit for schoolroom charts. The south polar cap glimmered like old enamel. Dawn crept along the terminator in a pale, slow curve. Somewhere under that curve lay Dome Lowell, the old road, the ridge called Neegan Spur, and his pressure cottage with the kitchen pump lying open on the floor.

That last thought irritated him beyond reason.

The pump’s secondary filter had been fouling for three weeks. He had finally stripped it down that morning, set the impeller on a rag, and found a crack in the ceramic throat no longer than his thumbnail. He had been deciding whether to patch it or curse it into working another month when the outer alarm chimed.

Not the soft two-note chime of a neighbour at the lock. Not the harsh repeating bark of pressure failure. A formal tone, one he had only heard on public channels.

Official arrival.

Arthur had wiped his hands on his trousers and gone to the north viewport. Three skimmers were descending through the dust haze with the absurd gentleness of expensive machines. They were black, narrow, and polished, their landing vanes folding like insect wings. On each hull was a silver mark: a star caught inside a laurel.

Antares.

He had muttered, “Diplomats,” and then counted eight rifles before the first boot touched his yard.

They had come in pressure armor too clean for Mars, blue-black with pale visors, moving with the practiced care of people who had drilled the difference between ceremony and assault. One of them, an officer with a narrow face and a lieutenant’s bar at the throat seal, walked up to the cottage lock alone. He kept his sidearm visible and his hands empty.

Arthur opened the inner speaker.

“If this is about the south access road,” he said, “you’re on the wrong claim.”

The officer inclined his head. “Mr. Arthur Neegan?”

“That depends on how expensive your question is.”

“I am Lieutenant Maro Hest, Antares Diplomatic Corps. Your presence is requested for an immediate consultation off-world.”

Arthur looked past him at the rifles spaced around the yard. One guard stood near the drill shed, another by the oxygen tank, another at the old survey mast his father had bolted into basalt twenty-six years ago. None aimed a weapon. None needed to.

“Requested,” Arthur said.

“Yes, sir.”

“Can I decline?”

Hest’s expression did not change, though Arthur could see only the lower half of his face beneath the raised visor. “Declining would introduce avoidable complications.”

“That’s a long word for no.”

“It is a shorter word than several alternatives.”

Arthur had disliked him less for that, which made him dislike the situation more.

He had not been allowed to pack properly. Allowed was the wrong word, perhaps. No one shoved him. No one raised a voice. Lieutenant Hest waited while Arthur sealed the pump housing, badly and with increasing anger, then stood at the wall safe while Arthur removed his identity spool, two claim keys, and the little metal case containing his mother’s paid-off transport lien and the original Neegan patent copy. When Arthur reached for his field cutter, two rifles shifted one degree toward him.

“Tools are not ordinarily permitted aboard diplomatic transfer craft,” Hest said.

“Then I pity your engineers.”

“I will see that it is secured and returned.”

“Will you also see that my pump doesn’t seize?”

Hest glanced toward the kitchen assembly. “It is sealed?”

“It is closed. That isn’t the same thing.”

The lieutenant had stepped inside—uninvited, but carefully—and crouched beside the open panel. His armored gloves were too clumsy for the fine work, but he checked the manual bypass and locked the intake valve with competent caution.

“I am not a miner,” he said, rising. “But your pump will not flood the line.”

Arthur had said nothing. Gratitude under armed escort was a poor habit to cultivate.

Now, aboard the transfer vessel, he watched a flake of red dust come loose from his cuff and drift in the cabin air. It turned slowly in the artificial gravity’s faint compromise, a tiny irregular thing, more real than the whole planet below.

The cabin door was not locked. Arthur had tested it twice.

The corridor beyond, however, contained a young Antarean marine with a rifle folded across his chest and the expression of a man prepared to be courteous until death.

Arthur opened the door a third time.

The marine looked at him. “Do you require anything, Mr. Neegan?”

“A return course.”

“I am not authorized to alter navigation.”

“Then you’re asking the wrong question.”

The marine considered this. “Do you require anything I am authorized to provide?”

“Coffee.”

A pause. “I will inquire.”

“Real coffee. Not diplomatic broth.”

“I will inquire specifically.”

Arthur let the door close. He had learned something, at least. They had instructions to keep him irritated but not uncomfortable. That meant they wanted him able to think. Or able to sign.

He turned back to the port.

The vessel itself was old-fashioned in the expensive way. The acceleration couch had brass-edged adjustment wheels beside a touch panel. Analog pressure dials lined one bulkhead, their needles steady as sermons. Somewhere behind the panels an atomic calculator chattered in brief bursts, like an insect trapped inside a wall. The air smelled faintly of oil, ionization, and filtered citrus.

His own cottage smelled of warm dust, machine grease, and the bitter little herb trays he kept trying to grow under the galley lamp. He wondered if they had sealed the outer door properly. Antareans were orderly, but Mars did not care for order imposed by visitors. Dust found prideful workmanship amusing.

The door chimed.

Arthur did not answer immediately. Petty resistance, but a man used what tools remained.

“Enter,” he said at last.

Lieutenant Hest came in carrying a bulb of coffee. He had removed his helmet. He was younger than Arthur had thought, perhaps thirty, with close-cropped dark hair and the composed face of someone trained to have no private reactions in public.

“The steward apologizes,” Hest said. “It is ship coffee.”

“Then the steward understands shame.”

A faint movement touched Hest’s mouth and vanished. He handed over the bulb.

Arthur tasted it. It was better than Dome Lowell coffee, worse than memory, and too hot. He held it anyway.

“Where are you taking me?”

“To the Antares legation habitat.”

“I gathered you weren’t taking me sightseeing.”

“You will be received by Minister Voss.”

Arthur waited.

Hest added nothing.

“This about Heliox?”

“I am not briefed on Minister Voss’s agenda.”

“Earth?”

No answer.

Arthur leaned back against the port frame. “My lower bore returned a bad assay three days ago.”

Hest’s eyes flickered once.

“There it is,” Arthur said.

“I did not speak.”

“You didn’t have to. Nobody sends three skimmers and a manners instructor over a bad water table.”

Hest looked at the red planet in the port, then back at him. “Mr. Neegan, I recommend you listen carefully to the minister.”

“I generally listen when abducted.”

“You are not—”

“Under arrest. Yes. Everyone keeps saying that as though there are prizes.”

Hest took the rebuke without visible offense. “There are situations in which vocabulary is used to preserve possibilities.”

“That’s what lawyers say when honest words have started a fire.”

“Sometimes honest words are the fire.”

Arthur studied him. “And Azra?”

The name entered the cabin like a change in pressure.

Hest’s face became perfectly still.

Arthur felt his stomach settle—not sink, but settle, as a load settles before a lift begins. So the impossible numbers had not been instrument error. The deep scan, the violet contamination on the sample bit, the radiation counter that aged its own calibration source into uselessness overnight: all of it had been real enough to bring Antares down on his roof.

Azra.

Until six months ago it had been a laboratory curiosity, a paragraph in technical bulletins, an exotic metal found in mean little seams under corporate ground. It accelerated radioactive decay. That was the village explanation. The imperial one, Arthur suspected, was why he was in orbit.

The intercom chimed. A woman’s voice, calm and nearly warm, filled the cabin.

“Lieutenant Hest, docking in four minutes. Please escort Mr. Neegan to reception lock three.”

Hest touched two fingers to his collar. “Acknowledged.”

Arthur finished the coffee because it had been given to him and he disliked waste.

The vessel turned. Mars slid out of the port, replaced by a structure catching sunlight along its rim: the Antares legation, a rotating wheel of black composite and silver spars. Beyond it, half-hidden by ceremonial screens, lay three narrow ships with armored spines. Their gun ports were covered by polished plates engraved with diplomatic seals.

Covered, Arthur thought. Not hidden.

Hest gestured toward the door. “Minister Voss is ready.”

Arthur tucked the metal case under his arm, felt the patent inside it shift against his ribs, and followed the armed diplomat into the corridor.

# Chapter 2 — The Offer

The Antares legation had been designed by people who believed fear could be polished into beauty.

Its corridors curved gently with the habitat’s rotation, black floors reflecting pale strips of light set into the walls. No surface was bare if it could carry a line, a seal, a map, or a discreet instrument. Arthur saw star charts etched into glass, pressure doors disguised as carved panels, and two guards standing beside a mural of linked hands between worlds. Their rifles spoiled the sentiment.

Reception lock three opened into a chamber that might have been a lounge if lounges were built for signing armistices. A viewport filled one side. Mars hung beyond it, rusty and remote. In the center stood a low table with two chairs, a silver water flask, and a stack of papers weighted by a black metal stylus.

Actual paper.

Arthur stopped before the table and looked at it.

“A calculated extravagance?” he asked.

“An old courtesy,” said a woman’s voice. “Paper contracts are harder to alter after the fact.”

Minister Cyrene Voss stood near the viewport. She wore dark blue, almost black, with the Antares laurel-star at her throat. She was tall, fine-boned, and so still that the station’s faint rotation seemed to happen around her rather than to her. Her hair, black threaded with silver, was drawn back severely. One glove lay on the table beside the papers.

“Mr. Neegan,” she said. “Thank you for coming.”

“I didn’t.”

Her eyes warmed by one degree. “Thank you for arriving.”

“Your lieutenant has better manners than his rifles.”

“He is valued for both.” She indicated the chair. “Please sit.”

Arthur remained standing. “I’ve been sitting since you took me off Mars.”

“Then stand. Diplomacy need not be cruel in small matters.”

“That depends on what it is in large ones.”

Voss inclined her head. “Fair.”

She took the opposite chair herself, a deliberate concession or a trap shaped like one. Arthur stood another moment, then sat because his legs were tired and because refusing comfort could become its own obedience.

Voss poured water into a bulb and slid it toward him.

He did not touch it.

She said, “Your claim at Neegan Spur has been reclassified.”

“By whom?”

“Everyone, by tomorrow. Antares, as of yesterday.”

“I own a basalt ridge with bad access, a disputed water table, and a pump that was half apart when your people arrived.”

“You owned that last week.”

Arthur looked at the papers. “And this week?”

“This week you own the richest known Azra formation in the settled system.”

The room was quiet enough that Arthur heard the faint tick of a cooling vent.

“That’s a large sentence,” he said.

“It is a large vein.”

“My assay showed contamination. Maybe a seam.”

“Your assay showed what your instruments survived long enough to show. The deep scan Heliox suppressed showed more.”

That moved him despite himself. “Suppressed?”

Voss’s mouth barely changed. “You are surprised?”

“I’m annoyed. There’s a difference.”

“Good. Annoyance is more useful.”

Arthur leaned back. “Say Azra like you’re not trying to sell it to me.”

Voss folded her bare hand over the gloved one. “Azra is an exotic metallic lattice that catalyzes radioactive decay. Crudely, it persuades unstable nuclei to finish old business quickly. In waste processing, it can burn certain poisons toward stability in months instead of millennia. In isotope drives, it can release stored decay energy fast enough to change interstellar transit. In weapons—”

“There it is.”

“In weapons,” Voss continued, “it makes many careful doctrines obsolete.”

Arthur remembered the counter in his shed, dead by morning, its calibration source aged out as if decades had passed while he slept.

“How obsolete?”

“Enough that Earth has dispatched observers from the Bureau of Radiological Equilibrium. Enough that Heliox has filed a patent irregularity notice against your family claim. Enough that three private military carriers lifted from Ceres twelve hours ago under false cargo codes.”

“And enough for Antares to steal a miner.”

“Invite.”

“Minister.”

“Compel,” she said. “If we are being precise.”

That won a reluctant silence from him.

Voss said, “Mr. Neegan, there are three currencies in a crisis: force, time, and legitimacy. Force is abundant. Time is scarce. Legitimacy is presently sitting in that chair with red dust on its cuffs.”

“I prefer Arthur.”

“I know. I am choosing not to presume.”

“You presumed enough to remove me from my kitchen.”

“Yes.”

She did not soften it. That, too, was a tactic.

“What do you want?”

Voss touched the top sheet and turned it so he could read the first page. “Antares proposes a custodial mineral lease. We will assume all claim debts, liens, and pending maintenance charges. We will rebuild your residence to current pressure code. We will provide personal protection, medical coverage, and a settlement of two hundred million solar credits held in your name outside corporate seizure.”

Arthur stared at her. It was a ridiculous number. So ridiculous it lost shape.

She went on. “In addition, Antares will purchase and extinguish the transport liens of the survey crews assigned to the Neegan Spur Azra project.”

Arthur’s eyes lifted.

Voss slid a second sheet forward. It held names.

He recognized three. Not friends. Mars was too large and too small for that distinction. A drill tech who had once helped him repair a seized crawler outside Lowell. A sampler from Heliox whose daughter sold printed charms near the west lock. Mira Saye, survey technician, whose name he had seen on a disputed data receipt.

“You bought a conscience with the contract,” Arthur said.

“No. I priced one.”

“That’s worse.”

“It is more honest.”

Arthur’s hand hovered over the list before he withdrew it. “And in return?”

“Exclusive extraction and containment jurisdiction for Antares beneath the specified claim volume.”

“There’s that word.”

“Jurisdiction?”

“Yes. Ore is a thing. Jurisdiction is a place.”

Voss’s eyes sharpened, and he knew he had touched the true mechanism.

“The vein cannot be secured by purchase alone,” she said. “It must be governed, guarded, studied, and if necessary denied to powers that would destabilize interstellar peace.”

“Meaning Earth.”

“Meaning any monopoly not ours.”

Arthur almost smiled. “That was honesty by accident.”

“No. By policy.”

He picked up the first page at last. The paper was heavy, faintly textured, warm from the room. His name appeared in three places before the second paragraph. Neegan Spur was defined not by surface acreage but by descending cones, subsurface volumes, access corridors, security perimeters, emergency authorities.

He said, “If I sign this, part of Mars stops being Mars.”

“Part of Mars becomes protected by Antares.”

“That’s the same sentence wearing a better coat.”

Voss looked toward the viewport. “Mr. Neegan, Earth will call its claim containment. Heliox will call its claim capacity. Your Council will call for deliberation until someone else owns the air in the chamber. Antares at least makes you an offer before events remove the courtesy.”

“Why not simply take it?”

“Because force without title is seizure. Seizure invites intervention. Intervention invites mobilization. Mobilization, with Azra in question, invites errors from which no one usefully apologizes.” She paused. “Also, you are inconveniently alive.”

“Conveniently, from my perspective.”

“Perspectives are why contracts exist.”

Arthur set the paper down. “You said Heliox suppressed a scan.”

“Yes.”

“Can I see it?”

“No.”

“Then we’re finished.”

Voss did not move. “You may see a redacted technical summary.”

“I didn’t ask for a sermon with numbers.”

“You are not in a position to demand classified Antarean intelligence.”

“I’m in the position you say matters. Legitimacy, was it? Red dust on the cuffs?”

For the first time, her expression changed enough to be called amusement.

“Careful, Arthur.”

“There. You presumed.”

“I adapted.” She considered him. “You want the raw survey record.”

“I want my mine. I want my instruments. I want to know whether everyone in this room is mad before I sell my roof.”

“You may return to Mars under escort. You may inspect Neegan Spur. You may consult one adviser not employed by Heliox, Earth, or Antares. You will have twelve hours.”

“That’s not time.”

“It is what remains of it.”

Arthur looked again at the list of names. Transport liens extinguished. Air debts cleared. Workers no longer itemized by breath and hour. He hated that she had put that where he could see it.

“What happens after twelve hours?”

“Heliox’s challenge enters the Lowell registry. Earth’s Equilibrium Office arrives with emergency authority papers. My instructions become less flexible. Politeness has a half-life, Mr. Neegan. Azra shortens all the others.”

He stood.

Voss rose with him.

“I haven’t agreed.”

“No. But you have begun calculating.”

“That isn’t consent.”

“It is better than panic.”

At the door, Arthur turned back. “Minister. Those vanished surveyors you mentioned. Did Antares vanish them?”

“No.”

He believed she was telling the truth. He did not know whether that comforted him.

“Did Heliox?”

“I do not know.”

“Would you tell me if you did?”

Voss placed her glove back on with slow precision. “If it served the prevention of war.”

Arthur laughed once, without humor. “That’s a poor answer.”

“It is the only durable kind.”

A steward led him to a guest compartment with a bed strapped neatly to the wall, a wash unit, and no visible lock. The contract waited in his hand like a tool designed by someone who hated fingers.

He sat beneath a lamp and read until the words blurred, then forced himself to read again.

Payment. Protection. Lien extinction. Containment rights. Emergency authority. Diplomatic immunity.

Jurisdiction.

The word appeared nineteen times.

Arthur took a pencil from the desk, circled the first occurrence, and beside it wrote one word of his own.

Soil.
